title: 1 Getting started: R basics
text:
NoteHow to read the examples



Every example comes in three tabs: R, Python and SAS. Pick a language once and the choice is kept across every page of the site.

The R and Python code is run each time the site is rebuilt, so the results shown are the real ones (R 4.x; Python 3.x with numpy, pandas, matplotlib and statsmodels).
The SAS code is not run automatically, because SAS requires a licence. You can try it for free with SAS OnDemand for Academics. Vector and matrix operations use PROC IML, the SAS matrix language.
The data files mentioned in the text are in the data/ folder of the repository.

title: 1 Getting started: R basics
text:
1.1 R: an open-source statistical environment
R is an open-source statistical computing environment released under the GNU-GPL licence. It is built on an object-oriented programming language and is by now well known well beyond specialist circles. It was created in 1996 by Ross Ihaka and Robert Gentleman at the University of Auckland as an offshoot of the S statistical language; indeed, at first most routines ran on either platform without any changes to the code. It is no coincidence that John M. Chambers, one of the creators of S, has been among the most active programmers supporting R.
More recent versions of R, however, have moved further away from S, emphasising the distinctive features of a language whose main strength is that it is entirely free. This is the real key to the success of R, which today offers a vast and ever-growing library of statistical routines, continually contributed by occasional programmers, experts and ordinary users alike: more than 10,000 packages at the beginning of 2018. It is therefore no surprise that on 7 January 2009 the prestigious New York Times ran an article devoted to R and its growing popularity among statisticians.
For these reasons, this book pays specific attention to R, with reference to release 3.4.3 (64-bit Microsoft Windows version), the latest at the time of writing. The commands used, however, also work with other versions of the software without any significant changes.
Files, data, additional materials, updates and errata for the book are available at http://www.unipa.it/persone/docenti/v/erasmo.vassallo/testo18a.
To begin with, Figure 1.1 shows the R start-up window with the cursor at the command line. Note that there are additional programs (almost always free or open source) that make the software easier to use through a minimal graphical interface and/or help with managing packages and the online help files; RStudio is one of the most popular. In any case, we keep to the command line, in keeping with the original philosophy of R and because it allows much greater flexibility with highly customisable scripts and commands.



Figure 1.1 – The R start-up window (Italian-language version)








TipPython and SAS: the equivalent environments






Python is a general-purpose, open-source language; for statistical analysis the main libraries are numpy (vectors and matrices), pandas (data tables), matplotlib (graphics) and statsmodels (statistical models). The most common environments are Jupyter, VS Code and RStudio/Positron itself.
SAS is commercial software, widely used in business, banking and official statistics. You work with programs made of DATA steps (data management) and PROC procedures (analysis). The SAS Studio web interface is included in SAS OnDemand for Academics.




In this book we will not dwell on a general introduction to R or on the generic use of its basic commands, unless they are useful for, or directly serve, the specific topics covered. The software is in fact familiar to the typical reader of this book, since many degree programmes in statistics, and certainly the Statistics programme at the University of Palermo, offer dedicated computer-literacy courses. Nevertheless, readers with less experience will still be able to follow the book by making use of the many excellent guides available online in several languages; in English, good starting points are An Introduction to R, the official manual, and the Italian-language guides by V. Muggeo and G. Ferrara (Nozioni di R) and by A.M. Mineo (Dispensa di R).
Here, as a starting point for whatever further study readers find necessary, we present a few simple commands that illustrate how R works.

title: 1 Getting started: R basics
text:
1.2 Assignment and workspace management
Starting with value assignment, the command x <- 4 assigns the value 4 to \(x\). Remember that R is case-sensitive, that is, \(x\) is different from \(X\). In the same way, y <- c(2,7,4,1) assigns the values (2, 7, 4, 1) to the vector \(y\).

RPythonSAS



x <- 4
y <- c(2, 7, 4, 1)
x

[1] 4

y

[1] 2 7 4 1





import numpy as np

x = 4
y = np.array([2, 7, 4, 1])   # numeric vectors are built with numpy
print(x)

4

print(y)

[2 7 4 1]




proc iml;                    /* the SAS matrix environment */
  x = 4;
  y = {2, 7, 4, 1};          /* column vector */
  print x, y;
quit;



While ls() lists the contents of the workspace, rm(PIL) removes the variable PIL from memory, provided of course that an object with that name already exists. To remove every variable whose name contains PIL, we would write rm(list=ls(pat="PIL")). Likewise, save(list=ls(), file="save.rda") saves the whole workspace to a file called save.rda. To delete all the data and variables in memory, clearing the entire workspace, we would write rm(list=ls()).
Once saved, for instance in prova.rda, the data can be loaded into a new R session simply with load("prova.rda"). After a series of computations, we may want to save only the objects \(V1\) and \(V2\), with save(V1, V2, file="save2.rda"). To store a complete snapshot of memory, including data and variables, we can use save.image().

RPythonSAS



ls()                               # workspace contents
rm(PIL)                            # remove the object PIL
rm(list = ls(pat = "PIL"))         # remove objects whose name contains "PIL"
save(list = ls(), file = "save.rda")   # save the whole workspace
rm(list = ls())                    # clear the workspace
load("prova.rda")                  # reload saved objects
save(V1, V2, file = "save2.rda")   # selective save
save.image()                       # full snapshot (.RData file)




import pickle

[n for n in dir() if not n.startswith("_")]   # defined objects (in Jupyter: %who)
del PIL                                       # remove the object PIL

# remove objects whose name contains "PIL"
for n in [n for n in list(globals()) if "PIL" in n]:
    del globals()[n]

# selective save and load with pickle
with open("save2.pkl", "wb") as f:
    pickle.dump({"V1": V1, "V2": V2}, f)
with open("save2.pkl", "rb") as f:
    objects = pickle.load(f)

# Python has no real "save.image()": to save a whole session
# you can use the dill library (dill.dump_session("session.pkl")).



/* Matrix objects in PROC IML */
proc iml;
  show names;            /* list matrices in memory (≈ ls()) */
  free PIL;              /* remove the matrix PIL (≈ rm(PIL)) */
  store V1 V2;           /* selective save (≈ save(V1, V2, ...)) */
  store _all_;           /* save all matrices (≈ save.image()) */
  free _all_;            /* clear memory (≈ rm(list = ls())) */
  load _all_;            /* reload saved matrices (≈ load()) */
quit;

/* Datasets in the temporary WORK library */
proc datasets library=work;
  delete PIL;            /* delete the dataset PIL */
  delete PIL:;           /* delete datasets whose name STARTS with PIL */
quit;
In SAS the working “memory” is the temporary WORK library, which is emptied at the end of the session; to keep data you use a permanent library (libname mylib "path";).

title: 1 Getting started: R basics
section: 1.3 Vectors, matrices, functions and data frames
text:
1.3 Vectors, matrices, functions and data frames
Let us continue with more examples in R. Readers can type in the commands and check how they behave.

RPythonSAS



x <- 4
y <- c(2, 7, 4, 1)
x * Y

Error:
! oggetto 'Y' non trovato





x * Y

NameError: name 'Y' is not defined




proc iml;
  x = 4;
  y = {2, 7, 4, 1};
  z = x * Y;     /* no error: SAS is NOT case-sensitive */
  print z;
quit;



The result is not what we expected, because \(Y\) does not exist. Indeed, \(y\) and \(Y\) are not the same object. As mentioned, R is case-sensitive; users familiar with programming languages or Unix systems will not be surprised. Python is case-sensitive too, whereas SAS is not: in SAS, y and Y refer to the same object.
The correct product, a scalar times a vector, gives a vector. Conversely, \(y\) times its transpose gives a scalar. Note the matrix product operator %*% and the transpose function t(). Whereas a row vector times a column vector gives a scalar, a column vector times a row vector gives a matrix.

RPythonSAS



x * y

[1]  8 28 16  4

t(y) %*% y

     [,1]
[1,]   70

z <- y %*% t(y)
z

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4]
[1,]    4   14    8    2
[2,]   14   49   28    7
[3,]    8   28   16    4
[4,]    2    7    4    1





print(x * y)

[ 8 28 16  4]

print(y @ y)            # inner product: @ is the matrix product

70

z = np.outer(y, y)      # column vector times row vector
print(z)

[[ 4 14  8  2]
 [14 49 28  7]
 [ 8 28 16  4]
 [ 2  7  4  1]]




proc iml;
  x = 4;
  y = {2, 7, 4, 1};
  a = x * y;
  b = t(y) * y;        /* in IML * is the matrix product; y` is the transpose */
  z = y * t(y);
  print a, b, z;
quit;



Matrices can also be built by filling. The command matrix(1:30,5,6) defines a matrix containing the values 1 to 30 in 5 rows and 6 columns. Similarly, to fill a \(2 \times 3\) matrix with zeros we would write matrix(0,2,3), while a \(3 \times 3\) unit diagonal matrix (the identity matrix) is diag(1,3,3).

RPythonSAS



a <- matrix(1:30, 5, 6)
a

     [,1] [,2] [,3] [,4] [,5] [,6]
[1,]    1    6   11   16   21   26
[2,]    2    7   12   17   22   27
[3,]    3    8   13   18   23   28
[4,]    4    9   14   19   24   29
[5,]    5   10   15   20   25   30

matrix(0, 2, 3)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    0    0    0
[2,]    0    0    0

diag(1, 3, 3)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    0    0
[2,]    0    1    0
[3,]    0    0    1





# R fills matrices by column: numpy needs order="F"
a = np.arange(1, 31).reshape(5, 6, order="F")
print(a)

[[ 1  6 11 16 21 26]
 [ 2  7 12 17 22 27]
 [ 3  8 13 18 23 28]
 [ 4  9 14 19 24 29]
 [ 5 10 15 20 25 30]]

print(np.zeros((2, 3)))

[[0. 0. 0.]
 [0. 0. 0.]]

print(np.eye(3))

[[1. 0. 0.]
 [0. 1. 0.]
 [0. 0. 1.]]




proc iml;
  /* shape() fills by row: build a 6x5 matrix and transpose it */
  a = t(shape(1:30, 6, 5));
  zeros = j(2, 3, 0);      /* 2x3 matrix of zeros */
  id = I(3);               /* 3x3 identity matrix */
  print a, zeros, id;
quit;









WarningMind the filling order



R fills matrices by column, whereas numpy and the SAS/IML shape() function fill them by row. To obtain the same matrix you need order="F" in Python and a transpose in SAS.


One of the most interesting features of R is the ability to define new commands through functions. For example, sm <- function(a,b) a+b defines a function that adds the arguments \(a\) and \(b\); a function with more than one statement must be enclosed in curly braces. So sm(6,8) returns the sum 14.

RPythonSAS



sm <- function(a, b) a + b
sm(6, 8)

[1] 14





def sm(a, b):
    return a + b

sm(6, 8)

14




proc iml;
  start sm(a, b);          /* define an IML function (module) */
    return(a + b);
  finish;
  s = sm(6, 8);
  print s;
quit;



Now let us build an object dati (data) as a data.frame(), entering the values directly at the command line, to fill a matrix with 5 rows and 2 columns, \(X1\) and \(X2\). The object \(X1\) does not exist unless it is called from within dati, either by the variable name or by the position of the column vector. Note that # lets you add comments, which the software ignores.

RPythonSAS



dati <- data.frame(matrix(c(3, 6, 8, 9, 1, 4, 3, 6, 7, 8), 5, 2))
dati

  X1 X2
1  3  4
2  6  3
3  8  6
4  9  7
5  1  8

X1        # the object X1 does not exist

Error:
! oggetto 'X1' non trovato

dati$X1

[1] 3 6 8 9 1

dati[, 1]

[1] 3 6 8 9 1





import pandas as pd

dati = pd.DataFrame(
    np.array([3, 6, 8, 9, 1, 4, 3, 6, 7, 8]).reshape(5, 2, order="F"),
    columns=["X1", "X2"],
)
print(dati)

   X1  X2
0   3   4
1   6   3
2   8   6
3   9   7
4   1   8

X1        # the object X1 does not exist

NameError: name 'X1' is not defined



print(dati["X1"].to_numpy())       # by name

[3 6 8 9 1]

print(dati.iloc[:, 0].to_numpy())  # by position (Python counts from 0)

[3 6 8 9 1]




data dati;                 /* in SAS, data tables are created with a DATA step */
  input X1 X2;
  datalines;
3 4
6 3
8 6
9 7
1 8
;
run;

proc print data=dati; run;
proc print data=dati; var X1; run;   /* column X1 only */



The last command displays all the values in the first column, whatever the row. To display all the values in the first row we would write dati[1,], while to display the single value in the second row and first column we would write dati[2,1].

RPythonSAS



dati[1, ]

  X1 X2
1  3  4

dati[2, 1]

[1] 6





print(dati.iloc[[0], :])   # first row

   X1  X2
0   3   4

print(dati.iloc[1, 0])     # second row, first column

6




proc print data=dati(obs=1); run;                     /* first row */
proc print data=dati(firstobs=2 obs=2); var X1; run;  /* second row, first column */



If, however, we want to work directly with the values in dati without referring to the data frame that contains them every time, we can use attach(). The reverse operation is detach().

RPythonSAS



attach(dati)
X1

[1] 3 6 8 9 1

X2

[1] 4 3 6 7 8

detach(dati)




# Python has no equivalent of attach(): extract the columns instead
X1, X2 = dati["X1"].to_numpy(), dati["X2"].to_numpy()
print(X1)

[3 6 8 9 1]

print(X2)

[4 3 6 7 8]




/* Not needed in SAS: inside a DATA step, or a PROC with data=dati,
   variables are referred to directly by name */
data _null_;
  set dati;
  put X1= X2=;
run;



Furthermore, if matrix(1:6,2,3) is a matrix with 2 rows and 3 unnamed columns, and VX and VY hold the column and row labels respectively, the dimnames argument lets us set the row and column names. (The labels mean low, medium, high and short, long.)

RPythonSAS



matrix(1:6, 2, 3)

     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    3    5
[2,]    2    4    6

VX <- c("basso", "medio", "alto")
VY <- c("corto", "lungo")
matrix(1:6, 2, 3, dimnames = list(VY, VX))

      basso medio alto
corto     1     3    5
lungo     2     4    6





VX = ["basso", "medio", "alto"]
VY = ["corto", "lungo"]
pd.DataFrame(np.arange(1, 7).reshape(2, 3, order="F"), index=VY, columns=VX)

       basso  medio  alto
corto      1      3     5
lungo      2      4     6




proc iml;
  m  = t(shape(1:6, 3, 2));
  VX = {"basso" "medio" "alto"};
  VY = {"corto" "lungo"};
  print m[rowname=VY colname=VX];
quit;



Data are usually not typed in at the command line but read from external files. Two widely used commands are read.table and write.table, which read and write tabular data respectively. R can also read and write data in the formats of the best-known statistical packages, in most cases through dedicated packages. For instance, the file pil.csv (Italian GDP, used in later chapters) uses the semicolon as separator, following the Italian convention, and is read with read.csv2().

RPythonSAS



pil <- read.csv2("data/pil.csv")
head(pil)

  Anni  PIL00   POP
1 1982 812365 56544
2 1983 821863 56564
3 1984 848375 56577
4 1985 872114 56593
5 1986 897056 56596
6 1987 925690 56602

# write.csv2(pil, "pil_copy.csv", row.names = FALSE)   # writing




pil = pd.read_csv("data/pil.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
print(pil.head())

   Anni   PIL00    POP
0  1982  812365  56544
1  1983  821863  56564
2  1984  848375  56577
3  1985  872114  56593
4  1986  897056  56596

# pil.to_csv("pil_copy.csv", sep=";", decimal=",", index=False)   # writing



proc import datafile="data/pil.csv" out=pil dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";";
  getnames=yes;
run;
proc print data=pil(obs=6); run;

/* writing */
proc export data=pil outfile="pil_copy.csv" dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";";
run;
In SAS OnDemand for Academics, files must first be uploaded to your personal space and the path adjusted accordingly (e.g. "/home/u1234567/data/pil.csv").

title: 1 Getting started: R basics
text:
1.4 First statistical computations
For our purposes, let us work through a few examples of statistical computation. Given a set of data \(X\), we compute the absolute and relative frequencies. The syntax needs no explanation.

RPythonSAS



X <- c(4, 6, 8, 3, 3, 7, 9, 6, 3, 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 5, 3)
table(X)

X
1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 
1 1 4 1 1 3 1 2 2 

table(X) / length(X)

X
     1      2      3      4      5      6      7      8      9 
0.0625 0.0625 0.2500 0.0625 0.0625 0.1875 0.0625 0.1250 0.1250 





X = pd.Series([4, 6, 8, 3, 3, 7, 9, 6, 3, 1, 2, 6, 8, 9, 5, 3], name="X")
print(X.value_counts().sort_index())

X
1    1
2    1
3    4
4    1
5    1
6    3
7    1
8    2
9    2
Name: count, dtype: int64

print(X.value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index())

X
1    0.0625
2    0.0625
3    0.2500
4    0.0625
5    0.0625
6    0.1875
7    0.0625
8    0.1250
9    0.1250
Name: proportion, dtype: float64




data es;
  input X @@;              /* @@ reads several values from the same line */
  datalines;
4 6 8 3 3 7 9 6 3 1 2 6 8 9 5 3
;
run;

proc freq data=es;
  tables X;                /* absolute, relative (%) and cumulative frequencies */
run;



To display a histogram of the data in \(X\), the command hist(X) produces the chart shown in Figure 1.2. R allows extensive customisation of its graphics. Readers can try standard commands such as plot(), boxplot() or pie(), to name just a few.

RPythonSAS



hist(X)




Figure 1.2 – Example of a histogram







import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.hist(X, bins=range(1, 10), edgecolor="black", color="lightgrey")
plt.title("Histogram of X")
plt.xlabel("X")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.show()




Figure 1.2 – Example of a histogram






proc sgplot data=es;
  histogram X / scale=count;
run;









Note



Each package chooses histogram classes in its own way: R closes them on the right, (a, b], whereas matplotlib and SAS close them on the left. With discrete data like these, bar heights may therefore differ slightly.


A general description of the dataset \(X\) is given by summary(), a very useful command for summarising and displaying the main results of any statistical analysis. In our example, it reports some descriptive statistics.

RPythonSAS



summary(X)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  1.000   3.000   5.500   5.188   7.250   9.000 





print(X.describe())

count    16.000000
mean      5.187500
std       2.561738
min       1.000000
25%       3.000000
50%       5.500000
75%       7.250000
max       9.000000
Name: X, dtype: float64




proc means data=es min q1 median mean q3 max maxdec=3;
  var X;
run;









WarningQuartiles: three packages, different definitions



By default R and pandas compute quartiles with the same method (linear interpolation, type 7 in R): \(Q_3 = 7.25\). SAS uses a different default definition (QNTLDEF=5) and returns \(Q_3 = 7.5\), the same value R gives with quantile(X, type = 2). This is not an error: there are several definitions of the sample quantile.

quantile(X, type = 2)

  0%  25%  50%  75% 100% 
 1.0  3.0  5.5  7.5  9.0 




To show how useful summary() is, we will apply it to a regression model. For this purpose, we load the cars data from the datasets package, which ships with R. The command for estimating a linear regression is lm(); the tilde ~ separates the dependent variable from the explanatory ones.

RPythonSAS



data(cars)
modello <- lm(dist ~ speed, data = cars)
summary(modello)


Call:
lm(formula = dist ~ speed, data = cars)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-29.069  -9.525  -2.272   9.215  43.201 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -17.5791     6.7584  -2.601   0.0123 *  
speed         3.9324     0.4155   9.464 1.49e-12 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 15.38 on 48 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.6511,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6438 
F-statistic: 89.57 on 1 and 48 DF,  p-value: 1.49e-12





import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

cars = pd.read_csv("data/cars.csv")       # the same data as in R, saved in data/
modello = smf.ols("dist ~ speed", data=cars).fit()
print(modello.summary())

                            OLS Regression Results                            
==============================================================================
Dep. Variable:                   dist   R-squared:                       0.651
Model:                            OLS   Adj. R-squared:                  0.644
Method:                 Least Squares   F-statistic:                     89.57
Date:                sab, 31 ott 2026   Prob (F-statistic):           1.49e-12
Time:                        19:13:39   Log-Likelihood:                -206.58
No. Observations:                  50   AIC:                             417.2
Df Residuals:                      48   BIC:                             421.0
Df Model:                           1                                         
Covariance Type:            nonrobust                                         
==============================================================================
                 coef    std err          t      P>|t|      [0.025      0.975]
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Intercept    -17.5791      6.758     -2.601      0.012     -31.168      -3.990
speed          3.9324      0.416      9.464      0.000       3.097       4.768
==============================================================================
Omnibus:                        8.975   Durbin-Watson:                   1.676
Prob(Omnibus):                  0.011   Jarque-Bera (JB):                8.189
Skew:                           0.885   Prob(JB):                       0.0167
Kurtosis:                       3.893   Cond. No.                         50.7
==============================================================================

Notes:
[1] Standard Errors assume that the covariance matrix of the errors is correctly specified.




/* Beware: SASHELP.CARS is a different dataset! Import the R data instead */
proc import datafile="data/cars.csv" out=cars dbms=csv replace;
  getnames=yes;
run;

proc reg data=cars;
  model dist = speed;
run;
quit;



In this way, R displays the estimates and a first set of diagnostics on the goodness of fit of the linear model between dist (the distance needed to stop the car) and speed (the speed of the same car); we will return later to the statistics produced by lm().
Finally, the commands plot(cars, main="Regression line") and abline(modello) draw the scatter plot of dist against speed and add the regression line estimated by OLS (Figure 1.3); note that abline() requires the graphics device to be already open.

RPythonSAS



plot(cars, main = "Regression line")
abline(modello)




Figure 1.3 – Example of a regression line







b0, b1 = modello.params
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.scatter(cars["speed"], cars["dist"], facecolors="none", edgecolors="black")
plt.axline((0, b0), slope=b1, color="black")   # equivalent of abline()
plt.title("Regression line")
plt.xlabel("speed")
plt.ylabel("dist")
plt.show()




Figure 1.3 – Example of a regression line






proc sgplot data=cars;
  title "Regression line";
  reg x=speed y=dist;      /* scatter plot + OLS line */
run;



It is not our aim here to describe further features and functions of R; rather, this first chapter provides a general, admittedly incomplete overview that is nonetheless sufficient for the purposes of the book.

title: 10 Statistical control charts for quality analysis
text:
10.3 The np chart
We could build a similar chart using the number of defective bolts instead of the defect rate, obtaining the \(np\) chart. Strictly speaking, this chart should be used with samples of constant size; we therefore carry out the exercise using the information on defective pins in the same file bulloni.csv (totperni = pins inspected, difperni = defective pins). We build and compare the \(p\) chart with the \(np\) chart, whose limits are now given by \(np\pm 3(np(1-p))^{1/2}\) (Figure 10.5)

RPythonSAS



pi <- difperni/totperni
p <- sum(difperni)/sum(totperni)
n <- sum(totperni)/32
lclnp <- n*p-3*(n*p*(1-p))^0.5
uclnp <- n*p+3*(n*p*(1-p))^0.5
lclnp; uclnp

[1] 10.47328


[1] 39.96422

par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(difperni, type="o", main="np chart", ylim=c(5,45))
abline(h=lclnp, lty=2); abline(h=uclnp, lty=2)
lcl <- p-3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
ucl <- p+3*sqrt(p*(1-p)/n)
lcl; ucl

[1] 0.01745546


[1] 0.06660704

plot(pi, type="o", main="p chart", ylim=c(0.01,0.08))
abline(h=lcl, lty=2); abline(h=ucl, lty=2)




Figure 10.5 – np chart and p chart of defective pins







difperni = bul["difperni"].to_numpy()
pi = difperni / bul["totperni"]
p = difperni.sum() / bul["totperni"].sum()
n = bul["totperni"].sum() / 32
lclnp = n * p - 3 * (n * p * (1 - p)) ** 0.5
uclnp = n * p + 3 * (n * p * (1 - p)) ** 0.5
lcl = p - 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
ucl = p + 3 * np.sqrt(p * (1 - p) / n)
print(lclnp, uclnp); print(lcl, ucl)

10.473277144694121 39.96422285530588
0.017455461907823534 0.06660703809217647



t = np.arange(1, 33)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9, 4.5))
for a, v, lo, hi, tit, yl in ((ax[0], difperni, lclnp, uclnp, "np chart", (5, 45)),
                              (ax[1], pi, lcl, ucl, "p chart", (0.01, 0.08))):
    a.plot(t, v, "o-", color="black", markerfacecolor="none")
    a.axhline(lo, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    a.axhline(hi, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
    a.set_ylim(*yl); a.set_title(tit); a.set_xlabel("Index")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()




Figure 10.5 – np chart and p chart of defective pins






/* np chart and p chart with SAS/QC (samples of 600 pins) */
proc shewhart data=bul;
  npchart difperni*gg / subgroupn=600;
  pchart  difperni*gg / subgroupn=600;
run;



Figure 10.5 shows the two charts; the process is under control, with the usual exception of the 26th observation. Note that when the two charts are applied to samples of identical size, and of course to the same data, they lead to conclusions that differ only in the scale of the values.

title: 10 Statistical control charts for quality analysis
text:
10.4 The c and u charts
The \(c\) chart is another control chart for attributes, based on the number of defects for samples of equal size. Figure 10.6 shows the example of defective pins from the file bulloni.csv

RPythonSAS



c <- sum(difperni)/32
lclc <- c-3*c^0.5; uclc <- c+3*c^0.5
plot(difperni, type="o", main="c chart", ylim=c(5,45))
abline(h=lclc, lty=2); abline(h=uclc, lty=2)




Figure 10.6 – c chart of defective pins



detach(bul)




cmedio = difperni.sum() / 32
lclc, uclc = cmedio - 3 * cmedio ** 0.5, cmedio + 3 * cmedio ** 0.5
carta(difperni, lclc, uclc, "c chart", (5, 45), "difperni")




Figure 10.6 – c chart of defective pins






proc shewhart data=bul;
  cchart difperni*gg;
run;



In this case the chart is built for samples of constant size, assuming that the number of defects \(X\) follows a Poisson random variable with parameter \(c\) (average number of defects), \(P(X=x)=e^{-c}c^{x}/x!\), \(x=0,1,2,...\), hence with limits
\[
LCL=c-3c^{1/2} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=c+3c^{1/2}
\tag{10.4}
\]
But if the number of defects, and hence the average number \(c\), refers to several production units, say \(n\), it may be useful to build the chart around the average number of nonconformities per unit, i.e. on \(u=c/n\), with limits \(LCL=u-3(u/n)^{1/2}\) and \(UCL=u+3(u/n)^{1/2}\), thus obtaining the \(u\) chart.
With the made-up data below, in the case of variable limits, we obtain the \(u\) chart shown in Figure 10.7

RPythonSAS



dif <- c(14,12,20,11,7,10,21,16,19,23) # no. of defects
nn <- c(10,8,13,10,9.5,10,12,10.5,12,12.5) # no. of units
c <- sum(dif)/10; n <- sum(nn)/10; u <- c/n; u

[1] 1.423256

lcl <- u-3*(u/nn)^0.5; ucl <- u+3*(u/nn)^0.5
ui <- dif/nn
plot(ui, type="o", main="u chart", ylim=c(0,3))
lines(lcl, lty=2); lines(ucl, lty=2)




Figure 10.7 – u chart of nonconformities per unit







dif = np.array([14, 12, 20, 11, 7, 10, 21, 16, 19, 23])          # no. of defects
nn = np.array([10, 8, 13, 10, 9.5, 10, 12, 10.5, 12, 12.5])       # no. of units
u = (dif.sum() / 10) / (nn.sum() / 10)
print(u)

1.4232558139534885



carta(dif / nn, u - 3 * (u / nn) ** 0.5, u + 3 * (u / nn) ** 0.5, "u chart", (0, 3), "ui")




Figure 10.7 – u chart of nonconformities per unit






data carta_u;
  input campione dif nn @@;
  datalines;
1 14 10   2 12 8   3 20 13   4 11 10   5 7 9.5
6 10 10   7 21 12  8 16 10.5 9 19 12  10 23 12.5
;
run;
proc shewhart data=carta_u;
  uchart dif*campione / subgroupn=nn;
run;

title: 10 Statistical control charts for quality analysis
text:
10.6 The X-bar and S charts
The \(R\) chart is preferable for small samples, but for sizes above 5 the estimate of \(\sigma\) based on the range becomes progressively less precise. Generally, with \(n>10\) or with variable sample sizes, a specific \(S\) or \(S^{2}\) chart is preferred to the \(R\) chart; of course the construction of the corresponding \(\bar{X}\) chart is also affected.
Let us assume, as usual, that the characteristic \(X\) of the product follows a normal distribution. If \(\sigma\) is known, the \(S\) chart has centre line \(c_{4}\sigma\), with lower and upper 3-sigma limits equal to
\[
LCL=B_{5}\sigma \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=B_{6}\sigma
\tag{10.8}
\]
where the constants \(c_{4}\), \(B_{5}\) and \(B_{6}\) take specific values tabulated by sample size, such that \(B_{5}=c_{4}-3(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}\) and \(B_{6}=c_{4}+3(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}\).
If the standard deviation is unknown, it must be estimated using the relationship \(\hat{\sigma}=\bar{S}/c_{4}\), where \(\bar{S}\) is the mean of the sample standard deviations. The \(S\) chart then has centre line \(\bar{S}\), with limits
\[
LCL=B_{3}\bar{S} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=B_{4}\bar{S}
\tag{10.9}
\]
where \(B_{3}=1-(3/c_{4})(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}\) and \(B_{4}=1+(3/c_{4})(1-c_{4}^{2})^{1/2}\).
The limits of the \(\bar{X}\) chart (whose centre line is still \(\bar{\bar{X}}\)) must then also be redefined
\[
LCL=\bar{\bar{X}}-A_{3}\bar{S} \qquad \text{and} \qquad UCL=\bar{\bar{X}}+A_{3}\bar{S}
\tag{10.10}
\]
where \(A_{3}=3/(c_{4}n^{1/2})\).
We load the data on the diameter of car piston rings in the file pistoni.csv (5 measurements for each of 25 samples). We build the two charts \(\bar{X}\) and \(S\) (Figure 10.10)

piston <- read.csv2("data/pistoni.csv")
med <- 0; dev <- 0
for (i in 2:26) med[i-1]=mean(piston[,i])
for (i in 2:26) dev[i-1]=sd(piston[,i])
media <- mean(med); mdev <- mean(dev)
media; mdev

Figure 10.10 – X-bar and S charts






data pistoni;
  infile "data/pistoni.csv" dlm=";" firstobs=2;
  input misura (c1-c25) (:commax10.);
  array c{25} c1-c25;
  do campione = 1 to 25;
    diametro = c{campione};
    output;
  end;
  keep campione diametro;
run;
proc sort data=pistoni; by campione; run;
/* X-bar and S charts with the tabulated constants A3, B3 and B4 */
proc shewhart data=pistoni;
  xschart diametro*campione;
run;



The process appears to be under control.
Building the \(\bar{X}\) and \(S\) charts is straightforward even with variable sample sizes. The centre lines are obtained using suitable weighted means instead of simple means, while the control limits, which are also variable, are computed each time with the constants for the corresponding sample size. Finally, note that some prefer the \(S^{2}\) chart, based on the sample variance, to the \(S\) chart.
In addition to the classical Shewhart charts presented here, the literature has proposed many other techniques, generally more detailed and more sensitive to small shifts in the process, such as CUSUM (cumulative sum) and EWMA (exponentially weighted moving average) charts; we will not dwell on them further.

title: 7 Poverty and income distribution
text:
Any definition of poverty involves a degree of arbitrariness on the part of the researcher. The most important definitions refer to a concept of relative poverty and to one of absolute poverty. In the first case a poverty threshold is chosen that depends on the level of well-being of the community; for example, if a family of two adults without children has a level of (net) disposable income, or a level of consumption expenditure, below the average of Italian families, it will be said to be (relatively) poor. A family that is poor in absolute terms, instead, cannot afford a specific basket of essential goods and/or services. Between absolute and relative poverty there is a variety of intermediate definitions, whose relevance is, however, more theoretical than empirical. Not by chance, in the most industrialised countries the notion of relative poverty is the one most widely adopted, also for policy purposes. Conversely, in developing countries absolute poverty is the main reference, since the interest generally lies in food-support policies for large sections of the population.
From a historical perspective, ISTAT data for 2007 show about 2 million 653 thousand families in relative poverty, 11% of resident families in 2007, while poor individuals numbered 7 million 542 thousand, 13% of the whole population.
The percentage of poor families and persons out of all resident families and persons is generally estimated on the basis of a conventional threshold (poverty line), which identifies the level of consumption expenditure below which a family is defined as poor in relative terms. The poverty threshold for a family of two adults (the standard reference) is the average monthly expenditure per person, which in 2007 was 986.35 euro (1.6% more than in 2006). Two-person families whose average monthly expenditure is equal to or below this value are classified as relatively poor. For families of different size (and composition) the poverty line is obtained by applying an equivalence scale that accounts for some economies of scale; for example, spending on lighting or heating depends little on the number of members compared with food expenditure (Table 7.1).

title: 7 Poverty and income distribution
text:
7.3 Poverty lines and equivalence scales
We have seen that in Italy the standard poverty line for 2007 was 986.35 euro. Computing poverty lines is generally rather complex, since it requires formulations based on demand systems such as QUAIDS (Quadratic Almost Ideal Demand System). For descriptive purposes, here we refer instead to a simple traditional approach based on Engel expenditure functions such that
\[
A/S=a+b\log S+c\log N
\tag{7.1}
\]
where \(A\) is food expenditure, \(S\) total expenditure and \(N\) the number of family members.
Other relevant information, such as age, social characteristics or consumer preferences, is ignored. Assuming that the ratio \(A/S\) stays constant and setting \(q=A/S-a\), we have \(\log S=q/b-(c/b)\log N\) and, reparameterising, \(S'=(q/b)-(c/b)N'\). The derivative of \(S'\) with respect to \(N'\) is then \(\partial S'/\partial N'=-c/b\), which is simply the elasticity \(E\) of \(S\) with respect to \(N\). This elasticity \(E=-c/b\) is the coefficient of economies of scale of total expenditure with respect to the number of members. Therefore,

\(E<1\): increasing economies of scale (expenditure \(S\) grows less than proportionally to the increase in the number of members \(N\)),
\(E=1\): constant economies of scale,
\(E>1\): decreasing economies of scale.

Once the elasticity \(E\) is known, the equivalence scale is
\[
U_{N+1}=U_{N}(1+E(\Delta N/N))
\tag{7.2}
\]
where \(U_{N}\) is the poverty line for a family of \(N\) members. If \(E=0.667\) with \(U_{2}=986.35\), the poverty line for a household of three and of four members will be

RPythonSAS



E <- 0.667; U2 <- 986.35
U3 <- U2*(1+E*((3-2)/2))
U4 <- U3*(1+E*((4-3)/3))
U3; U4

[1] 1315.298


[1] 1607.732





E, U2 = 0.667, 986.35
U3 = U2 * (1 + E * ((3 - 2) / 2))
U4 = U3 * (1 + E * ((4 - 3) / 3))
print(U3, U4)

1315.297725 1607.7322525249997




data _null_;
  E = 0.667; U2 = 986.35;
  U3 = U2*(1 + E*((3-2)/2));
  U4 = U3*(1 + E*((4-3)/3));
  put U3= U4=;
run;



which approximate well the values reported in Table 7.1.

title: 7 Poverty and income distribution
section: 7.4 Poverty indices: headcount, intensity and Sen
text:
7.4 Poverty indices: headcount, intensity and Sen
Entirely similar considerations apply to income levels. In particular, there are a number of useful indicators that help to analyse the poverty (of income or consumption) in a given area.
The headcount (diffusion) index, already computed (Table 7.2), is the ratio of the number of poor families (or persons) \(q\) to the total number of families \(n\)
\[
H=q/n
\tag{7.3}
\]
This index does not satisfy the monotonicity principle, according to which the index must increase if, other things being equal, the income (or consumption) of even a single poor individual falls. Nor does it satisfy the transfer principle, which requires the index to increase if income is transferred from a poor individual to another poor individual with higher income; moreover, it is insensitive to changes in the income distribution.
Another well-known index is the intensity (income-gap) index
\[
I=\sum_{i} g_{i}/qz
\tag{7.4}
\]
with \(i=1,...,q\), where \(z\) is the poverty line, \(g_{i}=z-y_{i}\) and \(y_{i}\) the income of the \(i\)-th poor individual. The index \(I\) satisfies the monotonicity principle, but it may fail to register changes in the number of poor individuals unless these come with changes in the total gap. Moreover \(I\), like \(H\), does not satisfy the transfer principle and is insensitive to changes in the income distribution.
Let us look at an example with made-up data.

RPythonSAS



x <- c(3,4,6,7,8,9,12,15) # incomes
x <- sort(x)
k <- 10 # poverty line
xp <- x[x<k]
H <- sum(x<k)/length(x)
H

[1] 0.75

I <- sum(k-xp)/(k*length(xp))
I

[1] 0.3833333





x = np.sort(np.array([3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15]))   # incomes
k = 10                                               # poverty line
xp = x[x < k]
H = np.mean(x < k)
I = np.sum(k - xp) / (k * len(xp))
print(H, I)

0.75 0.38333333333333336




proc iml;
  x = {3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 12, 15};   /* incomes (column vector)  */
  call sort(x, 1);
  k = 10;                           /* poverty line */
  xp = x[loc(x < k)];
  H = mean(x < k);
  I = sum(k - xp) / (k*nrow(xp));
  print H I;
quit;



The index \(H\) ranges from 0 (no poor) to 1 (everyone poor), while the index \(I\) ranges from zero (no poor), or from a minimum close to 0 (incomes just below the poverty line), to 1 (incomes far below the poverty line).
Another important index is Sen’s index
\[
S=H\left\{1-[1-I][1-G]\right\}
\tag{7.5}
\]
where \(G\) is the Gini index computed on the income distribution of the poor; we will return to the index \(G\), and hence to Sen’s index, shortly. Sen’s index satisfies three axioms: the weighting axiom (the weight given in the index to each gap equals its rank in the non-decreasing ordering of the gaps); monotonic welfare (if one individual’s income is higher than another’s, the welfare of the former is also higher than that of the latter); normalised poverty value (if all the poor have the same income, the index equals the product of the headcount index \(H\) and the intensity index \(I\)). Sen’s index satisfies the monotonicity and transfer principles, is an increasing function of \(H\), \(I\) and \(G\), and does not depend on the income distribution among the non-poor. Finally, Sen’s index ranges from 0 (no poor) to 1 (incomes far below the poverty line).

4 The decomposition approach to time series
text:
A set of data ordered in time defines a time series. For example, Italian GDP between 2000 and 2008 is a time series which, in this case, spans 8 periods and 9 years. Knowing how and why phenomena evolve over time allows us to formulate plausible hypotheses about their future evolution and to take corrective action where needed.
There are essentially two approaches to time-series analysis: the classical and the modern one (leaving aside spectral analysis). The first developed historically around empirical considerations, with techniques grounded in the analyst’s observation and experience. The idea behind the classical approach is that the series can be decomposed into a few specific factors. The modern approach, by contrast, assumes that there is a data-generating mechanism, of which the observed time series is one of many possible realisations; if certain initial assumptions hold, it is possible to find the statistical model that adequately represents the data. We will return to the modern approach later.
As we said, the classical approach decomposes the series into a few factors, namely



\(Y\)
\(T\)
\(C\)
\(S\)
\(A\)




series
trend
cycle
seasonality
random residual



The trend \(T\) is the most important component, since it represents the underlying tendency of the phenomenon. The cycle \(C\) expresses wave-like fluctuations over the medium term; in economics it can be represented by phases of recession and expansion, but it cannot always be clearly distinguished from the trend, so much so that trend and cycle are often treated as a single trend-cycle component \(TC\). Seasonality \(S\) is present only if the series consists of sub-annual observations, and expresses the typical seasonal pattern of the phenomenon. Finally, the random component \(A\) (sometimes denoted \(I\)) is a purely random residual factor, due to chance or to non-systematic errors.
These factors are combined through additive, multiplicative or mixed models (or other forms), respectively
\[
\begin{gathered}Y=T+C+S+A \\ Y=T\cdot C\cdot S\cdot A \\ Y=T\cdot C+S+A\end{gathered}
\tag{4.1}
\]
The additive model is simpler to compute but assumes a less plausible logical independence among the component factors; in this sense, the multiplicative model often appears the most appropriate for economic time series. Note also that in the multiplicative model, unlike the additive one, only the trend (or trend-cycle) component has the same unit of measurement as the series \(Y\), while the other components take the form of dimensionless coefficients; this makes the multiplicative model easy to read.

The cycle \(C\) expresses wave-like fluctuations over the medium term; in economics it can be represented by phases of recession and expansion, but it cannot always be clearly distinguished from the trend, so much so that trend and cycle are often treated as a single trend-cycle component \(TC\). Seasonality \(S\) is present only if the series consists of sub-annual observations, and expresses the typical seasonal pattern of the phenomenon. Finally, the random component \(A\) (sometimes denoted \(I\)) is a purely random residual factor, due to chance or to non-systematic errors.
These factors are combined through additive, multiplicative or mixed models (or other forms), respectively
\[
\begin{gathered}Y=T+C+S+A \\ Y=T\cdot C\cdot S\cdot A \\ Y=T\cdot C+S+A\end{gathered}
\tag{4.1}
\]
The additive model is simpler to compute but assumes a less plausible logical independence among the component factors; in this sense, the multiplicative model often appears the most appropriate for economic time series. Note also that in the multiplicative model, unlike the additive one, only the trend (or trend-cycle) component has the same unit of measurement as the series \(Y\), while the other components take the form of dimensionless coefficients; this makes the multiplicative model easy to read.

4.2 Moving averages
Figure 4.1 shows car sales by G.M. (General Motors) over a number of years; the values are in the file auto.csv. We load the data and plot the series Vendite (sales).

auto <- read.csv2("data/auto.csv")
attach(auto)
plot(Vendite, xlab="Years", ylab="Million cars sold",
     main="G.M. sales", xaxt="n", type="l")
axis(1, at=1:24, lab=c(1975:1998))




Figure 4.1 – G.M. sales, 1975-1998 (million units)







import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

auto = pd.read_csv("data/auto.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
Vendite = auto["Vendite"]
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.plot(auto["Anno"], Vendite, color="black")
plt.xlabel("Years"); plt.ylabel("Million cars sold")
plt.title("G.M. sales")
plt.show()




Figure 4.1 – G.M. sales, 1975-1998 (million units)






proc import datafile="data/auto.csv" out=auto dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
/* decimal comma: if Vendite is read as character, convert it with input(Vendite, commax8.) */

proc sgplot data=auto;
  title "G.M. sales";
  series x=Anno y=Vendite;
  xaxis label="Years"; yaxis label="Million cars sold";
run;



To bring out the underlying tendency of the series we must reduce the interference of short- and medium-term fluctuations. One way of doing this is to filter the data through, for example, an average computed over a number of adjacent values, that is, a “moving average” such as
\[
MA_{i}=(x_{i-1}+x_{i}+x_{i+1})/3 \qquad \text{for 3 terms}
\tag{4.2}
\]
An odd-order moving average is always centred, in the sense that the resulting value corresponds to the central term among those involved, with the same number of terms on either side. Clearly, a moving average cannot be computed at the lower and upper ends of the series, for lack of information outside the observed range: with 3 terms the first and last values are lost, but with 5 terms instead of 3, two values will be missing on the left and two on the right. In general, if \(L\) is the number of adjacent terms in the average, we lose \((L-1)/2\) terms at both the beginning and the end of the sequence. A larger number of terms smooths the series more, making the underlying tendency clearer, but loses more data at the beginning and end of the period under analysis.
Moving averages of even order can of course also be used, with the drawback that they are not centred to begin with; we will come back to this shortly.
To apply a moving average to the data of Figure 4.1 we use the filter() function. Below we consider a centred moving average of order 3 and then of order 5; note the syntax with the replication command rep(). In other words, the first run sums 3 adjacent values each weighted 1/3, the second 5 values each weighted 1/5.

title: 4 The decomposition approach to time series
text:
4.3 Exponential smoothing
Another way of smoothing a series in search of long-run patterns is exponential smoothing. The technique is particularly interesting because, unlike the previous one, it allows short-term forecasts. The simplest model is best applied to data with no seasonality and no particularly marked trend. Exponential smoothing is nothing but an exponentially weighted moving average
\[
M_{t}=\alpha x_{t}+(1-\alpha )M_{t-1}
\tag{4.3}
\]
where \(0<\alpha <1\) and \(M_{1}=x_{1}\), and

\(x_{t}\) is the value of the time series in period \(t\)
\(M_{t}\) is the weighted average in period \(t\)
\(M_{t-1}\) is the weighted average in period \(t-1\)
\(\alpha\) is the weighting coefficient, or smoothing parameter, chosen a priori.

A low \(\alpha\) filters out random fluctuations well, while a high \(\alpha\) adapts quickly to systematic changes in the series. A value of \(\alpha\) close to 0 gives strong smoothing, while a value close to 1 emphasises short-run fluctuations; the forecast for the first period after the observed values is set equal to the last smoothed value
\[
F_{t+1}=\hat{x}_{t+1}=M_{t}
\tag{4.4}
\]
The technique can be applied recursively to produce forecasts over several periods, but the probability of a wrong forecast then grows steadily.
Following the G.M. sales example, with \(\alpha = 0.25\) we have

RPythonSAS



alfa=0.25
M <- array(0, length(Vendite))
M[1] <- Vendite[1]
for (i in 2:24) M[i] <- alfa*Vendite[i] + (1-alfa)*M[i-1]
previsto <- M[24]
previsto

[1] 8.240602





alfa = 0.25
M = np.zeros(len(Vendite))
M[0] = Vendite[0]
for i in range(1, 24):
    M[i] = alfa * Vendite[i] + (1 - alfa) * M[i - 1]
previsto = M[23]
print(previsto)

8.240601804764333




data auto_es;
  set auto;
  retain M;
  alfa = 0.25;
  if _n_ = 1 then M = Vendite;
  else M = alfa*Vendite + (1-alfa)*M;
run;
/* the forecast is the last smoothed value */
proc print data=auto_es(firstobs=24) noobs; var Anno M; run;



The sales forecast for time \(t+1\) (1999) is 8.24 million cars, that is, the smoothed value at the last observed time. 4.6 Choosing the trend: a goodness-of-fit index
Let us proceed in this direction with an example on the file pil.csv, which contains Italian GDP in € million at constant 2000 prices and the resident population in thousands for 1982-2007. We compute GDP per capita as a proxy for a territory’s development and look for its linear and quadratic trends. The usual summary() function shows some results of interest.

pilpro <- PIL00/POP

tempo2 <- tempo^2

We postpone the statistical analysis of linear models to a later section and focus here only on a goodness-of-fit index based on the deviation of fitted from observed values
\[

title: 4 The decomposition approach to time series
text:
4.8 The seasonal component
We continue our treatment of the classical approach to time series by analysing phenomena with a seasonal component. For ease of interpretation we choose a multiplicative model.
Given the time series \(Y\), we want to identify its components. A moving average allows us to identify the trend, or rather the trend-cycle, but there is no unique answer to the choice of its order. A 3-term moving average has the advantage of losing only one observation at the beginning and one at the end, while a higher order smooths the data better but loses more observations. The choice of order depends largely on the desired degree of smoothing, but also on how many observations are available.
If a seasonal component is present, the order of the moving average must take the seasonal period into account, to make sure that the filter, matching the length of the season, cancels the seasonal component without distorting the trend-cycle. So the order of the average will be 12 for monthly data, 4 for quarterly data, 2 for half-yearly data, and so on; and since the number of terms is generally even, the moving average must also be centred, to ensure that its value can be unambiguously attributed to the time at the centre of the average. Consequently, with a 4-term moving average, centring amounts to taking the arithmetic mean of two adjacent 4-term moving averages, that is, a weighted average of 5 terms in which the first and last receive a weight of 0.5 (so in the end two values will be missing at the head and two at the tail of the moving-average series)
\[
MM(4)_{C}=(0.5\cdot x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}+0.5\cdot x_{5})/4
\tag{4.6}
\]
Using a moving average whose order equals the length of the seasonal period has an intuitive justification since, as we said, the series must be filtered so as to remove the seasonal effect without introducing distortions, as a moving average of a different order would: with quarterly data, for example, a 3-term average would always leave out some quarter, while a 5-term one would include one quarter twice.
Having obtained the trend or trend-cycle, since \(Y=T\cdot C\cdot S\cdot A\), the gross seasonal component (including the irregular component) is easily determined
\[
SA=Y/(T\cdot C)
\tag{4.7}
\]
Note straight away that, by construction, \(SA\) is an index number that fluctuates around one and has no unit of measurement. In an additive model little changes, except that we subtract instead of dividing
\[
SA=Y-(T + C)
\tag{4.8}
\]
In this case \(SA\) has the same unit of measurement as \(Y\), so the preference for a multiplicative model simplifies this point too.
The seasonal component obtained in this way is variable, since the values change slightly between the same periods of different years, whereas large fluctuations would be quite counter-intuitive: there is no strong reason why, especially in the short run, the season should change markedly from one year to the next; if it does, the change can hardly be attributed to seasonal factors as such. In practice, seasonal fluctuations are often numerically quite small relative to the average level of the series, and very similar from one year to the next; so it is not misleading to treat seasonality as a phenomenon that evolves at a constant rate. Thus, even for very long seasonal series, it is convenient and reasonable to represent the seasonal pattern by single values, for example 12 values for monthly seasonality, 4 for quarters, 2 for half-years, etc., simply by averaging within the same seasonal period.
This simplification consists in averaging the same seasonal factor year after year: with monthly data, for example, we average the seasonal factors for January over all the years of the series, then do the same for February and so on up to December, obtaining 12 single values (one per month) that replace the individual seasonal factors making up these averages. It may happen, however, simply because of numerical approximation, that the sum of these new constant seasonal coefficients is not exactly 12 (with a multiplicative model, or 0 with an additive one), as it should be, since they represent a seasonal phenomenon that begins and ends within the year. As seasonality must cancel out within the year, the seasonal factors below one (below 0 in the additive model) must be offset by those above one (above 0 in the additive model), so their sum must equal 4 for quarters, 3 for four-month periods, 12 for months, etc., or 0 in the additive model. This may fail to happen because of numerical approximation; so, assuming the hypothesis of constant seasonality is sound, a correction based on proportionality can be applied.
Specifically, consider a quarterly series covering 3 years; the table below shows the seasonal factors obtained from the ratio \(Y/(T\cdot C)\), where the trend-cycle is a centred 4-term moving average. The first two and the last two values are of course missing:

with \(m_1 + m_2 + m_3 + m_4 = somma\) (the sum). We compute the mean of each column; the sum of the means should be exactly 4, the seasonal period, apart from small fluctuations: for example, it is reasonable to get 4.01 or 3.90 (to keep the explanation intuitive), but certainly not 2 or 7, values far from 4; in fact the sum is never far from its theoretical value. At this point, the difference between the theoretical 4 and the value actually obtained is spread over the 4 quarters proportionally
\[
m_{i}\cdot 4/somma \qquad \text{for each } i \text{ from 1 to 4}
\tag{4.9}
\]
This gives the “corrected” seasonal indices, identical from year to year, whose sum is now, by construction, exactly 4. The procedure applies to any other seasonal period.

4.10 Seasonality with dummy variables
Besides trend analysis, regression can be used to isolate the seasonal component through dummy variables added to the explanatory variables and used as seasonal labels. With monthly data we add 11 dummy variables, taking the value 1 for observations in the month they represent and 0 otherwise; the twelfth dummy is not included, to avoid statistical redundancy, since its effect is already absorbed by the constant of the model. Which dummy to exclude is entirely arbitrary and does not affect the conclusions; we will return to this point in later sections.
Keeping to the example of monthly data, we estimate a model of the form
\[
Y=a+bt+c_{1}D_{1}+c_{2}D_{2}+...+c_{10}D_{10}+c_{11}D_{11}
\tag{4.11}
\]
where the twelfth dummy, for December, has been omitted; the seasonal component here therefore measures the impact of each month relative to December as the reference. \(a+bt\) is the trend or trend-cycle (in the latter case a polynomial of degree higher than one is usually assumed), while \(c_{1}D_{1}+c_{2}D_{2}+...+c_{10}D_{10}+c_{11}D_{11}\) is the seasonal component, with \(D_{i}=1\) in the \(i\)-th month and 0 otherwise. Note that the model implicitly imposes a constant seasonal structure.
We load the data in prodotto.csv, on sales in quintals of a generic consumer product between January 2001 and December 2006. We build a time index that R can use to create the dummy variables of interest.

title: 4 The decomposition approach to time series
text:
4.11 Autoregressive models
By their nature, the models discussed so far do not allow reliable forecasts except under particularly strict conditions, and in any case only in the short run. Dealing satisfactorily with forecasting requires more refined estimation methods and models, moving for example from the deterministic approach of many classical methods to a stochastic one, typical of ARIMA models. We will return to this later, but it is worth mentioning here a special case, useful for non-seasonal series not subject to wide and frequent fluctuations: the autoregressive model, which explains the series \(Y\) through the same variable lagged in time
\[
Y_{t}=a_{0}+a_{1}Y_{t-1}+...+a_{p}Y_{t-p}+e_{t}
\tag{4.13}
\]
that is, an autoregressive model of order \(p\), \(AR(p)\).
Note that estimating these models by OLS, as for linear models in general, requires certain conditions that must be checked. Given the autoregressive nature of the model, one can sense that least-squares estimates for specifications of order higher than one are inadequate; we will come back to this later.
We load the data in pil.csv on Italian GDP in € million at constant prices. We estimate a third-order autoregressive model. Note the use of embed() to build the matrix of the variable PIL00 at lag 0 (that is, unlagged) and at lags 1, 2 and 3. From the model’s summary() we extract the coefficients.

pildati <- read.csv2("data/pil.csv")
pil <- embed(pildati$PIL00, 4)

pil <- data.frame(pil)
modello <- lm(Y~Y1+Y2+Y3, data=pil)

  model Y = Y1;
run;

/* recursive 3-step-ahead forecasts */
data prev_ar;
  set pil_ar end=fine;
  if _n_ = 1 then set b_ar1(keep=Intercept Y1 rename=(Y1=a1));
  caso = _n_; output;
  if fine then do;
    do h = 1 to 3;
      Y = Intercept + a1*Y; caso + 1; Anni + 1; output;
    end;
  end;
  keep caso Anni Y;
run;

  title "Autoregressive model forecast";
  series x=caso y=Y;
  refline 23 / axis=x;
run;



The last observed year of GDP, 2007, no longer corresponds to observation 26 of the original data but to case 23, since lagging the variable \(Y\) removed the first 3 years. So 2007 corresponds to case 23, and the forecasts for 2008 and 2009 correspond to the fitted values for cases 24 and 25.

4.12 Distributed-lag models
In the autoregressive model of order \(p\), \(Y\) is explained by itself lagged up to period \(t-p\), but a more complex model might also include other explanatory variables \(X\), lagged or not, for example
\[
Y_{t}=\alpha +\beta_{1}Y_{t-1}+\beta_{2}Y_{t-2}+\gamma_{0}X_{t}+\gamma_{1}X_{t-1}
\tag{4.14}
\]
In the simplest case only \(X\), lagged for some periods, might be present; we then have a distributed-lag model of the form
\[
Y_{t}=\alpha +\gamma_{0}X_{t}+...+\gamma_{k}X_{t-k}+...+\gamma_{K}X_{t-K}
\tag{4.15}
\]
with \(k=0,...,K\).
We load a company’s data from the file corsi.csv, on losses in dollars due to workplace accidents (perdite) and on the hours of accident-prevention training given to employees (orecorsi). We estimate a distributed-lag model of losses on hours up to lag 4, over 60 months (5 years) of observations.

4.15 Trigonometric seasonality
Another interesting option is to represent the series through a trend-cycle component \(f(t)\) and a seasonal component built from sine and cosine functions. For the object prodotto, with monthly seasonality, we could estimate the model

\tag{4.16}

text:
4.16 The Holt-Winters method
Finally, R also offers built-in functions for exponential smoothing. The smoothing model presented earlier is rather simple and should not be used for forecasting series with a marked trend and/or seasonal fluctuations. In such cases the Holt-Winters procedure is preferable; with a multiplicative seasonal component, the forecast \(F\) at time \(t+Q\) becomes
\[
F_{t+Q}=(a_{t}+b_{t}Q)S_{t-L+Q}
\tag{4.17}
\]
with
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{t} &= M_{t}=\alpha (x_{t}/S_{t-L})+(1-\alpha )(M_{t-1}+b_{t-1}) \\
b_{t} &= \beta (M_{t}-M_{t-1})+(1-\beta )b_{t-1} \\
S_{t} &= \gamma (x_{t}/M_{t})+(1-\gamma )S_{t-L}
\end{aligned}
\]
and \(0<\alpha <1\), \(0<\beta <1\), \(0<\gamma <1\), where \(L\) is the length of the seasonal period (4 for quarters, 12 for months, etc.); additive seasonality can also be assumed, with some changes to the formulas not reported here.
Applying Holt-Winters to the series prodotto gives the following results. Since they were not set manually, the three parameters \(\alpha\), \(\beta\) and \(\gamma\) are chosen automatically by the algorithm through a specific optimisation procedure.

hwm <- HoltWinters(y, seasonal="mult")

section: Software used in this online edition
text:
Software used in this online edition

R: base packages and, in Chapters 6, 9 and 11, the tseries, lpSolve and fGarch packages.
Python: numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy, statsmodels and, in Chapter 11, arch.
SAS: Base SAS and SAS/STAT procedures, plus SAS/ETS (PROC ARIMA, PROC AUTOREG), SAS/IML, SAS/OR (PROC OPTMODEL, Chapter 9) and SAS/QC (PROC SHEWHART, Chapter 10).

title: Preface
text:
NoteAbout the online edition



This online edition is based on the book Statistica Economica con R (2018) and adds equivalent Python and SAS code alongside every R example. The R and Python code is run each time the site is rebuilt, so the output may differ in formatting details from that shown in the printed edition. The site is available in English and Italian.


This book grew out of the wish to reorganise the teaching materials and exercises handed out in my university courses and to make them easier for students to use.
This edition is a revised and updated version of a book first published in 2009 and, then, in 2018. It contains many changes from the previous edition: new topics have been added and some content that is no longer current has been removed. The book also aims more firmly at a broad readership, with an exposition suited to any student approaching Economic Statistics, even with only a minimal background in statistics. In particular, its integration with the software R, Python and SAS, which in practice accompanies every topic with numerous examples, gives it a strongly applied character. The resulting approach is therefore rather original: the book is easy to read and avoids excessive methodological and technical detail. Moreover, the chapters have been designed so that they can be read without necessarily following the order in which they are presented.
The site is divided into chapters.
Chapter 1 covers some basic notions of R, introducing the software to readers with less computing experience. It describes the functions for reading data and the most important commands for manipulating objects.
Chapter 2 sets out the main accounts of the National Accounts and works through some calculations for the aggregates considered most important.
Chapter 3 deals with Index Numbers, with particular attention to price indices, and with some deflation techniques. R is used to compute series at constant prices and to examine the differences between valuations at current and at constant prices, as well as how base changes are carried out and what they imply.
Chapter 4 describes time-series analysis in a classical framework, with a mainly, though not exclusively, macroeconomic slant. It shows how to decompose a series into its main trend, cycle and seasonal components using several techniques. The examples show how R can be used to smooth the data with moving averages of odd order, or of even order when the seasonal lag is even. The software is also used to compute more complex exponential smoothing functions for series with or without a seasonal period. In addition, a first look at the estimation of linear models makes it possible to identify trend, cycle and season through an appropriate model specification. The typical forms of autoregressive and distributed-lag models, widely used in economics, are introduced. This topic is treated in detail in the following chapter.
Chapter 5 therefore deals with the statistical, econometric and interpretive aspects of linear specification, with particular reference to its limits and to the precautions it requires. It addresses model misspecification through the omission of relevant variables and the inclusion of irrelevant ones, the presence of multicollinearity or of residual autocorrelation, and the lack of structural stability of the parameters or of homoscedasticity, to name just a few examples. A statistically reliable and robust model formulation, particularly for forecasting purposes, may require a specification that assumes a stochastic origin for the time series.
In this respect, Chapter 6 follows the modern approach, assuming that a time series is generated by a stochastic process and can be represented by a model with an autoregressive and/or a moving-average component. Extensive use of data and exercises in R makes it possible to assess the descriptive and forecasting performance of these models.
Chapter 7 is devoted to measures of poverty and income distribution. The software is used to compute the best-known indices of poverty incidence and intensity; in addition, several exercises compute the Gini concentration ratio and index, the Theil and Sen indices, and others.
Chapter 8 focuses on the concepts of production and productivity with reference to the production function and, in particular, to the Cobb-Douglas form, to which many exercises are devoted.
Chapter 9 is devoted to measuring the statistical efficiency of production processes through parametric and non-parametric procedures. Although the latter require knowledge of constrained maximisation and minimisation problems, a simple exposition is offered to introduce the reader to a topic of real importance in evaluating the performance of public services.
Chapter 10 covers the main Shewhart control charts, for attributes and for variables, which are used to monitor the evolution of a production process and detect possible anomalies. Once again, the topic is relevant to measuring and analysing process quality, with particular attention to public services.
Chapter 11 introduces particular autoregressive forms that focus on estimating the variance of financial time series. It presents autoregressive heteroscedastic models and their variants most widely used in analysing the characteristics and behaviour of financial markets. Economic time-series approaches rest essentially on a relationship of dependence along the time axis. It is intuitive, however, that data for one area are subject to a contagion effect and in turn affect data for neighbouring areas, so that their evolution is worth examining not only over time but also in space.
This topic, which also matters for analysing and interpreting territorial disparities, is introduced in Chapter 12, together with further examples that briefly recall some multivariate techniques; a more detailed treatment of these subjects is beyond the scope of the site.
It should be stressed that the chapters need not be read in order, although, for obvious expository reasons, later sections do not repeat the descriptions of software functions given earlier.
Clearly, the topics and applications covered in the site provide a general, didactically simplified and non-exhaustive overview of the main subjects of Economic Statistics; it is equally true, however, that they cover most of the basic training needs of the discipline in the various courses (both bachelor’s and master’s) offered by Italian universities.
Hoping to have produced useful material for students approaching Economic Statistics, given also its empirical and applied approach built around popular softwares, it only remains for the author to thank all those who will kindly point out errors, oversights and typos.

title: 3 Index numbers and deflation
text:
Comparing aggregates over time or across space requires the quantities compared to be homogeneous: we cannot compare the price of Tuscan cigars in lire with that of another type of cigar in euro, or compare speeds in km per hour and in miles per hour. Index numbers help us compare variables because they do not depend on the unit of measurement: we say that an index number is a pure number. There are obviously many ways of building an index number; it depends on what the analyst wants to know.
Suppose we want to compare the number of crimes against the person in two cities, say A and B. City A records 30 crimes per 100 victims, the second city 60 (again per 100). Clearly A is less “dangerous” than B, if crimes are a proxy for a community’s level of safety. The first city is less dangerous by \((30/60 - 1) \cdot 100 = (0.5-1) \cdot 100 = -50\%\), that is, by half. This ratio is an index number: a pure number expressing a relative change that does not depend on the original unit of measurement. And again: by what percentage did crimes per 100 victims increase in city A if they went from 20 in 2000 to 40 in 2008? The answer is immediate: \((40/20 - 1) \cdot 100 = (2-1) \cdot 100 = +100\%\); they doubled. In this way aggregates and variables can easily be compared both across space and over time. Since the denominator of an index number is the basis of comparison, over time it is usually the earlier period, so that the change reads intuitively from the more distant period to the more recent one.
Let us continue our example by choosing a product, say pork consumed by a given household in a given area over some period. If the Rossi family bought 1 kg of meat a week last year and buys 2 kg today, then \((2/1 - 1) \cdot 100 = 100\%\) is the increase in meat consumption (assuming that the quantity bought equals actual consumption); in other words, if \(q\) is the quantity, we can write \(q_{1}/q_{0}\), where 0 and 1 denote the two time periods. Likewise, for 2008 but for two different households, we have \(q_{famiglia1}/q_{famiglia2}\). The same reasoning applies to the price of meat in two different years, or in the same year for the same two households; we then write \(p_{1}/p_{0}\) or \(p_{famiglia1}/p_{famiglia2}\). These are examples of simple index numbers, which consider a single good (or service): a simple ratio.
We may be interested not only in comparing the price or the quantity of meat bought, but also the total value of the good. We may then want to compare the Rossi family’s spending on meat in one year with the same spending in the following year. The value of this spending depends on changes in price with quantity unchanged, on changes in quantity with price unchanged, or on changes in both price and quantity. The value of a purchase is of course the unit price times the quantity bought: spending on 5 kg of meat is \(q\cdot p\), that is, 5 kg times the price of 1 kg of meat. So the value of our spending is in general
\[
V=p\cdot q
\tag{3.1}
\]
The comparison between two years is obtained with the usual ratio; for periods 0 and 1 we have
\[
p_{1}q_{1}/p_{0}q_{0}
\tag{3.2}
\]
while across space, between areas \(r\) and \(s\), we have
\[
p_{r}q_{r}/p_{s}q_{s}
\tag{3.3}
\]
We focus on comparisons over time, as they are more relevant to what follows; everything also holds for spatial comparisons.
Saying that the Rossi family’s weekly spending on meat went from €25 to €36 between 2007 and 2008 is of limited interest; this value grew by \((36/25-1) \cdot 100 = 44\%\). What caused the increase? Did the Rossi family decide to buy more meat at unchanged prices, did prices rise with quantities unchanged, or did both prices and quantities increase? Bearing in mind that one could have risen and the other fallen, or vice versa.
So it clearly matters to establish what drives the change in value over time (quantities and/or prices) and to what extent. If we found that prices had in fact risen and the quantity of meat bought had fallen, but not by enough to offset the first change, we would know that the Rossi family is eating less meat even though it is spending more; by contrast, the initial information that spending had risen from 25 to 36 would intuitively have led us to believe that meat consumption had increased. Changes in prices and quantities must therefore be properly separated.
To do so we define two virtual values, combining the prices and quantities of the two periods 0 and 1:
\[
V'=p_{1}q_{0} \quad \text{and} \quad V''=p_{0}q_{1}
\tag{3.4}
\]
Comparing period 1 with these two virtual values, we get
\[
V/V'=p_{1}q_{1}/p_{1}q_{0} \quad \text{hence} \quad V/V'=q_{1}/q_{0}
\tag{3.5}
\]
and
\[
V/V''=p_{1}q_{1}/p_{0}q_{1} \quad \text{hence} \quad V/V''=p_{1}/p_{0}
\tag{3.6}
\]
So information on the change in quantities is obtained by holding prices constant, while information on the change in prices is obtained by holding quantities constant between periods 0 and 1. The first is a quantity index, the second a price index. We can generalise this principle to composite index numbers, that is, those that consider several goods and/or services.

title: 3 Index numbers and deflation
3 Index numbers and deflation
section: 3.3 Price indices, Fisher and chain indices
text:
3.3 Price indices, Fisher and chain indices
Let us focus on price indices only, which are particularly interesting because they allow useful considerations about inflation, that is, the relative change in the general price level recorded in a community over a given period.
Consider a given group of products, or a generic basket representative of the consumption spending of certain households. When prices tend to rise over a period (the usual pattern in a national economy), consumers end up replacing the goods and/or services whose prices have risen with cheaper products, buying and consuming less of the former and more of the latter. The Laspeyres price index will then tend towards higher values and the Paasche index towards lower values: we say that the first has an upward bias and the second a downward bias, since Laspeyres overstates inflation and Paasche understates it. Indeed, since a price index tracks prices through a particular weighted average with quantities as weights, it in fact measures, for the period and area considered, the general price dynamics of the basket of goods and/or services in question.
Recall that neither the product of the Laspeyres price and quantity indices nor that of the Paasche price and quantity indices gives the value index
\[
I_{v}=\sum_{i=1}^{n} p_{i1}q_{i1} \Big/ \sum_{i=1}^{n} p_{i0}q_{i0}
\tag{3.11}
\]
It is easy to show that only the product of the price index of one and the quantity index of the other, and vice versa, gives back the value index. Transitivity does not hold either: the price index between 0 and \(n\) is not equal to the combination of those between 0 and \(t\) and between \(t\) and \(n\), with \(t<n\). Simple index numbers, by contrast, have these properties too. Using a third index, the Fisher index, at least removes the bias of Laspeyres and Paasche by taking their geometric mean
\[
I_{p}^{F}=(I_{p}^{L}\cdot I_{p}^{P})^{1/2} \quad \text{and} \quad I_{q}^{F}=(I_{q}^{L}\cdot I_{q}^{P})^{1/2}
\tag{3.12}
\]
The Fisher index also solves the problem of recovering the value index, since
\[
I_{v}^{F}=I_{p}^{F}\cdot I_{q}^{F}
\tag{3.13}
\]
The main drawback is the computational effort and the amount of information required, since both Laspeyres and Paasche must be computed, and then their geometric mean.
ISTAT, like most national statistical institutes, prefers the Laspeyres index which, recall, does not in theory satisfy the transitivity (or circularity) property. Note, however, that since 2005 ISTAT has adopted chain index numbers, in line with new European directives. This implies continually updating the reference year and abandoning the old fixed-base index. In other words, each year a new price index based on the previous year is built and, through chain-linking, the index between, say, period 1 and period 3 is obtained as the product of the indices between periods 1 and 2 and between 2 and 3. In general terms,
\[
{}_{0}I_{t}={}_{0}I_{r}\cdot{}_{r}I_{s}\cdot{}_{s}I_{t} \qquad \text{with } r<s<t
\tag{3.14}
\]
Of course the corresponding fixed-base index between periods 1 and 3 will not coincide with the chain-linked one, but this is no longer a concern; in this way the lack of transitivity of the index loses its significance.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

ni = pd.read_csv("data/numeroindice.csv", sep=";")
p0, q0, p1, q1, p2, q2 = (ni[c] for c in ["p0", "q0", "p1", "q1", "p2", "q2"])
V0 = (p0 * q0).sum()
V1 = (p1 * q1).sum()

45 68 111




proc import datafile="data/numeroindice.csv" out=ni dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;

/* aggregate values are sums of products */
proc sql;
  create table valori as
  select sum(p0*q0) as V0, sum(p1*q1) as V1, sum(p2*q2) as V2,
         sum(p0*q1) as V01, sum(p1*q0) as V10
  from ni;
quit;
proc print data=valori noobs; var V0 V1 V2; run;



Let us look at the changes in value over time.

RPythonSAS



Iv1 <- ((V1/V0)-1)*100
Iv2 <- ((V2/V1)-1)*100

run;
proc print data=valori noobs; var Iv1 Iv2; run;



From period 0 to period 1 the value of the purchase grew from €45 to €68, an increase of about 51%, and by as much as 63% between periods 1 and 2; these are the value index numbers at periods 1 and 2.

V01 <- sum(p0*q1)

IqL <- (V01/V0)*100
IpL <- (V10/V0)*100
IqP <- (V1/V10)*100
IpP <- (V1/V01)*100
round(c(IqL,IqP,IpL,IpP),0)
