title: 3 Index numbers and deflation
section: 3.5 Inflation, purchasing power and revaluation coefficients
text:
3.5 Inflation, purchasing power and revaluation coefficients
ISTAT publishes price data monthly, both as year-on-year and as month-on-month changes. In February 2009 the national consumer price index for the whole population (NIC), including tobacco, stood at 137.0 (base 1995=100), up 0.2% on January 2009 (month-on-month change) and 1.6% on the same month of the previous year (year-on-year change): this is a measure of inflation for February 2009 over February 2008. If instead we looked at the FOI index (see below) with data updated to 2018, we would see an index of 102.9 in August 2018 against a base of 100 in 2015: an increase of 2.9% over the base period. Returning to the NIC in our historical assessment, the international crisis, which squeezed consumption and production, together with the substantial fall in energy commodity prices, led to a marked slowdown in the growth of all prices: over 2008 (compared with 2007) average annual inflation was 3.3%, peaking at 4% in the third quarter alone. Interestingly, in recent years price growth has been more moderate; for example, the year-on-year NIC figure for September 2018 shows annual growth of 1.5% (slightly below the 1.6% recorded in August 2018).
Knowing how prices evolve is particularly useful so as not to confuse changes in an aggregate with its real changes, where “real” here means net of the effect of prices. Suppose we want to study spending on bread in a neighbourhood of Palermo between 2007 and 2008: €10,000 in the first year and €12,000 in the second, an increase of 20%. But how much of this increase is due to prices? If we found that bread prices fully accounted for the increase in spending, we could conclude that people in the neighbourhood did not in fact eat more bread. We might even suppose that higher prices offset a fall in the quantities sold, so that the increase in spending hides a fall in real terms in the bread sold.
So, to interpret the data correctly, price effects must be stripped out, even though end users almost never have adequate information for individual products or product types; in most cases, with some important exceptions, a measure valid for prices as a whole has to suffice. This is the route usually followed to remove the effect of prices and obtain an aggregate in real terms.
In particular, besides the NIC, ISTAT computes a consumer price index for blue- and white-collar worker households (FOI); the FOI excluding tobacco is used to index rents, maintenance payments, etc. In February 2009 this index stood at 134.5 (base 1995=100), up 1.5% year on year on February 2008, while the annual index for 2007 and 2008 was 130.0 and 134.2 respectively, an increase of 3.23%. So, for a given amount of money, purchasing power fell by about 3% between 2007 and 2008. Similar considerations apply to more recent data.
We can now work out how much the value of, say, €1000 fell because of price erosion between 2007 and 2008. The 2008 index relative to 2007 (that is, rebased to 2007) is \((134.2/130.0) \cdot 100 = 103.23\); so \((1000 / 103.23) \cdot 100 = 968.70\) euro is what “really” remains of the initial €1000. More simply, \(1000 / (1 + 3.23\%) = 1000 / (1 + 0.0323) = 968.70\). By the same reasoning, to find the value of €1000 of 2008 in terms of 2007, we simply multiply 1000 by \((1+0.0323)\), that is, by the coefficient 1.0323 known as the “monetary revaluation coefficient”.

In essence, if we could travel back in time, one euro of 2008 would have had the purchasing power of about 8,514 euro in 1861, or of 67 euro in 1945; of course the coefficient equals 1 in 2008, the reference base of the whole series.
Revaluation coefficients are useful for deflating aggregates, removing from them the effect of prices as measured by the FOI index excluding tobacco. Although for simplicity these coefficients are used for most aggregates expressed in money terms, it would be logically correct to restrict their use to consumption items, using specific indices or deflators for the other demand items, and others still for supply and production items; for example, a specific implicit deflator is available for GDP.

title: 3 Index numbers and deflation
9 Statistical efficiency of production processes
text:
The concept of productivity introduced in the previous chapter is linked to the definition and measurement of efficiency. In particular, if productivity is measured by a ratio of output to input, efficiency is measured by the ratio of observed output to the maximum output attainable by a production process for some level of technology.
Let us assume and draw two different shapes for two production functions \(Y=f(X)\) for a simple process with one input and one output (Figure 9.1).



Figure 9.1 – Production functions


Let \(0C\) be, by construction, a straight line, precisely the bisector of the plane, i.e. such that its points all have the same output-to-input ratio (\(Y/X=a\); in the special case where output equals input, \(a=1\)). \(0C\) could represent a production function, however unrealistic, since it expresses a law transforming input into output for some process. Likewise, the curve \(0ABC\) could also represent a (more realistic) production function. Let us assume, however, that the curve \(0ABC\) is also the frontier of the production process: given a certain technology and some level \(x\) of input \(X\), a different level \(y\) of output \(Y\) can be obtained for each possible production function, but never above the value on the frontier, which by definition expresses the maximum the process can achieve given the inputs.
If \(0ABC\) is the set of points \((x,y)\) such that the output levels reached are the highest possible, we say that the efficiency of the productions, or combinations \((x,y)\), lying on this frontier is maximal, and therefore certainly greater than that of the points lying on the line \(0C\). We also say that the frontier \(0ABC\) is the set of technically efficient points (in terms of the combination of \(x\) and \(y\)) with output orientation, since it represents the maximum possible production given the input levels.
In Figure 9.1 points \(A\) and \(B\) have the same maximum efficiency but different productivity, since their output/input ratios differ; \(C\) and \(D\) have different efficiency (\(C\) is on the frontier and \(D\) is not) but the same productivity, since both lie on the line \(0C\) and therefore have a constant output-to-input ratio (equal to 1 here). In particular, the line \(0C\) represents a production process with constant returns to scale (CRS); indeed, at every point the tangent coincides with the line itself. The curve \(0ABC\), instead, shows increasing returns to scale at \(A\) and \(B\) (tangents steeper than the line \(0C\)) and decreasing returns at \(C\) (tangent flatter than \(0C\)). There is of course at least one point (in Figure 9.1, near the \(+\) symbol) whose tangent is parallel to the line \(0C\): here returns to scale are constant, and it is worth noting that if the production frontier is CRS, efficiency and productivity coincide (the CRS frontier is in fact a straight line).
So far the frontier has been defined with reference to production, meaning the maximum amount of output that can be produced for a given input level: this is an output-oriented approach. In exactly the same way, the production frontier can be seen as the minimum use of inputs for a given output level, with an input-oriented approach. Whatever the point of view, we refer to a concept of technical efficiency, since it concerns the levels, in quantity or value terms, of the inputs and outputs of the production process.



Figure 9.2 – Production frontier functions





Figure 9.3 – Cost frontier functions


If, instead, the frontier is defined from the point of view of costs, an efficiency condition, in this case allocative efficiency, requires minimising production costs given input prices and a fixed level of output; the frontier then no longer bounds the production possibility set from above but, on the contrary, from below (Figures 9.2 and 9.3).
Following Farrell’s well-known approach, and recalling that technical efficiency concerns the quantities (or values) of inputs and outputs while allocative efficiency concerns the costs of the process, one can also define overall efficiency as a combination of technical and allocative efficiency. To clarify the differences, consider Figure 9.4 in the input-oriented case; the transposition to the output-oriented case is straightforward.



Figure 9.4 – Farrell efficiency with input orientation


\(SS'\) is the isoquant corresponding to a fixed production level \(Y\), obtained by minimising the use of two inputs \(X_{1}\) and \(X_{2}\). At point \(P\) the same quantity of output as at \(Q\) is produced, but with greater use of inputs. We say that \(P\) represents a case of technical inefficiency with respect to the optimal point \(Q\), and hence that \(P\) is relatively inefficient with respect to \(Q\). This inefficiency can be measured by the ratio \(0Q/0P\), if we use a radial measure of the distance between \(Q\) and \(P\). \(AA'\) is instead an isocost line, along which the combination of inputs guarantees the same minimum cost for the fixed output \(Y\). Point \(Q\) is technically efficient but does not lie on the optimal isocost, so it shows allocative inefficiency with respect to point \(R\). Allocative inefficiency is therefore measured by the ratio \(0R/0Q\), which is again a radial measure. Overall inefficiency, interpretable as a combination of the two, can thus be measured by the product \((0Q/0P)\cdot (0R/0Q)=0R/0P\). Only at point \(Q'\) are full technical and allocative efficiency achieved at the same time.

title: 9 Statistical efficiency of production processes
9 Statistical efficiency of production processes
text:
9.3 Data Envelopment Analysis
Farrell’s approach gave rise to the non-parametric approach known as data envelopment analysis (DEA) which, in its original and still most widespread formulation, yields measures of technical inefficiency for the units of analysis (decision making units or DMUs). There are many versions of DEA, but here we restrict ourselves to the simplest and most classical formulation.
DEA is a technique that envelops the data, i.e. it determines a frontier without reference to production functions with forms known a priori. DEA was born in 1978 and uses computational algorithms typical of operations research, since it essentially looks for solutions to constrained minimum and maximum problems.
A great advantage is the possibility of analysing processes with several outputs, a typical condition of many non-industrial processes that we could hardly study with parametric approaches; the latter are typically based on regression functions which, while allowing many inputs as regressors, do not allow several dependent variables (our outputs) except with unusual and more complex methods that we leave aside here.
The following example helps to understand the logic of DEA. Suppose we want to examine 4 DMUs, for instance 4 firms whose industrial transformation process has a single output and a single input, both measured in tonnes

RPythonSAS



out <- c(125,44,80,23)
inp <- c(18,16,17,11)
es1 <- cbind(out,inp)
rownames(es1) <- c("A","B","C","D")
es1

  out inp
A 125  18
B  44  16
C  80  17
D  23  11





es1 = pd.DataFrame({"out": [125, 44, 80, 23], "inp": [18, 16, 17, 11]},
                   index=["A", "B", "C", "D"])
print(es1)

   out  inp
A  125   18
B   44   16
C   80   17
D   23   11




data es1;
  input dmu $ out inp;
  datalines;
A 125 18
B  44 16
C  80 17
D  23 11
;
run;
proc print data=es1 noobs; run;



To obtain a measure of technical efficiency we must compare actual output with the maximum possible, given the different input levels. So, by computing the ratio \(Y/X\) and dividing it by the largest observed value, it is easy to build the efficiency ranking

RPythonSAS



es1 <- cbind(es1,out/inp,(out/inp)/max(out/inp))
colnames(es1)[3:4] <- c("out/inp","(out/inp)/max")
es1

  out inp  out/inp (out/inp)/max
A 125  18 6.944444     1.0000000
B  44  16 2.750000     0.3960000
C  80  17 4.705882     0.6776471
D  23  11 2.090909     0.3010909





es1["out/inp"] = es1["out"] / es1["inp"]
es1["(out/inp)/max"] = es1["out/inp"] / es1["out/inp"].max()
print(es1)

   out  inp   out/inp  (out/inp)/max
A  125   18  6.944444       1.000000
B   44   16  2.750000       0.396000
C   80   17  4.705882       0.677647
D   23   11  2.090909       0.301091




proc sql;
  create table es1b as
  select *, out/inp as ratio, calculated ratio / max(calculated ratio) as efficiency
  from es1;
quit;
proc print data=es1b noobs; run;



The first unit is on the efficiency frontier, with score 1, while the fourth firm is the least efficient (score 0.30).
Let us work through another example for processes with two outputs and a single input; the setting is entirely analogous to the more familiar one with one output and two inputs

RPythonSAS



es2 <- cbind(out1=out,out2=c(50,20,55,12),inp)
rownames(es2) <- rownames(es1)
es2

  out1 out2 inp
A  125   50  18
B   44   20  16
C   80   55  17
D   23   12  11





es2 = pd.DataFrame({"out1": es1["out"], "out2": [50, 20, 55, 12], "inp": es1["inp"]})
print(es2)

   out1  out2  inp
A   125    50   18
B    44    20   16
C    80    55   17
D    23    12   11




data es2;
  input dmu $ out1 out2 inp;
  datalines;
A 125 50 18
B  44 20 16
C  80 55 17
D  23 12 11
;
run;
proc print data=es2 noobs; run;



and, as in the previous example,

RPythonSAS



es2 <- cbind(es2,oi1=es2[,1]/inp,oi2=es2[,2]/inp,
             maxo1=(es2[,1]/inp)/max(es2[,1]/inp),
             maxo2=(es2[,2]/inp)/max(es2[,2]/inp))
es2

  out1 out2 inp      oi1      oi2     maxo1     maxo2
A  125   50  18 6.944444 2.777778 1.0000000 0.8585859
B   44   20  16 2.750000 1.250000 0.3960000 0.3863636
C   80   55  17 4.705882 3.235294 0.6776471 1.0000000
D   23   12  11 2.090909 1.090909 0.3010909 0.3371901





es2["oi1"] = es2["out1"] / es2["inp"]
es2["oi2"] = es2["out2"] / es2["inp"]
es2["maxo1"] = es2["oi1"] / es2["oi1"].max()
es2["maxo2"] = es2["oi2"] / es2["oi2"].max()
print(es2.round(4))

   out1  out2  inp     oi1     oi2   maxo1   maxo2
A   125    50   18  6.9444  2.7778  1.0000  0.8586
B    44    20   16  2.7500  1.2500  0.3960  0.3864
C    80    55   17  4.7059  3.2353  0.6776  1.0000
D    23    12   11  2.0909  1.0909  0.3011  0.3372




proc sql;
  create table es2b as
  select *, out1/inp as oi1, out2/inp as oi2,
         calculated oi1 / max(calculated oi1) as maxo1,
         calculated oi2 / max(calculated oi2) as maxo2
  from es2;
quit;
proc print data=es2b noobs; run;



So with several outputs (or several inputs) things get more complicated, since the results may disagree: considering the first output the most efficient firm is \(A\), but considering the second output it becomes \(C\). Even if the efficiency rankings were consistent and pointed to the same firms, we would probably not obtain the same distance from the frontier; clearly the problem becomes even more complicated if the process has many inputs and many outputs. DEA provides a solution.



Figure 9.6 – Envelopment frontier


Figure 9.6 plots the four firms of the example. By definition, the frontier is given by the units with the highest output-to-input ratio, so it is built around units \(A\) and \(C\), in effect enveloping all the data. Firms \(A\) and \(C\) are therefore fully efficient: we say they dominate all the other units and by definition assign them a score of 1; the efficiency scores of the remaining firms \(B\) and \(D\), instead, are unknown.
We proceed as follows. We compute the ratio between the two outputs given the inputs, i.e. between \(Y_{1}/X\) and \(Y_{2}/X\), which amounts to comparing the two outputs directly

RPythonSAS



es2[,1]/es2[,2]

       A        B        C        D 
2.500000 2.200000 1.454545 1.916667 





print(es2["out1"] / es2["out2"])

A    2.500000
B    2.200000
C    1.454545
D    1.916667
dtype: float64




data _null_;
  set es2;
  ratio = out1/out2;
  put dmu= ratio=;
run;



The slope of the line through \(D\) and the origin (the process is assumed not to admit zero outputs or inputs unless jointly) is therefore known and equal to 1/1.92, and likewise for \(B\) we have 1/2.20 (the lines are drawn as dashed lines in Figure 9.6). Projecting \(D\) and \(B\) onto the frontier built around \(A\) and \(C\) identifies two fictitious firms \(D'\) and \(B'\), which are efficient and have the same output ratio as \(D\) and \(B\). The efficiency score of \(D\) is then computed with respect to its own virtual maximum \(D'\) and, in the same way, \(B\) is compared with \(B'\), giving a radial measure of efficiency; thus the score of \(D\) is \(0D/0D'\), while that of \(B\) is \(0B/0B'\).
For simplicity, let \(x=Y_{1}/X\) and \(y=Y_{2}/X\) denote the horizontal and vertical axes of the plane in Figure 9.6. Since the equation
\[
(x-x_{1})/(x_{2}-x_{1})=(y-y_{1})/(y_{2}-y_{1})
\tag{9.1}
\]
defines the line through any two points, the segment joining \(A\) and \(C\) is given by \(y=4.20-0.20x\). Point \(D\) instead lies on the line \(y=(1/1.92)x\); solving the two equations together easily gives the intersection point \(D'(5.82;\,3.03)\); similarly we find \(B'(6.42;\,2.92)\), which lies on the line \(y=(1/2.20)x\). Since the distance of a point from the origin \((0,0)\) equals
\[
(x^{2}+y^{2})^{1/2}
\tag{9.2}
\]
we have \(0D=2.36\) and \(0D'=6.56\), and also \(0B=3.02\) and \(0B'=7.05\). We now have the information needed to compute the efficiency scores of firms \(D\) and \(B\)

RPythonSAS



eff_D <- 2.36/6.56
eff_B <- 3.02/7.05
eff_D; eff_B

[1] 0.3597561


[1] 0.4283688





eff_D = 2.36 / 6.56
eff_B = 3.02 / 7.05
print(eff_D, eff_B)

0.3597560975609756 0.42836879432624114




data _null_;
  eff_D = 2.36/6.56;
  eff_B = 3.02/7.05;
  put eff_D= eff_B=;
run;



Firm \(D\) has an efficiency score of 0.36, lower than that of \(B\), equal to 0.43, and of course lower than those of \(A\) and \(C\), which are the benchmark and by definition score 1. To increase their efficiency, firms \(D\) and \(B\) should move along their dashed lines towards their projections on the frontier (Figure 9.6), increasing the ratio \(Y/X\) either by raising outputs for given inputs (output-oriented) or by reducing inputs for given outputs (input-oriented), or by both raising outputs and reducing inputs (this mixed approach is not allowed by traditional DEA techniques, but is available in more recent versions).

title: 9 Statistical efficiency of production processes
text:
9.4 The mathematical formulation of DEA
Efficiency can also be computed through a mathematical formulation, a generalisation that becomes necessary when the process has several inputs and outputs. For firm \(B\) the problem to solve, with obvious meaning of the symbols (peso = weight), is \(\max E_{B}\) subject to
\[
\begin{gathered}E_{A}=(125\,peso_{output1}+50\,peso_{output2})/(18\,peso_{input}) \\ E_{B}=(44\,peso_{output1}+20\,peso_{output2})/(16\,peso_{input}) \\ E_{C}=(80\,peso_{output1}+55\,peso_{output2})/(17\,peso_{input}) \\ E_{D}=(23\,peso_{output1}+12\,peso_{output2})/(11\,peso_{input}) \\ 0\le E_{i}\le 1,\quad peso_{k}\ge 0\end{gathered}
\tag{9.3}
\]
Since the problem is non-linear and hard to solve, a linear formulation is preferred, adding the condition \(16\,peso_{input}=1\); the efficiency of \(B\) to be maximised then becomes \(E_{B}=44\,peso_{output1}+20\,peso_{output2}\). The procedure is repeated in the same way for the other three units.
In practice, the DEA problem is usually more complex, since even the standard model admits different assumptions about the production process. For example, we could rewrite the problem in compact form (envelopment form) assuming constant returns to scale (CRS) in the output-oriented case, i.e.
\[
\begin{gathered}\max_{\phi ,\lambda}\phi \\ -\phi y_{i}+Y\lambda \ge 0,\ x_{i}-X\lambda \ge 0,\ \lambda \ge 0\end{gathered}
\tag{9.4}
\]
or, for each of the \(J\) units with \(M\) outputs and \(N\) inputs,
\[
\begin{gathered}1/efficiency_{i}=\max \phi_{i} \\ \sum_{j=1}^{J} \lambda_{j}y_{mj}-\phi_{i}y_{mi}\ge 0,\quad m=1,...,M \\ x_{ni}-\sum_{j=1}^{J} \lambda_{j}x_{nj}\ge 0,\quad n=1,...,N \\ \lambda_{j}\ge 0,\quad j=1,...,J\end{gathered}
\tag{9.5}
\]
where \(\lambda\) is a \((J\times 1)\) vector of non-negative weights and \(1\le \phi <\infty\). In this formulation the efficiency scores range from a minimum of 1, full efficiency, to a value that is larger the greater the inefficiency. Consequently, to obtain the usual range between 0 (minimum efficiency) and 1 (maximum efficiency), the reciprocal of the scores, \(1/\phi\), is used.
In the input-oriented case, instead, we have
\[
\begin{gathered}\min_{\theta ,\lambda}\theta \\ -y_{i}+Y\lambda \ge 0,\ \theta x_{i}-X\lambda \ge 0,\ \lambda \ge 0\end{gathered}
\tag{9.6}
\]
or
\[
\begin{gathered}efficiency_{i}=\min \theta_{i} \\ \sum_{j=1}^{J} \lambda_{j}y_{mj}-y_{mi}\ge 0,\quad m=1,...,M \\ \theta_{i}x_{ni}-\sum_{j=1}^{J} \lambda_{j}x_{nj}\ge 0,\quad n=1,...,N \\ \lambda_{j}\ge 0,\quad j=1,...,J\end{gathered}
\tag{9.7}
\]
where \(0\le \theta \le 1\).
To obtain efficiency scores under variable returns to scale (VRS) the following constraint must be added
\[
1'\lambda =1
\tag{9.8}
\]
where \(1\) is a vector of ones with \(J\) rows. If instead the additional constraint is
\[
1'\lambda \le 1
\tag{9.9}
\]
the scores are obtained under non-increasing returns to scale (NIRS); if the NIRS scores coincide with the VRS ones, decreasing returns to scale (DRS) are at work, while if they do not coincide but the CRS and VRS scores differ, increasing returns to scale (IRS) are at work.
If the technical efficiency score differs under constant returns to scale (CRS) and variable returns to scale (VRS), scale inefficiency is at work, which can be measured by the simple ratio of the efficiency scores obtained under the two assumptions; it is worth noting that, under constant returns to scale, the orientation does not affect the efficiency score.
Finally, we should mention that only the basic approach is presented here, but the family of DEA models is vast and today there is a very wide range of models and formulations, depending on the various working assumptions, such as the existence of slacks, discrete inputs and outputs, stochastic components, etc. We will not dwell further on this.
For an example we use the data in the file esdea.csv, on 2 outputs and 2 inputs of 10 firms

RPythonSAS



esdea <- read.csv2("data/esdea.csv")
attach(esdea)
X <- cbind(input1,input2)
Y <- cbind(output1,output2)
n <- dim(X)[1]
s <- dim(Y)[2]
m <- dim(X)[2]




esdea = pd.read_csv("data/esdea.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
X = esdea[["input1", "input2"]].to_numpy()
Y = esdea[["output1", "output2"]].to_numpy()
n, m = X.shape
s = Y.shape[1]



data esdea;
  infile "data/esdea.csv" dlm=";" firstobs=2;
  input aziende (output1 output2 input1 input2) (:commax12.);
run;



Solving the linear-programming problems in formulas (9.5) and (9.7) requires operations-research routines that are beyond the scope of this text. We therefore need to load a specific external package, since direct computation would require advanced knowledge; here we use lpSolve, distributed under the GNU licence and available on CRAN. In Python we use SciPy’s linprog function, in SAS the PROC OPTMODEL procedure (SAS/OR)

RPythonSAS



# this is the only external package used
# in the whole book (install.packages("lpSolve"))
library(lpSolve)




from scipy.optimize import linprog

def dea(X, Y, rts="crs", orient="io"):
    """DEA scores (between 0 and 1) for crs, vrs or nirs returns
    and input ("io") or output ("oo") orientation."""
    n, m = X.shape
    s = Y.shape[1]
    eff = np.zeros(n)
    for i in range(n):
        # variables: [theta (or phi), lambda_1, ..., lambda_n]
        if orient == "io":                       # min theta
            c = np.r_[1.0, np.zeros(n)]
            A = np.vstack([np.c_[np.zeros(s), -Y.T],     # Y'lambda >= y_i
                           np.c_[-X[i], X.T]])           # X'lambda <= theta x_i
            b = np.r_[-Y[i], np.zeros(m)]
        else:                                    # max phi
            c = np.r_[-1.0, np.zeros(n)]
            A = np.vstack([np.c_[Y[i], -Y.T],            # Y'lambda >= phi y_i
                           np.c_[np.zeros(m), X.T]])     # X'lambda <= x_i
            b = np.r_[np.zeros(s), X[i]]
        ones = np.r_[0.0, np.ones(n)][None, :]
        A_eq = b_eq = None
        if rts == "vrs":
            A_eq, b_eq = ones, [1.0]
        elif rts == "nirs":
            A, b = np.vstack([A, ones]), np.r_[b, 1.0]
        sol = linprog(c, A_ub=A, b_ub=b, A_eq=A_eq, b_eq=b_eq,
                      bounds=[(0, None)] * (n + 1), method="highs")
        eff[i] = sol.x[0] if orient == "io" else 1 / sol.x[0]
    return eff



/* macro solving problems (9.5) and (9.7) for all units with PROC OPTMODEL */
%macro dea(rts=crs, orient=io, out=);
  %if &orient = io %then %let val = e.sol; %else %let val = 1/e.sol;
  proc optmodel printlevel=0;
    set <num> DMU;
    set <str> INP  = {'input1', 'input2'};
    set <str> OUTP = {'output1', 'output2'};
    num x{DMU, INP};
    num y{DMU, OUTP};
    read data esdea into DMU=[aziende]
         {i in INP} <x[aziende,i]=col(i)> {o in OUTP} <y[aziende,o]=col(o)>;
    num k;                            /* unit being evaluated */
    var e >= 0;                       /* theta (input) or phi (output) */
    var lambda{DMU} >= 0;
    %if &orient = io %then %do;
      min obj = e;
      con c_inp{i in INP}:  sum{j in DMU} lambda[j]*x[j,i] <= e*x[k,i];
      con c_out{o in OUTP}: sum{j in DMU} lambda[j]*y[j,o] >= y[k,o];
    %end;
    %else %do;
      max obj = e;
      con c_inp{i in INP}:  sum{j in DMU} lambda[j]*x[j,i] <= x[k,i];
      con c_out{o in OUTP}: sum{j in DMU} lambda[j]*y[j,o] >= e*y[k,o];
    %end;
    %if &rts = vrs  %then %do; con c_rts: sum{j in DMU} lambda[j] =  1; %end;
    %if &rts = nirs %then %do; con c_rts: sum{j in DMU} lambda[j] <= 1; %end;
    num eff{DMU};
    for {kk in DMU} do;
      k = kk;
      solve with lp / logfreq=0;
      eff[kk] = &val;
    end;
    create data &out from [aziende] &out=eff;
  quit;
%mend dea;

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
In earlier sections we have repeatedly used the regression model for trend analysis or for extrapolation for forecasting purposes. The extensive use we make of linear models, not only for time series, calls for a dedicated treatment: on the one hand, to address the questions left unanswered so far and, on the other, to present in a unified and general way the important issue of model specification and of the interpretation of the corresponding estimates.
The file abitazioni.csv contains the sale prices (prezzo), lot size (dimensione), number of bedrooms (letto), number of bathrooms (bagno) and number of storage rooms (ripostiglio) of 546 houses. Assuming the model \(Y_{i}=\alpha +\beta X_{i}+\varepsilon_{i}\) for \(i=1,...,n\), OLS estimation with the lm() function gives the following results.

RPythonSAS



abit <- read.csv2("data/abitazioni.csv")
attach(abit)
modrg <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+letto+bagno+ripostiglio)
summary(modrg)


Call:
lm(formula = prezzo ~ dimensione + letto + bagno + ripostiglio)

from scipy import stats

modrg = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto + bagno + ripostiglio", data=abit).fit()
print(modrg.summary())

proc import datafile="data/abitazioni.csv" out=abit dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;

  modrg: model prezzo = dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio;

The estimates show that all the variables are significant except the intercept, which in any case takes an implausible negative value. The other estimates are positive, indicating that an increase in the \(X\) leads to an increase in the house price \(Y\). In particular, if lot size is measured in square metres and price in dollars, we can say that, other things being equal (that is, holding the other explanatory variables fixed), a 1 m² increase in lot size corresponds to an increase in house price of about $5.43. Likewise, with the other explanatory variables held fixed, an extra bedroom raises the house price by $2,825 on average, although the explanatory power of this variable appears less important than that of lot size (its p-value is higher); similar considerations apply to the other estimates. The p-value can be read as the lowest significance level at which the null hypothesis is rejected, which here is the hypothesis that the individual coefficient is zero. In other words, it is very unlikely that lot size has no influence on the prices in our sample and that what we observe is due to chance alone (the p-value is 0.000), whereas the same statement is riskier for the number of bedrooms (the p-value is 0.020).
The residual standard error shown in the output is
\[
rse\equiv s=\left(\sum (Y-\hat{Y})^{2}/df\right)^{1/2}
\tag{5.1}
\]
that is, explicitly or more concisely

RPythonSAS



y <- prezzo; ym <- mean(y)
yc <- modrg$fitted
n <- length(y)
u2 <- (y-yc)^2
dof <- n-5
rse <- (sum(u2)/dof)^(0.5); rse

[1] 18265.23

sqrt(deviance(modrg)/df.residual(modrg))

[1] 18265.23





y = abit["prezzo"]; ym = y.mean()
yc = modrg.fittedvalues
n = len(y)
dof = n - 5
rse = np.sqrt(((y - yc) ** 2).sum() / dof)
print(rse, np.sqrt(modrg.mse_resid))

18265.22711647008 18265.22711647008




/* "Root MSE" in the PROC REG output is the residual standard error */
proc reg data=abit outest=est_rg noprint;
  model prezzo = dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio / rsquare adjrsq;
run;
quit;
proc print data=est_rg noobs; var _RMSE_ _RSQ_ _ADJRSQ_; run;



Computing the coefficient of determination
\[
R^{2}=rgss/tss
\tag{5.2}
\]
is quite straightforward, where
\[
rgss=\sum (\hat{Y}-\bar{Y})^{2} \quad , \quad tss=\sum (Y-\bar{Y})^{2}
\tag{5.3}
\]
and \(tss=rgss+ssr\), with \(ssr=\sum (Y-\hat{Y})^{2}\).

RPythonSAS



rgss <- sum((yc-ym)^2)
tss <- sum((y-ym)^2)
Rqu <- rgss/tss
Rqu

[1] 0.5355473





rgss = ((yc - ym) ** 2).sum()
tss = ((y - ym) ** 2).sum()
Rqu = rgss / tss
print(Rqu, modrg.rsquared)

0.5355472817735653 0.5355472817735651




/* the sums of squares are in the "Analysis of Variance" table of PROC REG:
   Model = rgss, Error = ssr, Corrected Total = tss */



\(R^{2}\) measures the share of the total variance of \(Y\) that can be explained by \(X\) through the linear model; high values indicate a good fit of the model to the observed data.
When using a multiple regression model, however, the coefficient of determination should be adjusted to take into account the number of explanatory variables. Indeed, \(R^{2}\) tends to increase simply because variables are added, so the adjustment becomes necessary when comparing linear models with different numbers of explanatory variables. The adjusted \(R^{2}\) is
\[
R_{c}^{2}=1-[(1-R^{2})(n-1)/df]
\tag{5.4}
\]
The \(F\) statistic, by contrast, tests the significance of the regression as a whole, with null hypothesis \(\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=\beta_{4}=0\); it can also be computed from the relationship between \(F\) and \(R^{2}\).

RPythonSAS



Rqa <- 1-((1-Rqu)*(n-1)/dof)
Rqa

[1] 0.5321133

mrss <- rgss/4
ssr <- tss-rgss
mssr <- ssr/dof
F <- mrss/mssr
F

[1] 155.9529

Fcrit <- qf(0.05, 4, 541, lower.tail=FALSE)
Fcrit

[1] 2.38841

(Rqu/4)/((1-Rqu)/dof)

[1] 155.9529





Rqa = 1 - (1 - Rqu) * (n - 1) / dof
F = (rgss / 4) / ((tss - rgss) / dof)
Fcrit = stats.f.ppf(0.95, 4, 541)
print(Rqa, F, Fcrit, (Rqu / 4) / ((1 - Rqu) / dof))

0.5321132505851998 155.95294637625852 2.3884101059647223 155.95294637625855




data _null_;
  Fcrit = finv(0.95, 4, 541);   /* critical value of F */
  put Fcrit=;
run;



As the p-values show, both the \(F\) statistic and the \(\beta\) estimates are significant, which implies observed test statistics inside the rejection regions of the null hypothesis.
Given the relationship between \(F\) and \(R^{2}\), we can also find a critical value for the coefficient of determination under the null hypothesis that \(R^{2}\) equals 0
\[
R_{t}^{2}=((k-1)F_{t})/((k-1)F_{t}+(n-k))
\tag{5.5}
\]
where \(k\) is the number of parameters of the model, \(n\) the number of observations and \(F_{t}\) the critical value of the \(F\) statistic.

RPythonSAS



RqCr <- ((5-1)*Fcrit)/((5-1)*Fcrit+(546-5)); RqCr

[1] 0.01735279





print(((5 - 1) * Fcrit) / ((5 - 1) * Fcrit + (546 - 5)))

0.017352787671159085




data _null_;
  Ft = finv(0.95, 4, 541);
  RqCr = ((5-1)*Ft) / ((5-1)*Ft + (546-5));
  put RqCr=;
run;



The coefficient of determination is beyond the critical value; so, at 95% confidence, the null hypothesis \(R^{2}=0\) is rejected.

The estimates show that all the variables are significant except the intercept, which in any case takes an implausible negative value. The other estimates are positive, indicating that an increase in the \(X\) leads to an increase in the house price \(Y\). In particular, if lot size is measured in square metres and price in dollars, we can say that, other things being equal (that is, holding the other explanatory variables fixed), a 1 m² increase in lot size corresponds to an increase in house price of about $5.43. Likewise, with the other explanatory variables held fixed, an extra bedroom raises the house price by $2,825 on average, although the explanatory power of this variable appears less important than that of lot size (its p-value is higher); similar considerations apply to the other estimates. The p-value can be read as the lowest significance level at which the null hypothesis is rejected, which here is the hypothesis that the individual coefficient is zero. In other words, it is very unlikely that lot size has no influence on the prices in our sample and that what we observe is due to chance alone (the p-value is 0.000), whereas the same statement is riskier for the number of bedrooms (the p-value is 0.020).
The residual standard error shown in the output is
\[
rse\equiv s=\left(\sum (Y-\hat{Y})^{2}/df\right)^{1/2}
\tag{5.1}
\]
that is, explicitly or more concisely

y <- prezzo; ym <- mean(y)
yc <- modrg$fitted
n <- length(y)
u2 <- (y-yc)^2
dof <- n-5
rse <- (sum(u2)/dof)^(0.5); rse

  model prezzo = dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio / rsquare adjrsq;
run;
quit;
proc print data=est_rg noobs; var _RMSE_ _RSQ_ _ADJRSQ_; run;



Computing the coefficient of determination
\[
R^{2}=rgss/tss
\tag{5.2}
\]
is quite straightforward, where
\[
rgss=\sum (\hat{Y}-\bar{Y})^{2} \quad , \quad tss=\sum (Y-\bar{Y})^{2}
\tag{5.3}
\]
and \(tss=rgss+ssr\), with \(ssr=\sum (Y-\hat{Y})^{2}\).

RPythonSAS



rgss <- sum((yc-ym)^2)
tss <- sum((y-ym)^2)
Rqu <- rgss/tss
Rqu

[1] 0.5355473





rgss = ((yc - ym) ** 2).sum()
tss = ((y - ym) ** 2).sum()
Rqu = rgss / tss
print(Rqu, modrg.rsquared)

0.5355472817735653 0.5355472817735651




/* the sums of squares are in the "Analysis of Variance" table of PROC REG:
   Model = rgss, Error = ssr, Corrected Total = tss */



\(R^{2}\) measures the share of the total variance of \(Y\) that can be explained by \(X\) through the linear model; high values indicate a good fit of the model to the observed data.
When using a multiple regression model, however, the coefficient of determination should be adjusted to take into account the number of explanatory variables. Indeed, \(R^{2}\) tends to increase simply because variables are added, so the adjustment becomes necessary when comparing linear models with different numbers of explanatory variables. The adjusted \(R^{2}\) is
\[
R_{c}^{2}=1-[(1-R^{2})(n-1)/df]
\tag{5.4}
\]
The \(F\) statistic, by contrast, tests the significance of the regression as a whole, with null hypothesis \(\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta_{3}=\beta_{4}=0\); it can also be computed from the relationship between \(F\) and \(R^{2}\).

RPythonSAS



Rqa <- 1-((1-Rqu)*(n-1)/dof)
Rqa

[1] 0.5321133

mrss <- rgss/4
ssr <- tss-rgss
mssr <- ssr/dof
F <- mrss/mssr
F

[1] 155.9529

Fcrit <- qf(0.05, 4, 541, lower.tail=FALSE)
Fcrit

[1] 2.38841

(Rqu/4)/((1-Rqu)/dof)

[1] 155.9529





Rqa = 1 - (1 - Rqu) * (n - 1) / dof
F = (rgss / 4) / ((tss - rgss) / dof)
Fcrit = stats.f.ppf(0.95, 4, 541)
print(Rqa, F, Fcrit, (Rqu / 4) / ((1 - Rqu) / dof))

0.5321132505851998 155.95294637625852 2.3884101059647223 155.95294637625855




data _null_;
  Fcrit = finv(0.95, 4, 541);   /* critical value of F */
  put Fcrit=;
run;



As the p-values show, both the \(F\) statistic and the \(\beta\) estimates are significant, which implies observed test statistics inside the rejection regions of the null hypothesis.
Given the relationship between \(F\) and \(R^{2}\), we can also find a critical value for the coefficient of determination under the null hypothesis that \(R^{2}\) equals 0
\[
R_{t}^{2}=((k-1)F_{t})/((k-1)F_{t}+(n-k))
\tag{5.5}
\]
where \(k\) is the number of parameters of the model, \(n\) the number of observations and \(F_{t}\) the critical value of the \(F\) statistic.

RPythonSAS



RqCr <- ((5-1)*Fcrit)/((5-1)*Fcrit+(546-5)); RqCr

[1] 0.01735279





print(((5 - 1) * Fcrit) / ((5 - 1) * Fcrit + (546 - 5)))

0.017352787671159085




data _null_;
  Ft = finv(0.95, 4, 541);
  RqCr = ((5-1)*Ft) / ((5-1)*Ft + (546-5));
  put RqCr=;
run;



The coefficient of determination is beyond the critical value; so, at 95% confidence, the null hypothesis \(R^{2}=0\) is rejected.

5.2 Estimates and confidence intervals in matrix form
As with summary(), we could compute the estimated coefficients with their standard errors, Student’s t statistics and p-values “by hand”, with the following commands; the 95% confidence interval can be obtained in the same way.

xx <- cbind(intercetta, dimensione, letto, bagno, ripostiglio)

tstu <- stime/sec

proc iml;
  use abit;
  read all var {dimensione letto bagno ripostiglio} into X0;
  read all var {prezzo} into y;
  close abit;
  n = nrow(X0);  X = j(n,1,1) || X0;
  xtx = inv(X`*X);
  stime = xtx*X`*y;
  dof = n - ncol(X);
  rse = sqrt(ssq(y - X*stime)/dof);
  sec = sqrt(vecdiag(xtx))*rse;
  tstu = stime/sec;
  pvalue = 2*cdf("T", -abs(tstu), dof);
  tdx = quantile("T", 0.975, dof);
  matrice = stime || sec || tstu || pvalue || (stime - tdx*sec) || (stime + tdx*sec);
  print matrice[colname={"stime" "errori" "test-t" "p-value" "inferiore" "superiore"}
                rowname={"intercetta" "dimensione" "letto" "bagno" "ripostiglio"} format=12.3];
quit;

In fact the explanatory power of the model has fallen, because we have excluded variables that are significant both economically and (especially, in this case) statistically (although the two aspects are related); the adjusted coefficient of determination \(R_{c}^{2}\) shows the deterioration of the model, from 0.5321 to 0.1327. Such a high marginal effect ($13,270) compared with the full model ($2,825) precisely reflects the omission of important variables; the mistake would be to read the $13,270 as an effect due entirely to the extra bedroom, when an additional bedroom is typical of larger houses, sometimes with more outdoor space, more bathrooms, more storage rooms, etc. Indeed, if dati is the data frame containing the variables, the correlations among them reveal a positive interdependence.

Omitting relevant explanatory variables biases the estimator \(\beta\), and the bias is stronger the closer the relationship between the included and the excluded explanatory variables, since the omitted variables act through their correlation with those included in the model. The solution, however, is not to add as many variables as possible: there is a trade-off between adding variables and complicating the model, with the resulting difficulties of interpretation and sometimes of estimation. Rather, the effort should be to add the variables that the economic literature and the analyst’s experience indicate as most important, without losing sight of the advantages of a parsimonious model and accepting the risk of leaving out some important variable anyway; some will slip through regardless, if not through the analyst’s error then perhaps because the statistical information is unavailable.
We estimate a new model including only the first two explanatory variables, lot size and number of bedrooms. Lot size is clearly an important variable; through the direct relationship between the two explanatory variables we check the error we would make by excluding dimensione.

The opposite risk to excluding important variables is including statistically irrelevant ones. An irrelevant variable in the model generally has a low, but rarely zero, correlation with the other included explanatory variables; however low, this correlation affects the variance of the estimators: it can be shown that including an irrelevant variable does not bias the estimators of the other explanatory variables but increases their variance, and therefore reduces the precision of the estimates.

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.4 Multicollinearity
Obviously, everything is correlated with everything. But when the correlation among explanatory variables is too high, the statistical problem of multicollinearity may arise. With multicollinearity the model cannot properly attribute statistical weight to the individual explanatory variables and, in extreme cases, it signals a strong dependence of \(Y\) on the \(X\), with a high \(F\) statistic and a high \(R^{2}\), but no statistical significance for the individual explanatory variables; that is, the empirical values of the \(t\) statistics are low and fall in the acceptance region of the null hypothesis: an obvious contradiction.
With strong collinearity, a first simple step is to drop the explanatory variables that create statistical redundancy. But what if the variables are indicated by economic theory and their exclusion is justified statistically but not economically? In these cases, which are in fact the majority, the solution is not simple. One could transform the variables, try replacing them with different indicators or combine them into a new variable to replace those causing redundancy, but here too one risks stripping the model of economic meaning.
Let us build two artificial variables with strong collinearity. The dependent variable prezzo is correlated with both, and we might find it reasonable to estimate a model including them as explanatory variables.

RPythonSAS



var1 <- dimensione
var2 <- log(dimensione)/2
cor(var1, var2)

[1] 0.9642937

cor(prezzo, var1); cor(prezzo, var2)

The model modcor with both explanatory variables cannot attribute to them their proper role in explaining price, precisely because they are strongly correlated: both the estimated coefficient and its statistical significance are distorted.
A quick way to see whether the correlation among the explanatory variables is dangerously high is the statistic
\[
VIF_{j}=1/(1-R_{j}^{2})
\tag{5.6}
\]
where \(R_{j}^{2}\) is the coefficient of determination of the model in which the \(j\)-th explanatory variable is regressed on the others. The VIF follows an empirical rule whereby, if \(VIF_{j}>10\) (corresponding to an \(R^{2}\) above 0.90), \(X_{j}\) is considered highly correlated with the remaining explanatory variables. Since the VIF ranges from 1 (no collinearity) to infinity, its reciprocal is sometimes preferred
\[
TOL=1/VIF
\tag{5.7}
\]
known as tolerance; it ranges from 0 (greatest collinearity) to 1 (least collinearity). For our example

RPythonSAS



r <- cor(var1, var2)
vif <- 1/(1-(r^2)); tol <- 1/vif; vif; tol

[1] 14.25766


[1] 0.07013772





from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

Xv = sm.add_constant(abit[["var1", "var2"]])
vif = variance_inflation_factor(Xv.to_numpy(), 1)
print(vif, 1 / vif)

14.257662572989203 0.07013772382960415




/* VIF and TOL are already in the PROC REG output with the options / vif tol (see above) */



which signals a strong risk of multicollinearity.
Note, however, that time-series data tend to be correlated more easily than cross-section data; we will return to this later, but it should be stressed straight away that strong correlation is not always a bad thing. For example, the autoregressive model introduced in the previous chapter, like the distributed-lag model, often shows symptoms of multicollinearity. Nevertheless, strong correlation among the explanatory variables (within certain limits) is not a problem if we are not specifically interested in the coefficient estimates but are looking for a model that fits the data reasonably well and provides a satisfactory short-term forecast.

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.5 Centred and standardised variables
It may sometimes be useful to estimate the coefficients after subtracting the means from the variables or after standardising them. We again use the data in abitazioni.csv, taking house price, lot size and number of bedrooms.

RPythonSAS



nor <- lm(prezzo~dimensione+letto)
pre <- prezzo-mean(prezzo)
dim <- dimensione-mean(dimensione)
let <- letto-mean(letto); med <- lm(pre~dim+let)
pss <- pre/sd(prezzo); dss <- dim/sd(dimensione)
lss <- let/sd(letto); sta <- lm(pss~dss+lss)
round(summary(nor)$coeff,3); round(summary(med)$coeff,3); round(summary(sta)$coeff,3)

nor = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto", data=v).fit()
med = smf.ols("prezzo ~ dimensione + letto", data=v - v.mean()).fit()

{'Intercept': 5612.6, 'dimensione': 6.053, 'letto': 10567.352}

{'Intercept': -0.0, 'dimensione': 0.491, 'letto': 0.292}




/* the stb option of PROC REG gives the standardised ("beta") estimates directly */
proc reg data=abit;
  model prezzo = dimensione letto / stb;
run;
quit;



Three sets of estimates are reported. The first comes from the standard model and the second from the variables transformed by subtracting their means: note that in the second set the intercept becomes zero while the \(\beta\) do not change at all. In the third set the intercept is again zero, but standardising the variables gives “beta” estimates of the coefficients, which do not depend on the units of the original variables. So, if we wanted to compare the importance of the explanatory variables in influencing house prices, the second set of estimates would be misleading, because the corresponding \(X\) are measured in different units; by contrast, since the variables in the third set are standardised, we can say that a one-standard-unit change in dss causes a reaction in standardised prices about 68% larger than lss (0.491/0.292=1.68).

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.6 Dummy variables in regression
We introduced dummy variables for classical time series when specifying the seasonal component. We now generalise the use of these special variables in multiple regression models.
The file case.csv contains further information on our 546 houses; besides the price, there are now 5 dummy variables taking the value 0 or 1 for the absence or presence of: a driveway (accesso), a games room (giochi), a cellar (cantina), gas heating (gas) and air conditioning (clima). We assume that the presence or absence of these features may influence house prices. For simplicity, we focus on the OLS estimates of the model with only the first two dummies as regressors.

RPythonSAS



case <- read.csv2("data/case.csv")
attach(case)
dum <- lm(prezzo~accesso+giochi)
dum$coeff[1]+dum$coeff[2]*0+dum$coeff[3]*0

(Intercept) 
   84282.67 





case = pd.read_csv("data/case.csv", sep=";")
dum = smf.ols("prezzo ~ accesso + giochi", data=case).fit()
combinazioni = pd.DataFrame({"accesso": [0, 1, 0, 1], "giochi": [0, 0, 1, 1]})
print(dum.predict(combinazioni).round(2).to_numpy())

[47099.08 68258.99 63122.77 84282.67]




proc import datafile="data/case.csv" out=case dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc glm data=case;
  model prezzo = accesso giochi / solution;
  estimate "no driveway, no games room" intercept 1;
  estimate "driveway only"           intercept 1 accesso 1;
  estimate "games room only"            intercept 1 giochi 1;
  estimate "both"               intercept 1 accesso 1 giochi 1;
run;
quit;



The first result is the average price of houses with neither a driveway nor a games room ($47,099), the second that of houses with a driveway only ($68,258), the third that of houses with a games room only ($63,122) and, finally, the fourth that of houses with both ($84,282). Note straight away that the choice of coding 0 rather than 1 is arbitrary: 0 is logically used for absence and 1 for presence of the feature, but we could swap them without changing anything for interpretation.
Dummy variables make several specifications possible; for example (for ease of notation without subscripts and random error term):

as in the previous case, with effects on the intercept only: \(Y=\alpha +cX+\beta D\)
with effects only on the strength of the relationship between \(Y\) and \(X\): \(Y=\alpha +cX+\beta XD\)
with effects on both the intercept and the slope: \(Y=\alpha +cX+\beta D+\gamma XD\)

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
section: 5.7 Parameter restrictions and the F test
text:
5.7 Parameter restrictions and the F test
The \(F\) test is particularly useful for assessing specific restrictions on the parameters. Suppose we want to check whether the coefficients of dimensione and dimcli can be considered different only by chance. Then \(Y=\alpha +\beta_{1}X_{1}+\beta_{2}X_{2}+e\) is the extended model, while \(Y=\alpha +\beta_{1}(X_{1}+X_{2})+e\) is the restricted model to be tested (now there is a single \(\beta\)). Since
\[
\begin{gathered}F=((rsum-usum)/m)/(usum/(n-k))\equiv \\ \equiv ((r_{u}^{2}-r_{r}^{2})/m)/((1-r_{u}^{2})/(n-k))\end{gathered}
\tag{5.8}
\]
where \(rsum\) is the residual sum of squares of the restricted model and \(usum\) that of the unrestricted (or extended) model, with \(m\) the number of restrictions and \(k\) the number of parameters of the extended model, we have

RPythonSAS



n <- nrow(case)
riduz <- dimensione+dimcli
modris <- lm(prezzo~riduz)
round(summary(modris)$coeff, 4)

              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 40409.5835  1689.4359 23.9190        0
riduz           3.9557     0.2056 19.2356        0

usum <- anova(modnid)$Sum[3]
rsum <- anova(modris)$Sum[2]
Frestr <- ((rsum-usum)/1)/(usum/(n-3))
Frestr

[1] 3.912474

smodnid <- summary(modnid)
smodris <- summary(modris)
ru <- smodnid$r.square
rr <- smodris$r.square
((ru-rr)/1)/((1-ru)/(n-3))

[1] 3.912474





n = len(case)
case["riduz"] = case["dimensione"] + case["dimcli"]
modris = smf.ols("prezzo ~ riduz", data=case).fit()

riduz            3.955682

/* equivalent: the TEST statement shown above */



The \(F\) test is also useful for testing the structural stability of the coefficients of a model estimated over two different time periods, in two different areas or on two different groups of cases (for example, less and more affluent consumers). This particular test statistic is known as the Chow test
\[
\begin{gathered}F_{Chow}=\left((rsum-(usum_{a}+usum_{b}))/k\right)/ \\ \left((usum_{a}+usum_{b})/(n_{a}+n_{b}-2k)\right)\sim F_{k,(n_{a}+n_{b}-2k)}\end{gathered}
\tag{5.9}
\]
where \(k\) is the number of parameters, \(rsum\) is the residual sum of squares of the restricted model with structural stability (a single model for all observations), while \(usum_{a}\) and \(usum_{b}\) are the corresponding sums for the unrestricted models, estimated separately for the two groups (\(a\) and \(b\)) of observations.

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
section: 5.8 The Chow test and structural stability
text:
5.8 The Chow test and structural stability
We load the data in redditousa.csv on US saving (risparmio) and disposable income (reddito) from 1970 to 1995. We want to check whether a structural break in the linear saving function occurred between 1981 and 1982. We estimate a first model for 1970-1981, a second for 1982-1995 and a third for the whole period 1970-1995.

RPythonSAS



usa <- read.csv2("data/redditousa.csv")
attach(usa)
t(anno)

[1,]  1984  1985  1986  1987  1988  1989  1990  1991  1992  1993  1994  1995

ant <- summary(ante); pos <- summary(post)
tut <- summary(tutto)

proc autoreg data=usa;
  model risparmio = reddito / chow=(13);
run;



So the null hypothesis of structural stability of the coefficients over the whole period 1970-1995 is rejected.
Note that the Chow test requires the error variance to be the same in the two models. Let us check whether this is the case.

RPythonSAS

Fvar

proc reg data=usa outest=s_post noprint; where anno >= 1982; model risparmio = reddito; run;
quit;
data _null_;
  merge s_ante(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s_a)) s_post(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s_p));
  Fvar = s_p**2 / s_a**2;
  p = 1 - probf(Fvar, 12, 10);
  put Fvar= p=;
run;

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.9 Dummies and models without intercept
This also allows a further remark on the use of dummy variables. Suppose we are interested only in the level of saving, and hence in the effect of the historical period on it, regardless of income. Consistently with what we have seen, we should introduce a single dummy, equal for example to 0 between 1970 and 1981 and 1 between 1982 and 1995; we cannot introduce two dummies, as that would cause perfect multicollinearity. In fact we can get around this problem by not including the intercept.

RPythonSAS



d1 <- rep(NA,26); d2 <- rep(NA,26)
d1[1:12] <- 0; d1[13:26] <- 1
d2[1:12] <- 1; d2[13:26] <- 0
modd <- lm(risparmio~d1+d2)
summary(modd)$coeff

            Estimate Std. Error   t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 106.4417   10.35161 10.282615 2.844306e-10
d1          103.3440   14.10687  7.325794 1.445638e-07

5.10 Residual diagnostics
Let us go back to the model modum and use plot() to obtain some diagnostics (Figure 5.1). The first par() instruction tells R to arrange the plots in two columns and two rows within a single graphics device; the second par() restores the default layout, while plot() draws the four basic diagnostic plots.

Figure 5.1 – Diagnostic plots of the model modum

ax[1, 1].set_title("Residuals vs Leverage")

plt.show()




Figure 5.1 – Diagnostic plots of the model modum






/* PROC REG produces the diagnostic panel automatically (ODS Graphics) */
ods graphics on;
proc reg data=usa plots=diagnostics;
  model risparmio = reddito d1 d1x;
run;
quit;



The four plots of Figure 5.1 are easy to interpret, with evidence of anomalies in cases 15, 23, 25 and, partly, 12. Recall that the standardised residual is \(r_{i}=\hat{\varepsilon}_{i}/(\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1-h_{ii}})\), where the \(h_{ii}\) (leverage of the \(i\)-th observation) are the elements on the main diagonal of the matrix \(H=X(X'X)^{-1}X'\). The Jarque-Bera test of normality of the residuals is also useful here
\[
JB=n(S^{2}/6+(K-3)^{2}/24)
\tag{5.10}
\]
with \(S\) a measure of skewness (0 for the Normal) and \(K\) a measure of kurtosis (3 for the Normal). The JB statistic is asymptotically distributed as \(\chi_{(2)}^{2}\). Hence,

RPythonSAS

m4 <- mean((ee-mean(ee))^4); K <- m4/(sd(ee)^4)

JB = 26 * (S ** 2 / 6 + (K - 3) ** 2 / 24)

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.11 Functional form: the MWD test
A typical issue in model specification is the choice of functional form. In most cases the alternative is between a linear and a log-linear form, and generally economic theory itself or the analyst’s specific interests lead to one or the other. In some cases the MacKinnon, White and Davidson (MWD) test helps guide the choice.
We load the data in rose.csv on quintals of roses sold, the price of the main variety (prvar1) and the price of a substitute flower, the carnation (prvar2). We estimate the linear and the log-linear model, adding the variables z1 and z2 as specified below.

RPythonSAS



rosedf <- read.csv2("data/rose.csv")
attach(rosedf)
mo1 <- lm(rose~prvar1+prvar2)
mo2 <- lm(log(rose)~log(prvar1)+log(prvar2))
z1 <- log(fitted(mo1))-fitted(mo2)
z2 <- exp(fitted(mo2))-fitted(mo1)
mod1e <- lm(rose~prvar1+prvar2+z1)
mod2e <- lm(log(rose)~log(prvar1)+log(prvar2)+z2)
round(summary(mod1e)$coeff,3); round(summary(mod2e)$coeff,3)

5.12 The likelihood-ratio test
To check whether an explanatory variable can be dropped from the model without significantly worsening it, the likelihood-ratio test can also be used. We take the linear model mo1, re-estimate it without prvar2 (mo3) and extract the value of the log-likelihood function, which we compare using an (asymptotic) approximation to a \(\chi^{2}\) with 1 degree of freedom (there is 1 restriction).

RPythonSAS



ll1 <- logLik(mo1)
mo3 <- lm(rose~prvar1)
ll3 <- logLik(mo3)
ll1; ll3

'log Lik.' -132.3601 (df=4)


'log Lik.' -136.5061 (df=3)

lambda

[1] 0.003982102

lam = 2 * (mo1.llf - mo3.llf)
print(mo1.llf, mo3.llf, lam, stats.chi2.sf(lam, 1))

-132.36008243110132 -136.50606171002818 8.291958557853718 0.0039821017249386725




/* PROC MIXED (maximum likelihood) reports -2 log-likelihood */
proc mixed data=rosedf method=ml;
  model rose = prvar1 prvar2 / solution;

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.13 Heteroscedasticity
When estimating linear models, a condition that is often not met is homoscedasticity, that is, the assumption of constant variance. The error variance may not be constant for various reasons, for example because of an incorrectly specified functional form, the presence of outliers, etc. With heteroscedasticity the estimators are unbiased and consistent but not efficient. One way of dealing with the problem is to use generalised least squares (GLS), weighting, for example, the observations in inverse proportion to the size of the variance (weighted least squares, WLS).
There are several techniques and tests for detecting heteroscedasticity; one of them is the Goldfeld-Quandt test, which assumes that the variance is positively related to a specific explanatory variable.
To run the test we assume a simple model with a single explanatory variable and load the data in consusa.csv on the income (reddito) and consumption (consumo) of 30 US households. We sort the data by the explanatory variable and, dropping \(c\) central observations, estimate one model for the first part of the observations and one for the rest, then compare the residual sums of squares with an \(F_{(n-c-2k)/2,(n-c-2k)/2}\) test.

RPythonSAS



tabella <- read.csv2("data/consusa.csv")
attach(tabella)
tabord <- tabella[order(reddito),]
modet1 <- lm(tabord$consumo[1:13]~tabord$reddito[1:13])
modet2 <- lm(tabord$consumo[(30-13+1):30]~tabord$reddito[(30-13+1):30])
rss1 <- anova(modet1)$Sum[2]
rss2 <- anova(modet2)$Sum[2]
lam <- (rss2/11)/(rss1/11)
lam

[1] 4.074595

qf(0.95, 11, 11)

[1] 2.81793





tabella = pd.read_csv("data/consusa.csv", sep=";")
tabord = tabella.sort_values("reddito").reset_index(drop=True)
modet1 = smf.ols("consumo ~ reddito", data=tabord.iloc[:13]).fit()
modet2 = smf.ols("consumo ~ reddito", data=tabord.iloc[17:]).fit()
lam = (modet2.ssr / 11) / (modet1.ssr / 11)
print(lam, stats.f.ppf(0.95, 11, 11))

4.074594580988356 2.8179304699530854




proc import datafile="data/consusa.csv" out=tabella dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc sort data=tabella out=tabord; by reddito; run;
data tabord; set tabord; oss = _n_; run;
proc reg data=tabord outest=gq1 noprint; where oss <= 13; model consumo = reddito; run;
proc reg data=tabord outest=gq2 noprint; where oss >= 18; model consumo = reddito; run;
quit;
data _null_;
  merge gq1(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s1)) gq2(keep=_RMSE_ rename=(_RMSE_=s2));
  lam = s2**2 / s1**2;    /* same degrees of freedom (11) in the two groups */
  Fcrit = finv(0.95, 11, 11);
  put lam= Fcrit=;
run;



The null hypothesis is rejected, so the data show significant heteroscedasticity.
Many other tests exist in the literature; White’s test is among the most general. It is based on an auxiliary regression of the squared residuals of the model on the regressors, their squares and their cross-products; the test statistic is the coefficient of determination of the auxiliary regression multiplied by the number of observations, and is asymptotically distributed as a \(\chi^{2}\) with degrees of freedom equal to the number of regressors in the auxiliary regression. Hence

RPythonSAS



modwh <- lm(consumo~reddito)
reddito2 <- reddito^2
u2 <- (residuals(modwh))^2
modu2 <- lm(u2~reddito+reddito2)
raux <- summary(modu2)$r.squared
white <- 30*raux
white

[1] 5.330902

pchisq(white, 2, lower.tail=FALSE)

[1] 0.06956796

detach(tabella)




from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import het_white

modwh = smf.ols("consumo ~ reddito", data=tabella).fit()
white, pval, _, _ = het_white(modwh.resid, modwh.model.exog)
print(white, pval)

5.330902406871207 0.06956795714944981




/* the spec option of PROC REG runs White's test */
proc reg data=tabella;
  model consumo = reddito / spec;
run;
quit;



At 95% confidence the null hypothesis of homoscedasticity is accepted (narrowly): note that the conclusions of the last two tests contradict each other. If heteroscedasticity is present, there are reweighting techniques that help reduce its consequences, including the so-called White procedure, run by default by most software; we will not go into this further.

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.14 Autocorrelation of the residuals
Another common violation of the basic assumptions in estimating a model is autocorrelation of the residuals; it appears over time in time series, across space in cross-section data, or both in more complex situations. The last two cases call for a more detailed treatment that is beyond our scope, but we can give some examples of serial autocorrelation.
If the model can be written as \(Y_{t}=\alpha +\beta_{1}X_{1}+\beta_{2}X_{2}+u_{t}\), where \(u_{t}\) is not the classical white noise \(\varepsilon_{t}\) but a disturbance correlated with itself over time, then in the simplest case we can write
\[
u_{t}=\rho u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{t}
\tag{5.11}
\]
which is very reminiscent of a first-order autoregressive model, \(AR(1)\); \(\rho\) is called the first-order autocorrelation coefficient. Of course the dependence of the errors over time could follow a more complex structure with a higher lag, but in most cases the first-order assumption is satisfactory. If we used OLS with serial autocorrelation (as with heteroscedasticity), the estimators would be unbiased and consistent but not efficient.
We load the data in salari.csv on hourly wages (salari) and hourly productivity (produtt) in US industry between 1959 and 1998, and estimate a log-linear model.

RPythonSAS



sal <- read.csv2("data/salari.csv")

modsal <- lm(log(salari)~log(produtt))

\[
d=\sum_{t=2}^{n} (\hat{u}_{t}-\hat{u}_{t-1})^{2}\Big/\sum_{t=1}^{n} \hat{u}_{t}^{2}
\tag{5.12}
\]
It can be shown that, if \(\hat{\rho}\) is the autocorrelation coefficient between \(\hat{u}_{t}\) and \(\hat{u}_{t-1}\),
\[
d\approx 2(1-\hat{\rho})
\tag{5.13}
\]

0.9186959977748962 0.15423059406016035 0.16260800445020762




/* PROC AUTOREG reports Durbin-Watson and its p-value */
proc autoreg data=sal;
  model ls = lp / dw=1 dwprob;
run;



The critical values of the Durbin-Watson test for \(n=40\), \(k=2\) and 95% confidence are \(d_L=1.44\) and \(d_U=1.54\). Since the statistic is below the lower bound, the null hypothesis is rejected in favour of positive autocorrelation. In particular, if

\(0<d<d_{L}\): positive autocorrelation
\(4-d_{L}<d<4\): negative autocorrelation
\(d_{U}<d<4-d_{U}\): no autocorrelation
\(d_{L}\le d\le d_{U}\): inconclusive region
\(4-d_{U}\le d\le 4-d_{L}\): inconclusive region.

Note that the Durbin-Watson statistic is symmetric around \(d=2\). Moreover, its correct application requires strict conditions, including the absence of the lagged dependent variable among the explanatory variables.
Finally, note that in some cases strong autocorrelation, as already pointed out for heteroscedasticity, may result from model misspecification rather than from genuine serial dependence in the data.

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.15 Correcting for autocorrelation
Suppose now that \(\rho\) is known and equal to the correlation between \(\hat{u}_{t}\) and \(\hat{u}_{t-1}\). We estimate a transformed model which, while not eliminating serial autocorrelation entirely, at least reduces it and its consequences for the estimates. The procedure applies OLS to the transformed model, which is equivalent to GLS on the original model \(Y=f(X)+u\), that is, \((Y_{t}-\rho Y_{t-1})=\beta_{0}(1-\rho )+\beta_{1}(X_{t}-\rho X_{t-1})+\varepsilon_{t}\), where by construction \(\varepsilon_{t}=(u_{t}-\rho u_{t-1})\sim WN\).

RPythonSAS



y <- log(salari)
x <- log(produtt)
y1 <- 0; x1 <- 0
y1[2:40] <- y[1:39]
x1[2:40] <- x[1:39]
yy <- (y-rho*y1)
xx <- (x-rho*x1)
yy[1] <- y[1]*((1-rho^2)^0.5)
xx[1] <- x[1]*((1-rho^2)^0.5)
modrh <- lm(yy~xx)
u <- residuals(modrh)
ut0 <- embed(u,2)[,1]
ut1 <- embed(u,2)[,2]
cor(ut0, ut1)

[1] 0.3528248

dw <- (sum((ut0-ut1)^2))/(sum(u^2))
dw

[1] 1.290367

rho <- cor(ut0, ut1)
dd <- 2*(1-rho)
dd

[1] 1.29435





def prais_winsten(y, x, rho):
    """Transform y and x with the given rho, keeping the first observation."""
    yy = np.r_[y[0] * np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2), y[1:] - rho * y[:-1]]
    xx = np.r_[x[0] * np.sqrt(1 - rho ** 2), x[1:] - rho * x[:-1]]
    return yy, xx

y = np.log(sal["salari"].to_numpy()); x = np.log(sal["produtt"].to_numpy())
yy, xx = prais_winsten(y, x, rho)
modrh = sm.OLS(yy, sm.add_constant(xx)).fit()
u = modrh.resid

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.16 Dynamic forecasting
An autoregressive form in the residuals of the model can be exploited for forecasting. By appropriate substitution we have \(Y_{t}=\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}X_{t}+\rho u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{t}\) and therefore
\[
\hat{Y}_{t+1}=\hat{\beta}_{0}+\hat{\beta}_{1}X_{t+1}+\hat{\rho}\hat{u}_{t}
\tag{5.14}
\]
This is an example of dynamic forecasting, since we take into account the errors \(u\) of the previous period. The following commands compare, ex post, the static and dynamic forecasts at time \(t+1\) for the log-linear model of wages on productivity, estimated over 1959-1996, for 1997.

RPythonSAS

modf$coeff[1]+modf$coeff[2]*log(produtt[39])

modf$coeff[1]+modf$coeff[2]*log(produtt[39])+rh*residuals(modf)[38]

(Intercept) 
   4.621213 

log(salari)[39]

[1] 4.61611

5.19 Non-nested models: the J test
So far we have applied tests useful for choosing between two models when one is a special case of the other. If this is not the case, one can use the usual estimation statistics and diagnostics, but also a special encompassing F test, which specifies a new general model combining the two original models and applies the standard \(F\) statistic for nested models. Another frequently used test is the Davidson-MacKinnon \(J\) test, which estimates extended models by adding the fitted values of the dependent variable from the alternative models under analysis; we apply this test to the data in conspro.csv on per capita consumption (cpro) and income (rpro) in the United States between 1970 and 1991, in dollars.

title: 5 Specification of linear economic models
text:
5.20 Information criteria: AIC and SIC
Comparing more complex models, especially when specified quite differently from one another, requires a more reliable statistic; this is the case of the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) and the Schwarz Information Criterion (SIC).
With the usual meaning of the symbols, the first can be defined as
\[
\log AIC=(2k/n)+\log (rss/n)
\tag{5.15}
\]
and suggests choosing the model with the lowest value. For the second criterion we have
\[
\log SIC=(k/n)\log n+\log (rss/n)
\tag{5.16}
\]
and again the preferred model has the lowest value.
Let us work through an example with the previous models modA and modB.

RPythonSAS



rssA <- sum(residuals(modA)^2)
rssB <- sum(residuals(modB)^2)
aicA <- (2*3/21)+log(rssA/21)
aicB <- (2*3/21)+log(rssB/21)
sicA <- (3/21)*log(21)+log(rssA/21)
sicB <- (3/21)*log(21)+log(rssB/21)
aicA; aicB

[1] 10.08096


[1] 9.831612

sicA; sicB

[1] 10.23018


[1] 9.98083





for nome, m in (("A", modA), ("B", modB)):
    aic = 2 * 3 / 21 + np.log(m.ssr / 21)
    sic = 3 / 21 * np.log(21) + np.log(m.ssr / 21)
    print(nome, aic, sic)

A 10.080959791950459 10.230177283053804
B 9.831612187213253 9.980829678316598

   (on a different scale from the text, but ranking the models in the same way) */
proc reg data=fAB;
  modA: model cpro = rpro r1 / aic sbc;
  modB: model cpro = rpro c1 / aic sbc;

On the basis of these two criteria, model modB would be preferred. This is consistent with the slight superiority that emerged earlier; in particular, while the contribution of the added regressor in modAx is highly significant, that in modBx has a confidence only slightly above 95%, indicating limited additional information relative to the original specification of modB.

title: 12 Further applied examples
text:
The territory, with its specific characteristics, plays an essential role in correctly interpreting an aggregate. Aggregates often take similar values in neighbouring areas and dissimilar values in distant ones. For example, Lombardy and Sicily have very different levels of GDP per capita, while Sicily and Calabria record more similar values (the so-called first law of Tobler): just as values that are closer in time are generally more correlated, areas that are closer in space tend to be more correlated than distant ones.
The existence of strong spatial correlation, positive or negative, implies that the observations are not independent; it is therefore always advisable to check whether the data depend strongly on space.
To compute autocorrelation one can use traditional correlation indices, adjusted with a suitable matrix \(W\) that indicates the spatial proximity of the areas. The simplest form is a contiguity matrix, which takes the value 0 when two areas have no common border and 1 otherwise. However, different definitions of contiguity could be used, or weights based on the inverse of the geographical distances between the centres of the areas. The choice of the type of contiguity or weight, and of the techniques for measuring distances and locating centres, is relatively arbitrary, which is an obvious limitation of these tools.



Figure 12.1 – The 9 provinces of the Sicily Region


Let us take as an example the 9 provinces of the Sicily Region, whose borders are shown in Figure 12.1 with their abbreviations and ISTAT codes. Setting 1 where two provinces share a border and 0 otherwise (0 also on the main diagonal), we obtain the following square matrix, built from the contiguity information in the file confinanti.csv, which also contains value added per capita for 2001 and 2006 (vap01 and vap06)

To obtain the spatial autocorrelation of GDP per capita for the 9 Sicilian provinces in 2001 and 2006, we use Moran’s I index, defined as
\[
I=\left(n\Big/\sum_{i} \sum_{j} w_{ij}\right)\sum_{i} \sum_{j} (x_{i}-\bar{x})(x_{j}-\bar{x})w_{ij}\Big/\sum_{i} (x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}
\tag{12.1}
\]
whose central value (no autocorrelation) is \(-1/(n-1)\), which tends to 0 for sufficiently large \(n\). In general, if the computed index is below the central value there is negative autocorrelation, if it is above there is positive autocorrelation.
Another well-known index of spatial autocorrelation is Geary’s c
\[
c=\left((n-1)\Big/2\sum_{i} \sum_{j} w_{ij}\right)\sum_{i} \sum_{j} (x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}w_{ij}\Big/\sum_{i} (x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}
\tag{12.2}
\]
When this index is greater than 1 there is evidence of negative autocorrelation, when it is below 1 we say there is positive autocorrelation, while autocorrelation is nil when the statistic is close to one.
We compute Moran’s index for GDP per capita in 2001

RPythonSAS



num <- matrix(0,9,9)
for (i in 1:9) for (j in 1:9) num[i,j] <- (vap01[i]-mean(vap01))*(vap01[j]-mean(vap01))*matw[i,j]
num2 <- sum(num)
den <- 0
for (i in 1:9) den[i] <- (vap01[i]-mean(vap01))^2
den1 <- sum(den)
IMoran <- 9/sum(matw)*num2/den1
IMoran

[1] -0.01025151

centr <- -1/(9-1); centr

[1] -0.125

IMoran > centr

[1] TRUE





def moran(x, W):
    z = x - x.mean()
    return len(x) / W.sum() * (z @ W @ z) / np.sum(z ** 2)

def geary(x, W):
    z = x - x.mean()
    diff2 = (x[:, None] - x[None, :]) ** 2
    return (len(x) - 1) / (2 * W.sum()) * np.sum(diff2 * W) / np.sum(z ** 2)

IMoran = moran(vap01, W)
centr = -1 / (9 - 1)
print(IMoran, centr, IMoran > centr)

-0.010251513230766713 -0.125 True




proc iml;
  use matt; read all var {TP PA ME AG CL EN CT RG SR} into W;
            read all var {vap01 vap06} into V; close matt;
  start moran(x, W);
    z = x - mean(x);
    return( nrow(x)/sum(W) * (z` * W * z) / ssq(z) );
  finish;
  start geary(x, W);
    n = nrow(x); z = x - mean(x);
    D = (repeat(x, 1, n) - repeat(x`, n, 1))##2;
    return( (n-1)/(2*sum(W)) * sum(D # W) / ssq(z) );
  finish;
  IMoran01 = moran(V[,1], W);  CGeary01 = geary(V[,1], W);
  IMoran06 = moran(V[,2], W);  CGeary06 = geary(V[,2], W);
  centr = -1/(9-1);
  print IMoran01 CGeary01 IMoran06 CGeary06 centr;
quit;

title: 12 Further applied examples
text:
The territory, with its specific characteristics, plays an essential role in correctly interpreting an aggregate. Aggregates often take similar values in neighbouring areas and dissimilar values in distant ones. For example, Lombardy and Sicily have very different levels of GDP per capita, while Sicily and Calabria record more similar values (the so-called first law of Tobler): just as values that are closer in time are generally more correlated, areas that are closer in space tend to be more correlated than distant ones.
The existence of strong spatial correlation, positive or negative, implies that the observations are not independent; it is therefore always advisable to check whether the data depend strongly on space.
To compute autocorrelation one can use traditional correlation indices, adjusted with a suitable matrix \(W\) that indicates the spatial proximity of the areas. The simplest form is a contiguity matrix, which takes the value 0 when two areas have no common border and 1 otherwise. However, different definitions of contiguity could be used, or weights based on the inverse of the geographical distances between the centres of the areas. The choice of the type of contiguity or weight, and of the techniques for measuring distances and locating centres, is relatively arbitrary, which is an obvious limitation of these tools.



Figure 12.1 – The 9 provinces of the Sicily Region


Let us take as an example the 9 provinces of the Sicily Region, whose borders are shown in Figure 12.1 with their abbreviations and ISTAT codes. Setting 1 where two provinces share a border and 0 otherwise (0 also on the main diagonal), we obtain the following square matrix, built from the contiguity information in the file confinanti.csv, which also contains value added per capita for 2001 and 2006 (vap01 and vap06)

RPythonSAS

# matt is the name chosen for the full matrix

matw

To obtain the spatial autocorrelation of GDP per capita for the 9 Sicilian provinces in 2001 and 2006, we use Moran’s I index, defined as
\[
I=\left(n\Big/\sum_{i} \sum_{j} w_{ij}\right)\sum_{i} \sum_{j} (x_{i}-\bar{x})(x_{j}-\bar{x})w_{ij}\Big/\sum_{i} (x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}
\tag{12.1}
\]
whose central value (no autocorrelation) is \(-1/(n-1)\), which tends to 0 for sufficiently large \(n\). In general, if the computed index is below the central value there is negative autocorrelation, if it is above there is positive autocorrelation.
Another well-known index of spatial autocorrelation is Geary’s c
\[
c=\left((n-1)\Big/2\sum_{i} \sum_{j} w_{ij}\right)\sum_{i} \sum_{j} (x_{i}-x_{j})^{2}w_{ij}\Big/\sum_{i} (x_{i}-\bar{x})^{2}
\tag{12.2}
\]
When this index is greater than 1 there is evidence of negative autocorrelation, when it is below 1 we say there is positive autocorrelation, while autocorrelation is nil when the statistic is close to one.
We compute Moran’s index for GDP per capita in 2001

RPythonSAS



num <- matrix(0,9,9)
for (i in 1:9) for (j in 1:9) num[i,j] <- (vap01[i]-mean(vap01))*(vap01[j]-mean(vap01))*matw[i,j]
num2 <- sum(num)
den <- 0
for (i in 1:9) den[i] <- (vap01[i]-mean(vap01))^2
den1 <- sum(den)
IMoran <- 9/sum(matw)*num2/den1
IMoran

[1] -0.01025151

centr <- -1/(9-1); centr

[1] -0.125

IMoran > centr

[1] TRUE





def moran(x, W):
    z = x - x.mean()
    return len(x) / W.sum() * (z @ W @ z) / np.sum(z ** 2)

def geary(x, W):
    z = x - x.mean()
    diff2 = (x[:, None] - x[None, :]) ** 2
    return (len(x) - 1) / (2 * W.sum()) * np.sum(diff2 * W) / np.sum(z ** 2)

IMoran = moran(vap01, W)
centr = -1 / (9 - 1)
print(IMoran, centr, IMoran > centr)

-0.010251513230766713 -0.125 True




proc iml;
  use matt; read all var {TP PA ME AG CL EN CT RG SR} into W;
            read all var {vap01 vap06} into V; close matt;
  start moran(x, W);
    z = x - mean(x);
    return( nrow(x)/sum(W) * (z` * W * z) / ssq(z) );
  finish;
  start geary(x, W);
    n = nrow(x); z = x - mean(x);
    D = (repeat(x, 1, n) - repeat(x`, n, 1))##2;
    return( (n-1)/(2*sum(W)) * sum(D # W) / ssq(z) );
  finish;
  IMoran01 = moran(V[,1], W);  CGeary01 = geary(V[,1], W);
  IMoran06 = moran(V[,2], W);  CGeary06 = geary(V[,2], W);
  centr = -1/(9-1);
  print IMoran01 CGeary01 IMoran06 CGeary06 centr;
quit;
