title: 12 Further applied examples
text:
12.2 Cluster analysis
Every territory has specific characteristics that can influence a phenomenon, whether economic or social. Moreover, many of these specific effects depend on the spatial location of the territory, since two neighbouring areas generally behave more similarly than distant ones. It is therefore reasonable to expect neighbouring territories to show similar macroeconomic patterns, in effect forming macro-areas that are fairly homogeneous internally; this is typically the case of the Centre-North and the South (Mezzogiorno) of Italy. Cluster analysis is therefore very useful for identifying areas that are similar with respect to certain characteristics.
Here we give an example with metric variables measured in the same unit. Suppose we examine the 9 Sicilian provinces with reference to hourly labour productivity, in euro, in the textile industry (\(X\)) and in the engineering industry (\(Y\))

RPythonSAS



X <- c(12,25,16,81,55,70,18,48,51)
Y <- c(23,20,27,26,21,35,52,64,69)




X = np.array([12, 25, 16, 81, 55, 70, 18, 48, 51])
Y = np.array([23, 20, 27, 26, 21, 35, 52, 64, 69])



data prod;
  input provincia X Y @@;
  datalines;
1 12 23  2 25 20  3 16 27  4 81 26  5 55 21
6 70 35  7 18 52  8 48 64  9 51 69
;
run;



We compute the matrix of Euclidean distances (other choices are of course possible, but this is one of the simplest and most widely used). Since the Euclidean distance between two points \(z_{i}\) and \(z_{j}\) is
\[
d(z_{i},z_{j})=\left(\sum_{k} (z_{i,k}-z_{j,k})^{2}\right)^{1/2}
\tag{12.3}
\]
the distance between the first and second province is 178 (omitting the square root for convenience)

RPythonSAS



d12 <- (X[1]-X[2])^2+(Y[1]-Y[2])^2; d12

[1] 178





d12 = (X[0] - X[1]) ** 2 + (Y[0] - Y[1]) ** 2
print(d12)

178




data _null_;
  set prod(obs=2);
  retain x1 y1;
  if _n_ = 1 then do; x1 = X; y1 = Y; end;
  else do; d12 = (x1-X)**2 + (y1-Y)**2; put d12=; end;
run;



so, to obtain the full matrix, we write

RPythonSAS



d <- matrix(0,9,9)
for (i in 1:9) for (j in 1:9) d[i,j] <- (X[i]-X[j])^2+(Y[i]-Y[j])^2




d = (X[:, None] - X[None, :]) ** 2 + (Y[:, None] - Y[None, :]) ** 2



proc iml;
  use prod; read all var {X Y} into Z; close prod;
  d = distance(Z, "L2")##2;          /* squared Euclidean distances */
  print d;
  create dist from d; append from d; close dist;
quit;



We now need a criterion for merging the areas, for example the minimum distance (or single linkage), according to which the two points with the smallest value are merged into a single point

/* the matrix is printed by the previous block (print d) */



There are other criteria, such as the maximum distance, the average distance and others, but the minimum distance is perhaps the most intuitive and simple choice. The minimum distance between the cluster formed by points \(a\) and \(b\) and the one formed by point \(c\) is therefore \(d(ab,c)=\min \left\{d(a,c),d(b,c)\right\}\)

RPythonSAS



dn <- d; d0 <- d; ind <- dim(dn)[2]; aggr <- 0
dn[lower.tri(dn,TRUE)] <- NA
for (j in 1:(ind-2)) {
  coord <- which(dn==min(dn,na.rm=TRUE),arr.ind=TRUE)
  minimo <- min(dn,na.rm=TRUE)
  aggr[j] <- minimo; dd <- 0
  for (i in 1:ind) dd[i] <- min(d0[coord[1],i],d0[i,coord[2]])
  dn[coord[1],] <- dd
  dn[,coord[1]] <- dd
  dn <- dn[,-coord[2]]
  dn <- dn[-coord[2],]
  d0[coord[1],] <- dd
  d0[,coord[1]] <- dd
  d0 <- d0[,-coord[2]]
  d0 <- d0[-coord[2],]
  ind <- ind-1
  dn[lower.tri(dn,TRUE)] <- NA
}
aggr[j+1] <- dn[1,2]
gruppi <- matrix(0,(dim(d)[2]-1),2)
for (i in 1:(dim(d)[2]-1)) gruppi[i,1:2] <- which(d==aggr[i],arr.ind=TRUE)[1:2]
gruppi <- cbind(gruppi,aggr)
colnames(gruppi) <- c("cl1","cl2","dist")




from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage
from scipy.spatial.distance import squareform

# single linkage on the (squared, as in the text) distance matrix
Z = linkage(squareform(d), method="single")
members = {i: [i + 1] for i in range(9)}          # provinces numbered from 1
rows = []
for k, (a, b, dist, _) in enumerate(Z):
    members[9 + k] = sorted(members[int(a)] + members[int(b)])
    rows.append({"step": k + 1, "group": members[9 + k], "dist": dist})
gruppi = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("step")



/* PROC CLUSTER directly accepts a distance matrix (TYPE=DISTANCE) */
data dist(type=distance);
  set dist;
  provincia = _n_;
run;
proc cluster data=dist method=single nonorm outtree=albero;
  id provincia;
run;

/* the "Cluster History" table of PROC CLUSTER reports, step by step,
   the clusters joined and the minimum distance ("Minimum Distance") */



At the first step points 3 and 1 are merged and at the second points 9 and 8. At the third step point 3, which already includes point 1, is merged with point 2; the group is therefore formed by points 1, 2 and 3. At the fourth step points 6 and 4 are merged and at the fifth 6 and 5, so the cluster at the fifth step consists of points 4, 5 and 6. Proceeding in this way, the sixth group contains points 1, 2, 3 and 7, the seventh points 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and the eighth all the previous ones, thus including all nine points.
Going back to the example of the 9 Sicilian provinces, we can say that provinces 1 (Trapani) and 3 (Messina) are the first to show a strong similarity in terms of hourly labour productivity in the textile and engineering industries, followed by provinces 8 (Ragusa) and 9 (Syracuse), and so on.
If the clustering procedure is carried out to the last step, all units end up in a single group; instead, the procedure must be stopped at the most appropriate point to identify a limited number of groups. For this purpose a similarity index can be used, choosing the merge corresponding to the most significant step-by-step change (Figure 12.2)

RPythonSAS



simil <- (1-gruppi[,3]/max(d))*100; round(simil,2)

[1] 99.33 99.29 97.27 95.77 91.17 86.81 81.11 78.11

plot(round(simil,2), type="l", main="Similarity", xlab="Steps", ylab="Values")
abline(v=4, lty=2)




Figure 12.2 – Similarity index







simil = (1 - gruppi["dist"] / d.max()) * 100
print(simil.round(2).to_numpy())

[99.33 99.29 97.27 95.77 91.17 86.81 81.11 78.11]



plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.plot(gruppi.index, simil.round(2), color="black")
plt.axvline(4, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8)
plt.title("Similarity"); plt.xlabel("Steps"); plt.ylabel("Values")
plt.show()




Figure 12.2 – Similarity index






/* similarity index from the merging distances of PROC CLUSTER */
proc iml;
  use dist; read all var ("COL1":"COL9") into D; close dist;
  call symputx("dmax", max(D));
quit;
data simil;
  set albero;
  where _ncl_ < 9;
  passo = 9 - _ncl_;
  simil = round((1 - _height_/&dmax)*100, 0.01);
run;
proc sort data=simil; by passo; run;
proc sgplot data=simil noautolegend;
  title "Similarity";
  series x=passo y=simil;
  refline 4 / axis=x lineattrs=(pattern=dash);
  xaxis label="Steps"; yaxis label="Values";
run;



Figure 12.2 shows the pattern of the similarity index, indicating step 4 as the candidate for defining the clusters; specifically, this implies a partition into 5 groups: {1,2,3}, {8,9}, {4,6}, {5} and {7}.

title: 12 Further applied examples
text:
12.3 Factor analysis and principal components
Factor analysis is another technique that can usefully be applied to the analysis of territorial units. Suppose we know the current surplus (\(X1\)) and the net lending (\(X2\)) of 12 municipal administrations. We are interested in summarising the data so as to better represent the accounting position of the units under study. Factor analysis can help, since it summarises the information in a smaller number of new variables (the factors) than the original ones. In general, for each variable \(x\) we define
\[
x_{i}=\sum_{j} A_{ij}F_{j}+U_{i} \quad \text{with} \quad F_{j}=\sum_{i} W_{ij}x_{i}
\tag{12.4}
\]
where \(F_{j}\) is the \(j\)-th factor common to all the \(x_{i}\), while \(U_{i}\) is the \(i\)-th unique factor. The main method for extracting the factors is based on principal components, which are simply linear combinations of the variables; in particular, the first component captures the largest share of the variance, the second (uncorrelated with the first) the largest share of the remaining variance, and so on. To choose the number of factors at which to stop the extraction, one refers precisely to the percentage of variance explained by each factor.
Suppose that the accounting position of our 12 municipal administrations is described by the following two variables

RPythonSAS



X1 <- c(16,12,13,11,10,9,8,7,5,3,2,0)
X2 <- c(8,10,6,2,8,-1,4,6,-3,-1,-3,0)

X2 = np.array([8, 10, 6, 2, 8, -1, 4, 6, -3, -1, -3, 0], dtype=float)

  input X1 X2 @@;

  datalines;
16 8  12 10  13 6  11 2  10 8  9 -1
8 4  7 6  5 -3  3 -1  2 -3  0 0

The same result can be obtained by a step-by-step computation. The general equation is
\[
(S-\lambda I)w=0
\tag{12.5}
\]
where \(\lambda\) is the eigenvalue and \(w\) the eigenvector. Excluding the trivial solution \(w=0\), we have the characteristic equation \(|S-\lambda I|=0\), i.e.
\[
\left|\begin{matrix}23.09-\lambda & 16.45 \\ 16.45 & 21.09-\lambda \end{matrix}\right|=0
\]
which is equivalent to
\[

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
Classical time-series analysis proposes models in which the observed values of a series are expressed, for each period, as the combination of a deterministic systematic component, which is the main object of interest, and a residual random component to which no particular importance is attached. The components are generally not computed with formal statistical procedures, in the sense that many of these techniques rest on criteria that are valid mainly empirically. The immediate advantage is that computation is easy and fast and the results are often easier to interpret, with no need to meet strict conditions of applicability or to have a large number of observations. On the other hand, the stronger statistical framework provided by a stochastic approach would allow an in-depth analysis of the series, searching for its components with more refined and precise procedures able to adapt to the specific data, as well as better forecasting ability. For these reasons the stochastic (or modern) approach should be seen as complementary to, not an alternative to, the classical methods discussed earlier in the book.
In the modern approach the observed series \(Y\) does not derive from a combination of deterministic effects plus a random component, but is generated by a stochastic process. A stochastic process is a family of random variables \(X(t)\) ordered by a time parameter \(t\in T\), continuous or discrete; in typical economic series the time index is discrete.
From this perspective, a time series is interpreted as a finite part of a realisation of a stochastic process whose probabilistic structure is unknown, where \(T\) is the set of time points at which the process is defined. The same stochastic process can give rise to many different time series, just as different samples can be drawn from the same population.
Our aim is to estimate the characteristics of the stochastic process generating the series on the basis of the observed data of the only series available. We are therefore forced to restrict attention to specific and quite special stochastic processes, so that the link between process and series is stable and strong enough to infer information about the process from the series observed in reality; of particular importance are processes that are stationary in the strict or weak sense.
Weak stationarity, the less restrictive, holds when the three conditions below are met
\[
\begin{aligned}
&E(X(t))=m && \text{for every } t \\
&E(X(t)-m)^{2}=\sigma^{2} && \text{finite, for every } t \\
&E(X(t)-m)(X(s)-m)=\gamma (|s-t|) && \text{for every pair } t, s
\end{aligned}
\tag{6.1}
\]
As \(t\) varies, the mean is constant, the variance is finite and constant and, for every \(t\) and \(s\), the autocovariance function depends only on the lag \(|s-t|\). For Gaussian processes, weak stationarity also guarantees strict stationarity (which holds when the distribution of the multivariate random variable \((X(t_{1}),...,X(t_{n}))\) does not depend on \((t_{1},...,t_{n})\) for every \(n>1\)). We therefore assume that the process is always Gaussian.
A first important property is thus stationarity. Another is invertibility, that is, the possibility of expressing a process \(X(t)\) through past random variables, namely
\[
X(t)=\sum_{j} \delta_{j}X(t-j)+a_{t}
\tag{6.2}
\]
for \(j\) from 1 to \(\infty\), where \(a_{t}\) is a \(WN\) (white noise) process, normally distributed with mean 0 and constant variance.
From the single observed series we must therefore work back to the generating process; the autocorrelation function, that is, the autocorrelations at different time lags, helps us do this. First of all the process must be stationary; only then does the autocorrelation function have the meaning of an internal measure of the process, that is, of the linear relationship between the random variables \(X(t)\) and \(X(t-k)\) as \(k\) varies. Besides the (global) autocorrelation function, the partial autocorrelation function is computed (which considers the relationship between \(X(t)\) and \(X(t-k)\) holding \(X(t-1),...,X(t-k+1)\) fixed); both are shown graphically in correlograms.
Estimating the properties of a process from a single time sample of finite length is not obvious; it is legitimate, however, if the process is ergodic. A stochastic process is ergodic with respect to a parameter if the estimate of the parameter obtained from a time series tends to the parameter of the process as \(n\) tends to \(\infty\). Ergodicity guarantees that statistically consistent estimates of the stationary process can be obtained from the available information (the observed time series). The literature has shown that stationary processes are generally also ergodic, but this is not a sufficient condition.
Usually one is content to check stationarity and, if it does not hold, to try to achieve it by suitably transforming the original series; in many cases one or two successive differences are enough to come very close to stationarity.
The observed time series is regarded as a finite realisation of some underlying stochastic process. A general aim of modern time-series analysis is therefore also to make inferences about the properties of the stochastic process from the information contained in the observed series. In fact, statistical analysis does not succeed in identifying the stochastic process itself; starting from the data, it merely identifies a statistical model whose properties and characteristics are similar to those of the mechanism generating the process. The focus thus shifts to building a model that represents the stochastic process and summarises its main features.

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
section: 6.2 AR, MA, ARMA and ARIMA models
text:
6.2 AR, MA, ARMA and ARIMA models
We already know the autoregressive model of order \(p\), \(AR(p)\), now defined by the following relationship
\[
X(t)=\phi (1)X(t-1)+...+\phi (p)X(t-p)+a(t)
\tag{6.3}
\]
where the \(\phi (i)\) are constants and \(a(t)\sim WN\). If we define the lag operator \(B\) such that \(BX(t)=X(t-1)\), then
\[
B^{j}X(t)=X(t-j)
\tag{6.4}
\]
and so
\[
AR(p):\ \phi (B)X(t)=a(t)
\tag{6.5}
\]
with \(\phi (B)\) called the autoregressive operator of order \(p\). Essentially, \(AR\) models try to explain the present as a function of the past up to a certain time lag \(p\). It can be shown that an \(AR(p)\) process is always invertible, while it is stationary if and only if all the solutions of the characteristic equation \(\phi (B)=0\) are greater than 1 in modulus.
Besides the autoregressive form, a moving-average model of order \(q\), \(MA(q)\), is also often used, defined by the following relationship
\[
X(t)=a(t)-\theta (1)a(t-1)-...-\theta (q)a(t-q)
\tag{6.6}
\]
where again the \(\theta (i)\) are constants and \(a(t)\sim WN\). As in the previous case, it immediately follows that
\[
MA(q):\ X(t)=\theta (B)a(t)
\tag{6.7}
\]
with \(\theta (B)\) called the moving-average operator of order \(q\). \(MA(q)\) models thus try to explain the present as the result of a sequence of random shocks. It can be shown that an \(MA(q)\) process is always stationary, while it is invertible if and only if all the solutions of the characteristic equation \(\theta (B)=0\) are greater than 1 in modulus.
A third class, the so-called mixed models, combines \(AR(p)\) and \(MA(q)\). The generic \(ARMA(p,q)\) model can therefore be defined as
\[
\begin{gathered}X(t)-\phi (1)X(t-1)-...-\phi (p)X(t-p)= \\ =a(t)-\theta (1)a(t-1)-...-\theta (q)a(t-q)\end{gathered}
\tag{6.8}
\]
that is
\[
\phi (B)X(t)=\theta (B)a(t)
\tag{6.9}
\]
Consequently, an \(ARMA(p,q)\) process is stationary when all \(p\) roots of the characteristic equation of the \(AR\) component, \(\phi (B)=0\), are greater than 1 in modulus; it is invertible when all \(q\) roots of the characteristic equation of the \(MA\) component, \(\theta (B)=0\), are greater than 1 in modulus.
We can say that it is always necessary to achieve stationarity. There are apparent exceptions in cointegration analysis, where a linear combination of non-stationary time series may give rise to a stationary structure.
Non-stationarity in variance and covariance (the second and third conditions) is dealt with before attempting to formulate a suitable model, while non-stationarity in the mean is removed through a specific transformation that can be built into the structure of the model itself. In this case we speak of the generalisation to \(ARIMA(p,d,q)\) models, where \(d\) is the order of integration, that is, the number of times the series must be differenced. If \(\nabla\) is the difference operator such that
\[
\nabla^{d}X(t)=\nabla (\nabla^{d-1}X(t))=\nabla^{d-1}X(t)-\nabla^{d-1}X(t-1)=W(t)
\tag{6.10}
\]
we can write
\[
ARIMA(p,d,q):\ \phi_{p}(B)\nabla^{d}X(t)=\theta_{q}(B)a(t)
\tag{6.11}
\]
or (also without subscripts)
\[
\phi (B)W(t)=\theta (B)a(t)
\tag{6.12}
\]
The aim is now to find the ARMA or ARIMA model that is statistically best for the observed series.

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.3 Identification and seasonal SARIMA models
In practice, given the time series, we estimate the global and partial autocorrelation functions up to a certain lag. Knowing these functions is generally not enough to identify the model; however, restricting attention to stationary and invertible ARMA models, there is a one-to-one correspondence between model and autocorrelation function. Moreover, assuming Gaussian as well as stationary and invertible processes, knowing the autocorrelation function is equivalent to knowing the process itself.
Note that the ARIMA notation alone is generally preferred, since ARMA models are the special case \(d=0\), just as AR and MA models are special cases.
In fact, the key step in analysing a time series is identifying the ARIMA model, that is, the values to give the parameters \((p,d,q)\) once all the required statistical conditions have been checked. The values of \(p\) and \(q\) are determined by studying the global autocorrelation function \(\rho (k)\) and the partial autocorrelation function \(\pi (k)\) (where \(k\) is the time lag), that is, by comparing the observed pattern with the theoretical pattern for \(AR(p)\), \(MA(q)\) and \(ARMA(p,q)\) processes (for which all the required conditions hold).
In particular, the global autocorrelation function of an \(MA(q)\) process is identically zero for \(k>q\), while its partial autocorrelation function decays exponentially towards 0 without ever vanishing. Conversely, the global autocorrelation function of an \(AR(p)\) process decays towards 0 as a linear combination of decaying exponentials and/or damped sine waves, without ever vanishing, while its partial autocorrelation function is zero for \(k>p\).
Consequently, the global autocorrelation function of an \(ARMA(p,q)\) process combines the AR and MA patterns: it never vanishes but decays exponentially towards 0 for lags \(k>(q-p)\); its partial autocorrelation function also combines the patterns of the AR and MA components, never vanishing but decaying exponentially towards 0 for lags \(k>(p-q)\).
Finally, once the order and type of model have been identified and the parameters estimated, the residuals are analysed to assess whether the model is correctly specified. If the outcome is unsatisfactory, the identification procedure is repeated in search of a better alternative.
If a series is seasonal, more complex SARIMA models must be formulated, that is, ARIMA models with a seasonal component of period \(s\). In this case we introduce the further seasonal difference operator \(\nabla_{s}\) (possibly of order \(D\)), such that
\[
\nabla_{s}X(t)=(1-B^{s})X(t)=X(t)-X(t-s)
\tag{6.13}
\]
The seasonal ARIMA is structured as two linked ARIMA models: if, for example, seasonality is monthly, a first model of order \((P,D,Q)\) studies the relationship between the values of the same month in successive years
\[
\Phi_{P}(B^{s})\nabla_{s}^{D}X(t)=\Theta_{Q}(B^{s})\alpha (t)
\tag{6.14}
\]
and a second model of order \((p,d,q)\) studies the relationship between values in different months of the same year, applied to the residuals \(\alpha (t)\) of the previous model
\[
\phi_{p}(B)\nabla^{d}\alpha (t)=\theta_{q}(B)a(t) \quad \text{with} \quad a(t)\sim WN
\tag{6.15}
\]
These two expressions easily give the general form of the seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) model, with the obvious meaning of the symbols
\[
ARIMA(p,d,q)(P,D,Q)_{s}:\quad \phi_{p}(B)\Phi_{P}(B^{s})\nabla^{d}\nabla_{s}^{D}X(t)=\theta_{q}(B)\Theta_{Q}(B^{s})a(t)
\tag{6.16}
\]

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.5 Spurious regression
What we have said so far makes clear the importance of working with stationary series, that is, integrated of order 0; first differences are useful in many cases and, if \(d\) differences make the series \(Y\) stationary, we say that \(Y_{t}\sim I(d)\). When series are not stationary, apart from some specific exceptions, analysing them over time leads to misleading results. To see this, we generate 500 observations from two random-walk models; the two series are integrated of order 1 and certainly unrelated, since they are generated by drawing random components from two Normal distributions with mean 0 and variance 1. So there should be no significant relationship between the two series; yet, if we estimate a linear model, we might obtain results such as the following.

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.6 Autocorrelation functions
The variables \(X\) and \(Y\) were generated by a random-walk model without drift, that is, an \(AR(1)\) without constant and with the coefficient of the regressor equal to 1. In reality we have observed time series whose generating process, and hence the appropriate model, is not known a priori; the global and partial autocorrelation functions are very useful for this purpose. Recalling that the estimated covariance at lag \(k\) is
\[
\hat{\gamma}_{k}=\sum (Y_{t}-\bar{Y})(Y_{t+k}-\bar{Y})/n
\tag{6.19}
\]
with \(\hat{\gamma}_{0}=\sum (Y_{t}-\bar{Y})^{2}/n\), the estimated autocorrelation function at lag \(k\) is
\[
\hat{\rho}_{k}=\hat{\gamma}_{k}/\hat{\gamma}_{0}
\tag{6.20}
\]
It is then fairly easy to build the corresponding correlograms. For convenience we use the functions acf() and pacf(), first on the white noise (Figure 6.3) and then on the random walk without drift (Figure 6.4).

RPythonSAS



par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
awn <- acf(u, main="ACF: White Noise")
pwn <- pacf(u, main="PACF: White Noise")




Figure 6.3 – Correlograms of a white noise







from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
plot_acf(u, ax=ax[0], lags=25, title="ACF: White Noise")
plot_pacf(u, ax=ax[1], lags=25, title="PACF: White Noise")
plt.show()




Figure 6.3 – Correlograms of a white noise






/* PROC ARIMA, IDENTIFY statement: ACF, PACF and Ljung-Box test */
proc arima data=spuria plots=(series(acf pacf));
  identify var=u nlag=25;
run;
quit;




RPythonSAS



par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
arw <- acf(Y, main="ACF: random walk without drift")
prw <- pacf(Y, main="PACF: random walk without drift")




Figure 6.4 – Correlograms of a random walk without drift







fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
plot_acf(Y, ax=ax[0], lags=25, title="ACF: random walk without drift")
plot_pacf(Y, ax=ax[1], lags=25, title="PACF: random walk without drift")
plt.show()

quit;

While the correlogram of the white noise shows no systematic pattern worth noting, with values almost always inside the non-significance bands (the dashed lines in the plots, built using \(\hat{\rho}_{k}\sim N(0,1/n)\)), the random walk shows a pattern reminiscent of autoregressive models but with a very slow decay of the ACF: at the fifth lag the autocorrelation is still extremely high (0.967 in the printed edition); this is a classic consequence of non-stationarity. The problem arises because the autoregressive coefficient equals one. Indeed, if \(Y_{t}=\rho Y_{t-1}+u_{t}\), but now \(-1<\rho <1\), for example \(\rho =0.3\), we obtain Figure 6.5

  retain G 0;

run;

  identify var=G nlag=25;
run;
quit;

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.7 The Box-Pierce and Ljung-Box tests
To assess the significance of the autocorrelation at the various time lags, besides the confidence bands shown by default in the plots, the Box-Pierce \(Q\) statistic is often used
\[
Q_{m}=n\sum_{k=1}^{m} \hat{\rho}_{k}^{2}
\tag{6.21}
\]
which tests the hypothesis of zero autocorrelation up to lag \(m\) against a \(\chi^{2}\) distribution with \(m\) degrees of freedom. Another well-known test is based on the Ljung-Box statistic
\[
LB=n(n+2)\sum_{k=1}^{m} (\hat{\rho}_{k}^{2}/(n-k))
\tag{6.22}
\]
which also follows a \(\chi^{2}\) distribution with \(m\) degrees of freedom. In R both tests are available through Box.test(); let us apply them, for example up to lag 10, to the white noise \(u\) and to the series \(G\).

RPythonSAS



Box.test(u, lag=10, type="Box-Pierce")


    Box-Pierce test

data:  u
X-squared = 7.7978, df = 10, p-value = 0.6486

Box.test(G, lag=10, type="Ljung-Box")


    Box-Ljung test

data:  G
X-squared = 50.167, df = 10, p-value = 2.487e-07





from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox

print(acorr_ljungbox(u, lags=[10], boxpierce=True))

      lb_stat  lb_pvalue    bp_stat  bp_pvalue
10  16.812408   0.078619  16.605751   0.083556

print(acorr_ljungbox(G, lags=[10]))

     lb_stat  lb_pvalue
10  23.83487   0.008051




/* PROC ARIMA reports the Ljung-Box test ("Autocorrelation Check for White Noise")
   in groups of 6 lags in the IDENTIFY output */
proc arima data=ar1;
  identify var=G nlag=12;
run;
quit;

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.9 An example: US income
We load the constant-price data in logreddito.csv on the logarithm of disposable income and the logarithm of household consumption in the United States from the first quarter of 1954 to the fourth quarter of 1994. We want to check whether the log of income is stationary (Figure 6.8).

RPythonSAS



lr <- read.csv2("data/logreddito.csv")
reddito <- lr$lreddito
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(ts(reddito), main="Income")
plot(diff(ts(reddito)), main="First differences of income")




Figure 6.8 – Income series and first differences







lr = pd.read_csv("data/logreddito.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
reddito = lr["lreddito"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
ax[0].plot(reddito, color="black"); ax[0].set_title("Income")
ax[1].plot(reddito.diff(), color="black"); ax[1].set_title("First differences of income")
plt.show()




Figure 6.8 – Income series and first differences






proc import datafile="data/logreddito.csv" out=lr dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
data lr; set lr; t = _n_; dreddito = dif(lreddito); run;
proc sgplot data=lr; title "Income"; series x=t y=lreddito; run;
proc sgplot data=lr; title "First differences of income"; series x=t y=dreddito; run;



The income series clearly shows strong signs of non-stationarity. In particular, estimating a first-order autoregression gives a coefficient very close to one, that is, a \(\rho -1\) very close to 0. We estimate the model for the \(DF\) test, where the t statistic must be assessed with great caution, since it now follows a different distribution (here the p-value produced by default by the software cannot be used).

YY <- embed(reddito,2); Y <- YY[,1]; Y1 <- YY[,2]
modello <- lm(Y~Y1)
coef(modello)

In particular, one can check that the augmented Dickey-Fuller test (\(ADF\)), unlike the traditional \(t\) test, accepts the null hypothesis \(\delta =0\) and therefore signals that income is not stationary, with ADF = −0.7729 up to lag 5 and p-value = 0.9621; likewise, it indicates that the first differences are stationary, with ADF = −5.4756 up to lag 5 and p-value = 0.01.
Base R has no function for the ADF statistic: external packages are needed, such as tseries, which provides adf.test() (model with constant and trend; by default the number of lags is \(\lfloor (n-1)^{1/3} \rfloor\), here 5).

RPythonSAS



library(tseries)
adf.test(reddito)


    Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  reddito
Dickey-Fuller = -0.77285, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.9621
alternative hypothesis: stationary

adf.test(diff(reddito))


    Augmented Dickey-Fuller Test

data:  diff(reddito)
Dickey-Fuller = -5.4756, Lag order = 5, p-value = 0.01
alternative hypothesis: stationary





from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller

for nome, x in (("reddito", reddito), ("differenze", reddito.diff().dropna())):
    stat, pval = adfuller(x, maxlag=5, regression="ct", autolag=None)[:2]
    print(nome, round(stat, 4), round(pval, 4))

reddito -0.7729 0.9679
differenze -5.4756 0.0




/* PROC AUTOREG: ADF test (with constant and trend) with 5 lags */
proc autoreg data=lr;
  model lreddito = / stationarity=(adf=5);
  model dreddito = / stationarity=(adf=5);
run;









Note



The p-values of the ADF test are computed with different approximations: adf.test() interpolates the Dickey-Fuller tables and truncates the values at the extremes (0.01 and 0.99), while statsmodels and SAS use MacKinnon’s approximations. The test statistic is the same.


The series may be stationary around a deterministic trend; in that case, removing the trend may be enough to achieve stationarity, without taking differences. We add a linear trend to the initial model.

Note the use of I() to build the time index inside lm(). There is no significant deterministic trend; so the series appears to be difference-stationary rather than stationary around a linear deterministic trend, although the trend could take more complex forms, such as quadratic or cubic ones (our income series in fact shows a clearly linear pattern). Let us nevertheless detrend the income series and repeat the Dickey-Fuller test.

RPythonSAS



modello4 <- lm(reddito~I(1:length(reddito)))
detrend <- residuals(modello4)
adf.test(detrend)

  model lreddito = t;
  output out=lr_det r=detrend;
run;
quit;
proc autoreg data=lr_det;
  model detrend = / stationarity=(adf=5);
run;



Given how modello4 is defined, its residuals are the detrended series \(Y\). On the series detrend, the augmented DF statistic up to lag 5 equals −0.7729, with p-value 0.9621; so, confirming the previous result, the linearly detrended log income series is still non-stationary.
A remark on the logarithmic transformation of the previous series. It is widely used for time series because, on the one hand, it linearises the trend (for example in the log-linear model) and, on the other, it reduces and tends to stabilise the variance, with considerable advantages for data analysis. Moreover, in the log-linear model the coefficients typically have the economic interpretation of elasticities. If, for example, consumption and income are linked by an exponential model, the double-log transformation makes the model linear and gives the estimates the meaning of the elasticity of consumption with respect to income, which is clearly useful for interpretation.

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.10 Cointegration and the error-correction model
We have already seen that regressing one non-stationary series on another can produce entirely misleading results (spurious regression) and that modelling variables over time is generally wrong if the series are not stationary. There is at least one important exception.
We load the data in gdpusa.csv, which for the United States reports (at constant prices) GDP (pil), disposable income (redd), household consumption (cons), and the profits and dividends of some companies, for 88 quarters from 1970Q1 to 1991Q4. We estimate a simple linear consumption function with income as the explanatory variable
\[
C=\alpha +\beta R+u
\tag{6.23}
\]

RPythonSAS



gdp <- read.csv2("data/gdpusa.csv")
attach(gdp)
modc <- lm(cons~redd)
round(summary(modc)$coeff, 3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) -171.441     22.917  -7.481        0
redd           0.967      0.008 119.871        0





gdp = pd.read_csv("data/gdpusa.csv", sep=";", decimal=",")
modc = smf.ols("cons ~ redd", data=gdp).fit()
print(modc.summary().tables[1])

==============================================================================
                 coef    std err          t      P>|t|      [0.025      0.975]
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Intercept   -171.4412     22.917     -7.481      0.000    -216.999    -125.883
redd           0.9672      0.008    119.871      0.000       0.951       0.983
==============================================================================




proc import datafile="data/gdpusa.csv" out=gdp dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
proc reg data=gdp;
  modc: model cons = redd;
  output out=gdp_res r=uc;
run;
quit;



It is easy to check that both consumption and income are \(I(1)\), a first difference being enough to make them stationary. So the results of model modc are wrong, with one important exception: if the residual series turns out to be stationary.

RPythonSAS



uc <- residuals(modc)
u <- embed(uc,2)
du <- u[,1]-u[,2]
u1 <- u[,2]
modu <- lm(du~u1-1)
round(summary(modu)$coeff, 3)

   Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
u1   -0.275      0.073  -3.779        0





from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import coint

uc = modc.resid.to_numpy()
modu = sm.OLS(np.diff(uc), uc[:-1]).fit()
print(modu.params, modu.tvalues)

[-0.27531223] [-3.77907067]

# Engle-Granger test with the appropriate critical values
print(coint(gdp["cons"], gdp["redd"], maxlag=0, autolag=None))

CointResult(coint_t=-3.7790706719922773, pvalue=0.014451783159283802, critical_values=array([-4.02675342, -3.40726247, -3.09355879]))




/* with a regressor, the stationarity=(adf) option of PROC AUTOREG
   also reports the Engle-Granger cointegration test */
proc autoreg data=gdp;
  model cons = redd / stationarity=(adf=0);
run;



As in the direct stationarity test, where the empirical t value is compared not with Student’s t but with the Dickey-Fuller \(\tau\) distribution, for the residuals of a model with non-stationary series specific theoretical values are used, such as those tabulated by Engle and Granger (other distributions are also available); the test carried out under these conditions is known as a test of cointegration between consumption and income.
Base R cannot run these tests without loading external packages, but it suffices to know that in our example the empirical t value lies beyond the acceptance region of the non-stationarity hypothesis under the Engle-Granger distribution, so the residuals are stationary. Consequently, modc is not a spurious regression but a cointegrating regression, which identifies the long-run equilibrium relationship between consumption and income. Thus 0.967 is the long-run marginal propensity to consume.
If the cointegrating relationship represents a long-run equilibrium, there will be short-run disequilibrium, represented by departures from that relationship, that is, by the residual \(u=C-\alpha -\beta R\). Since consumption and income in our example are cointegrated, by the Granger representation theorem it can be shown that changes in consumption depend on changes in income up to the correction factor \(u\), hence the name “error-correction model” (ECM)
\[
\Delta C_{t}=\alpha_{0}+\alpha_{1}\Delta R_{t}+\alpha_{2}u_{t-1}+\varepsilon_{t} \quad \text{where} \quad \varepsilon \sim WN
\tag{6.24}
\]
For our example

RPythonSAS



cc <- embed(cons,2); dc <- cc[,1]-cc[,2]
rr <- embed(redd,2); dr <- rr[,1]-rr[,2]
modecm <- lm(dc~dr+u1); round(summary(modecm)$coeff, 3)

            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)   11.692      2.196   5.325    0.000
dr             0.291      0.070   4.172    0.000
u1            -0.087      0.054  -1.600    0.113

detach(gdp)




ecm = pd.DataFrame({"dc": gdp["cons"].diff(), "dr": gdp["redd"].diff(),
                    "u1": pd.Series(uc).shift(1)}).dropna()
modecm = smf.ols("dc ~ dr + u1", data=ecm).fit()
print(modecm.summary().tables[1])

==============================================================================
                 coef    std err          t      P>|t|      [0.025      0.975]
------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Intercept     11.6918      2.196      5.325      0.000       7.325      16.058
dr             0.2906      0.070      4.172      0.000       0.152       0.429
u1            -0.0867      0.054     -1.600      0.113      -0.194       0.021
==============================================================================




data gdp_ecm;
  set gdp_res;
  dc = dif(cons); dr = dif(redd); u1 = lag(uc);
run;
proc reg data=gdp_ecm;
  modecm: model dc = dr u1;
run;
quit;



Simplifying somewhat, we could say that the estimated correction coefficient is not statistically significant, suggesting an instantaneous adjustment of consumption to changes in income; in particular, the short-run marginal propensity to consume is 0.291.
Of course the problem is much more complex than presented here, and there are many theoretical considerations and practical and interpretive cautions that must be studied in specific advanced courses.

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.13 A SARIMA model for consumption
We load the data on consumption of non-durable goods (at constant prices) in the United Kingdom from the first quarter of 1955 to the fourth quarter of 1988, in the file consnd.csv. We look for an ARIMA model for these data, restricting the series to 1955-1970 so as to use the remaining years to assess forecasting performance ex post.
For the reasons already mentioned, the series has been log-transformed. Figure 6.14 shows the corresponding ACF and PACF.

RPythonSAS



consnd <- read.csv2("data/consnd.csv")$consnd
consumiuk <- ts(consnd, start=1955, frequency=4)
consumo <- window(log(consumiuk), end=c(1970,4))
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
acf(consumo, main="ACF consumption series")
pacf(consumo, main="PACF consumption series")




Figure 6.14 – ACF and PACF of the consumption series







cnd = pd.read_csv("data/consnd.csv", sep=";")
consumiuk = pd.Series(cnd["consnd"].to_numpy(dtype=float),
                      index=pd.period_range("1955Q1", periods=len(cnd), freq="Q"))
consumo = np.log(consumiuk[:"1970Q4"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
plot_acf(consumo, ax=ax[0], lags=16, title="ACF consumption series")
plot_pacf(consumo, ax=ax[1], lags=16, title="PACF consumption series")
plt.show()




Figure 6.14 – ACF and PACF of the consumption series






proc import datafile="data/consnd.csv" out=cnd dbms=dlm replace;
  delimiter=";"; getnames=yes;
run;
data cnd;
  set cnd;
  data = yyq(anno, trimestre); format data yyq6.;
  lc = log(consnd);
run;
proc arima data=cnd(where=(anno <= 1970)) plots=(series(acf pacf));
  identify var=lc nlag=16;
run;
quit;



The series shows seasonal peaks and does not appear stationary. We difference it; lag 1 is not enough, so we also difference at the seasonal lag (the data have a seasonal period of 4, matching the quarterly cycle): the result is much better (Figure 6.15).

RPythonSAS



par(mfrow=c(2,2))
acf(diff(consumo), main="ACF consumption lag 1")
pacf(diff(consumo), main="PACF consumption lag 1")
acf(diff(diff(consumo),4), main="ACF consumption lags 1 and 4")
pacf(diff(diff(consumo),4), main="PACF consumption lags 1 and 4")




Figure 6.15 – ACF and PACF of the differenced series







d1 = consumo.diff().dropna()
d14 = consumo.diff().diff(4).dropna()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(8, 7))
plot_acf(d1, ax=ax[0, 0], lags=16, title="ACF consumption lag 1")
plot_pacf(d1, ax=ax[0, 1], lags=16, title="PACF consumption lag 1")
plot_acf(d14, ax=ax[1, 0], lags=16, title="ACF consumption lags 1 and 4")
plot_pacf(d14, ax=ax[1, 1], lags=16, title="PACF consumption lags 1 and 4")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()




Figure 6.15 – ACF and PACF of the differenced series






proc arima data=cnd(where=(anno <= 1970)) plots=(series(acf pacf));
  identify var=lc(1) nlag=16;      /* difference at lag 1 */
  identify var=lc(1,4) nlag=16;    /* differences at lags 1 and 4 */
run;
quit;



The autocorrelation functions do not point to a clear model specification, but they certainly suggest the two differencing operations, at lag 1 for the non-seasonal part and at the seasonal lag for the seasonal part.
We try a few models, choosing the best in terms of the AIC criterion and with residuals as close as possible to white noise. For brevity we estimate only low-order models. The first model is an \(ARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1)_{4}\), the second an \(ARIMA(1,1,0)(1,1,0)_{4}\), the third an \(ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)_{4}\).

RPythonSAS



modtsa <- arima(consumo, order=c(1,1,1), seasonal=c(1,1,1))
modtsb <- arima(consumo, order=c(1,1,0), seasonal=c(1,1,0))
modtsc <- arima(consumo, order=c(0,1,1), seasonal=c(0,1,1))
modtsa$coef; modtsb$coef; modtsc$coef

       ar1        ma1       sar1       sma1 
 0.5218448 -0.8598077  0.4278748 -0.9996419 


       ar1       sar1 
-0.2749615 -0.3981325 


       ma1       sma1 
-0.3530235 -0.5827546 

modtsa$aic; modtsb$aic; modtsc$aic

[1] -368.7176


[1] -365.3164


[1] -370.2744





from statsmodels.tsa.statespace.sarimax import SARIMAX

ordini = {"a": ((1, 1, 1), (1, 1, 1, 4)), "b": ((1, 1, 0), (1, 1, 0, 4)), "c": ((0, 1, 1), (0, 1, 1, 4))}
modelli = {k: SARIMAX(consumo, order=o, seasonal_order=s).fit(disp=False) for k, (o, s) in ordini.items()}
for k, m in modelli.items():
    print(k, m.params.drop("sigma2").round(4).to_dict(), "AIC:", round(m.aic, 2))

a {'ar.L1': 0.5019, 'ma.L1': -0.8374, 'ar.S.L4': 0.4079, 'ma.S.L4': -0.9654} AIC: -368.68

  identify var=lc(1,4) noprint;
  estimate p=(1)(4) q=(1)(4) method=ml;   /* ARIMA(1,1,1)(1,1,1)4 */
  estimate p=(1)(4) method=ml;            /* ARIMA(1,1,0)(1,1,0)4 */
  estimate q=(1)(4) method=ml;            /* ARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)4 */
run;
quit;



Note that arima() does not include the period option, since the consumption series has already been defined as a seasonal time series with period 4; otherwise it must be specified.
The AIC criterion suggests the third model; note that both coefficients are negative and significant, while the correlograms of the residuals are shown in Figure 6.16.

RPythonSAS



modtsc


Call:
arima(x = consumo, order = c(0, 1, 1), seasonal = c(0, 1, 1))

Coefficients:
         ma1     sma1
      -0.353  -0.5828
s.e.   0.143   0.1382

sigma^2 estimated as 9.649e-05:  log likelihood = 188.14,  aic = -370.27

par(mfrow=c(1,2))

pacf(modtsc$resid, main="PACF of residuals")




Figure 6.16 – Residual diagnostics of the third SARIMA model







modtsc = modelli["c"]
print(modtsc.summary().tables[1])

==============================================================================

------------------------------------------------------------------------------
ma.L1         -0.3491      0.112     -3.116      0.002      -0.569      -0.130

res = modtsc.resid[5:]          # drop the first values, affected by initialisation
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))

proc arima data=cnd(where=(anno <= 1970)) plots=(residual(acf pacf));
  identify var=lc(1,4) noprint;
  estimate q=(1)(4) method=ml;
run;
quit;



The residuals appear to be white noise, supporting the choice of the third model, whose forecasting ability we now check for the years 1971-1988, left out of the analysis. In total the model must forecast \((1988-1970)\cdot 4 = 72\) observations: the full series has 136 and the part used for estimation 64.

RPythonSAS



(1988-1970)*4

[1] 72

previsione <- predict(modtsc, n.ahead=72)
length(consumiuk)

[1] 136

136-72

[1] 64

errp <- log(consumiuk)[65:136]-previsione$pred
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(log(consumiuk), main="Forecast")
lines(previsione$pred, type="o")
plot(errp, main="Observed - forecast")
abline(h=0)




Figure 6.17 – Observed and forecast values







previsione = modtsc.forecast(72)
osservato = np.log(consumiuk)
errp = osservato.iloc[64:].to_numpy() - previsione.to_numpy()
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))
ax[0].plot(osservato.to_timestamp(), color="black")
ax[0].plot(previsione.to_timestamp(), "o-", color="black", markersize=2)
ax[0].set_title("Forecast"); ax[0].tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45)
ax[1].plot(previsione.index.to_timestamp(), errp, color="black"); ax[1].axhline(0, color="black")
ax[1].tick_params(axis="x", labelrotation=45)
ax[1].set_title("Observed - forecast")
plt.show()




Figure 6.17 – Observed and forecast values






/* estimation over 1955-1970 and forecast of the next 72 quarters */
data cnd_stima; set cnd; if anno > 1970 then lc = .; run;
proc arima data=cnd_stima;
  identify var=lc(1,4) noprint;
  estimate q=(1)(4) method=ml noprint;
  forecast lead=72 id=data interval=qtr out=prev_cnd;
run;
quit;
data confronto;
  merge prev_cnd cnd(keep=data lc rename=(lc=osservato));
  by data;
  errp = osservato - FORECAST;
run;
proc sgplot data=confronto;
  title "Forecast";
  series x=data y=osservato;
  series x=data y=FORECAST / markers;
run;



Figure 6.17 shows the observed and forecast values (dotted line) and their difference; the result, though not optimal, is sufficient for our purposes: in any case, the fitted values do not stray far from the observed ones. It should be stressed, however, that with real series it is hard to find a parsimonious model that fits the data very well.

title: 6 Stochastic models for time-series analysis
text:
6.14 Airline passengers
Let us look at another example, the number of international airline passengers in the United States from January 1949 to December 1960; these well-known data are included in R’s standard packages (for Python and SAS we saved them in airpassengers.csv). We follow the classical approach to separate the seasonal from the non-seasonal component; we already know the commands needed.

RPythonSAS



dati <- AirPassengers
scomponi <- stl(dati, s.window="period")
scomponi$time.series[1:5,]

       seasonal    trend  remainder
[1,] -25.497718 127.1873 10.3103699
[2,] -35.220935 126.6495 26.5714028
[3,]  -3.027478 126.1117  8.9157625
[4,]  -8.299054 126.1989 11.1001224
[5,]  -5.737289 126.2861  0.4511408





from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import STL

air = pd.read_csv("data/airpassengers.csv")
dati = pd.Series(air["passeggeri"].to_numpy(dtype=float),
                 index=pd.period_range("1949-01", periods=len(air), freq="M"))
# note: statsmodels STL has no equivalent of R's "periodic" option; with a very wide
# seasonal window the result is similar but not identical
scomponi = STL(dati.to_timestamp(), period=12, seasonal=999).fit()
print(pd.DataFrame({"seasonal": scomponi.seasonal, "trend": scomponi.trend,
                    "remainder": scomponi.resid}).head())

             seasonal       trend  remainder
1949-01-01  -7.367864  119.595482  -0.227618
1949-02-01   2.521788  120.951594  -5.473382

proc import datafile="data/airpassengers.csv" out=air dbms=csv replace;
  getnames=yes;
run;
data air;
  set air;
  data = mdy(mese, 1, anno); format data monyy7.;
run;
/* decomposition into trend-cycle and seasonality */
proc timeseries data=air outdecomp=scomp_air;
  id data interval=month;
  var passeggeri;
  decomp tcc sc / mode=add;
run;



We can use this decomposition to obtain information on the order of the ARIMA models to fit to the seasonal and non-seasonal parts of the series and, consequently, to specify the corresponding SARIMA as well as possible (Figure 6.18).

RPythonSAS



stagione <- scomponi$time.series[,1]
tendenza <- scomponi$time.series[,2]
par(mfrow=c(2,2))
acf(tendenza, main="ACF of the trend")
pacf(tendenza, main="PACF of the trend")
acf(stagione, main="ACF of the season")

print(modpass.summary().tables[1])

res = modpass.resid[13:]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8, 4))

plot_pacf(res, ax=ax[1], lags=24, title="PACF of residuals")

proc arima data=air plots=(residual(acf pacf));
  identify var=passeggeri(1,12) noprint;
  estimate p=(1)(12,24) method=ml;   /* ARIMA(1,1,0)(2,1,0)12 */
  forecast lead=24 id=data interval=month out=prev_air;
run;
quit;



The model modpass performs well (Figure 6.19) and can be kept, although it is always advisable to estimate and compare several models. Finally, Figure 6.20 shows the observed values and those forecast by our SARIMA for 1961 and 1962.

RPythonSAS



prev <- predict(modpass, n.ahead=24)
serie <- append(dati, prev$pred)
serie <- ts(serie, start=1949, frequency=12)
plot(serie, main="Observed 1949-1960 and forecast 1961-1962")
abline(v=1961)




Figure 6.20 – Observed data up to 1960 and forecasts for 1961 and 1962







prev = modpass.forecast(24)
serie = pd.concat([dati, prev])
plt.figure(figsize=(5, 5))
plt.plot(serie.to_timestamp(), color="black")
plt.axvline(pd.Timestamp("1961-01-01"), color="black")
plt.title("Observed 1949-1960 and forecast 1961-1962", fontsize=10)
plt.show()




Figure 6.20 – Observed data up to 1960 and forecasts for 1961 and 1962






proc sgplot data=prev_air;
  title "Observed 1949-1960 and forecast 1961-1962";
  series x=data y=FORECAST;
  scatter x=data y=passeggeri / markerattrs=(size=4);
  refline '01jan1961'd / axis=x;
run;

title: 8 Production and productivity of economic systems
text:
The production function expresses a relationship between input and output: the former represents the factors used to produce (factors of production), the most important of which are labour \(L\) and capital \(K\); the latter the value of the goods and/or services produced (GDP or value added). The advent of technology and of new forms of production processes has in fact excluded other variables, such as land, from the econometric specification, and in other cases has included additional factors, such as the energy required by the process or the education and skills of the workforce. In any case, labour and capital are still the most relevant inputs and often the only ones considered in the statistical and econometric specification of the function, if only because of the difficulty of defining and measuring the other variables.
In a form such as
\[
Y=f(L,K)
\tag{8.1}
\]
output \(Y\) is usually measured by value added (VA), especially in a macroeconomic approach. For consistency of sources and proper comparability of the data, \(L\) is commonly measured by the number of full-time equivalent labour units (ULA), while \(K\) is measured by gross private fixed capital, given the difficulty of subtracting depreciation (the value of capital consumption) without excessive arbitrariness.
Value added and labour units raise fewer estimation problems, while capital is generally computed indirectly, not without complications, by applying the perpetual inventory method to investment: an estimate of the capital stock at some date in the past is obtained, and investment is added while retirements are subtracted and depreciation is taken into account (at least for the net valuation); but even the valuation of retirements is not simple, being represented by mathematical forms based on somewhat arbitrary assumptions.
The difficulty of estimating private capital is quite evident from the ISTAT time series (among them, those valued at replacement cost are preferable); for the country as a whole, time series cover fewer than 30 years, while territorially disaggregated estimates and estimates for the most recent years are missing.
The problems increase if, following a more complex formulation, one decides to add an estimate of public capital, usually denoted by \(G\) and corresponding in practice to public works. The working assumptions are even stronger in this case: is it right to assume that the value of an investment in a motorway lasts 80 years? How can a secondary road be distinguished from a main road? Should one not account for some wear (more in some places, less in others) of public works? And so on.
Function (8.1) does not satisfy part of the literature, which proposes adding an estimate of public capital \(G\) and an estimate of the capabilities, skills and, in general, abilities of the workforce through a suitable measure of human capital \(H\). The educational level of the employed can be a good proxy for \(H\), on the assumption that higher levels of education (especially technical and scientific training) are strongly correlated with the ability to perform a given job.
The production function might therefore become
\[
Y=f(L,K,G,H)
\tag{8.2}
\]
The statistical limits in defining and measuring some of the inputs that characterise mathematical forms such as (8.2) go together with non-negligible difficulties in the correct economic interpretation of the estimated coefficients. In short, weighing the pros and cons, it is advisable to use the simpler and more easily interpretable traditional forms, in particular the Cobb-Douglas production function which, moreover, with slight adjustments allows technological change to be taken into account, a rather complex operation in more elaborate mathematical forms. Hence, despite the many criticisms raised, the Cobb-Douglas is still widely applied, mainly because its estimates are easier to interpret.

The production function expresses a relationship between input and output: the former represents the factors used to produce (factors of production), the most important of which are labour \(L\) and capital \(K\); the latter the value of the goods and/or services produced (GDP or value added). section: 8.3 Elasticities, marginal productivities and Euler’s theorem
text:
8.3 Elasticities, marginal productivities and Euler’s theorem
Recalling that
\[
\partial Y/\partial L=a\alpha L^{\alpha -1}K^{1-\alpha}
\tag{8.7}
\]
and since the elasticity \(e\) is the ratio of two relative changes, which in the case of labour are \(\Delta Y/Y\) and \(\Delta L/L\), we have
\[
e=(\Delta Y/Y)/(\Delta L/L)
\tag{8.8}
\]
and, in continuous terms,
\[
e=(\partial Y/\partial L)/(Y/L)=a\alpha L^{\alpha -1}K^{1-\alpha}/a(K/L)^{1-\alpha}=\alpha
\tag{8.9}
\]
so the elasticity of \(Y\) with respect to \(L\) (i.e. \(e_{L}\)) is exactly \(\alpha\). Similarly, the elasticity of \(Y\) with respect to capital \(K\) (\(e_{K}\)) is \(\beta =1-\alpha\). Therefore, if \(L\) increases by \(k\%\), \(Y\) increases by \(k\alpha \%\), and if \(K\) increases by \(k\%\), \(Y\) increases by \(k(1-\alpha )\%\).
Hence, if
\[
e_{L}=(\partial Y/\partial L)/(Y/L)=\alpha \qquad \text{and} \qquad e_{K}=(\partial Y/\partial K)/(Y/K)=\beta
\tag{8.10}
\]
then also
\[
\partial Y/\partial L=\alpha (Y/L) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \partial Y/\partial K=\beta (Y/K)=(1-\alpha )(Y/K)
\tag{8.11}
\]
Consequently, the marginal productivity of labour is \(\alpha\)-proportional to the average productivity of labour, while the marginal productivity of capital is \(\beta\)-proportional to the average productivity of capital.
Indeed, with the data for Mexico we obtain approximately (in the restricted model the estimated coefficient is \(\beta\), hence \(\alpha =1-\beta\))

while by Euler’s theorem we can also write
\[
Y=(\partial Y/\partial L)L+(\partial Y/\partial K)K
\tag{8.12}
\]
since
\[
\begin{gathered}Y/Y=1=(\partial Y/\partial L)(L/Y)+(\partial Y/\partial K)(K/Y)= \\ \alpha (Y/L)(L/Y)+(1-\alpha )(Y/K)(K/Y)=\alpha +(1-\alpha )=1\end{gathered}
\tag{8.13}
\]
and, therefore, output \(Y\) is entirely attributed to the two factors of production \(L\) and \(K\) according to their productivities. It is easy to obtain the corresponding decomposition and to check that it adds back up to output \(Y\) with the data for Mexico

Note the unusual negative value for the labour factor.
Following marginalist theory under perfect competition, the productivity of a factor must equal its relative price
\[
\partial Y/\partial L=P_{L}=\alpha (Y/L) \qquad \text{and} \qquad \partial Y/\partial K=P_{K}=(1-\alpha )(Y/K)
\tag{8.14}
\]
It follows that
\[
\begin{gathered}Y=P_{L}L+P_{K}K=\alpha (Y/L)L+(1-\alpha )(Y/K)K= \\ \alpha Y+(1-\alpha )Y=Y\end{gathered}
\tag{8.15}
\]
that is, \(\alpha\) is also the share of \(Y\) attributable to labour and \((1-\alpha)\) the share attributable to capital.
If \(Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}\) with \(\log Y=\log a+\alpha \log L+\beta \log K\), defining \(\nabla Z=Z_{t}-Z_{t-1}\) for any variable \(Z\) at each time \(t\), it follows that
\[
\nabla \log Y=\alpha \nabla \log L+\beta \nabla \log K
\tag{8.16}
\]
Since \(\nabla \log\) is the growth rate, we conclude that the growth rate of output \(Y\) is approximately the weighted sum of the growth rates of the inputs labour \(L\) and capital \(K\). We obtain

round(diff(log(Y))-dL-dK,1)

  set mex;
  dY = dif(log(Y)); dL = dif(log(L))*(1-&beta); dK = dif(log(K))*β
  if _n_ > 1 then gap = round(dY - dL - dK, 0.1);
run;
proc print data=growth(firstobs=2) noobs; var anni gap; run;



The implicit assumptions, legitimate for adjacent periods, are the stability of the coefficients \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) and an unchanged technology, which become untenable over long periods.
Therefore, to account explicitly for the effect of technology, one can use Solow’s well-known formulation, in which technical progress is computed as a residual. We can write (the usual conditions of neoclassical theory hold, with \(\alpha +\beta =1\))
\[
Y=A(t)L^{\alpha}K^{\beta}
\tag{8.17}
\]
where \(A(t)\) represents the effect of technical progress.
Hence \(\log Y=\log A(t)+\alpha \log L+\beta \log K\) and, differencing over periods, \(\nabla \log Y=\nabla \log A(t)+\alpha \nabla \log L+\beta \nabla \log K\), which gives the Solow residual
\[
\nabla \log A(t)=\nabla \log Y-(\alpha \nabla \log L+\beta \nabla \log K)
\tag{8.18}
\]
It is also interesting to note that \(Y=A(t)L^{\alpha}K^{\beta}\) can be rewritten as
\[
A(t)=Y/L^{\alpha}K^{\beta}=TFP
\tag{8.19}
\]
In this formulation \(A(t)\) is not linked to the Solow residual but to a measure of total factor productivity (TFP), since it is the ratio of output \(Y\) to a combination of the two factors of production through a geometric mean with weights \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\). Thus an index of how TFP changes over time (or space) is simply a total productivity index, given by the ratio of two TFPs for different periods (or areas). In essence, this is a non-parametric method with strict assumptions: perfectly competitive markets, constant returns to scale, Hicks-neutral technical progress (i.e. technical progress changes the marginal productivity of the factors in the same proportion), and no adjustment costs (so firms always tend towards a long-run equilibrium).

8.5 Technical progress in the Cobb-Douglas
The functional specification of the Cobb-Douglas can be enriched by an additional variable expressing technical progress acting over time; in this way one could capture improvements in input quality over time, such as a progressively better-qualified workforce or machinery able to produce faster and with less waste. In this case we could write
\[
Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}e^{ut}
\tag{8.20}
\]
Clearly, if \(\alpha +\beta =1\) were imposed when it does not hold, the term \(e^{ut}\) would also absorb the effects of returns to scale.

data prod;
  set prod;
  logVA = log(VA00); logL = log(L); logK = log(K00);
  t = _n_;
run;
proc reg data=prod;
  progress: model logVA = logL logK t;
run;
quit;



Only capital appears significant, while the trend factor (which here represents the effect on output of technical progress as the mere passing of time) is not only non-significant but even has a slightly negative coefficient. Note that the intercept is also negative. We will not dwell on these anomalous results, since the discussion would move on to topics already covered in the previous chapters on the statistical analysis of linear models, the limits of functional-form specification and the problems of stationarity of the series.
Finally, note that in the Cobb-Douglas specification with technical progress, changes in labour quality can also be considered explicitly through a measure of hours worked. For example
\[
Y=aL^{\alpha}K^{\beta}h^{T}e^{ut}
\tag{8.21}
\]
where \(h\) is the average number of hours worked per employee.

title: 8 Production and productivity of economic systems
section: 8.6 More general forms: CES, VES and translog
text:
8.6 More general forms: CES, VES and translog
To conclude, it is worth mentioning production functions that are more general than the CD, but also less used in empirical analysis because they are harder to interpret and to estimate statistically. In particular, the Cobb-Douglas has a constant elasticity of substitution (between \(L\) and \(K\)) equal to one; this assumption is not always admissible. There are more complex forms that remove some of these constraints, for example functions with a constant elasticity of substitution not necessarily equal to one, the so-called CES functions. VES functions, similarly, generalise to the case of a non-constant elasticity of substitution; among these forms the best known is the translog
\[
\begin{gathered}\log Y=b_{0}+b_{1}\log L+b_{2}\log K+b_{3}(\log L)^{2}+ \\ b_{4}(\log K)^{2}+b_{5}(\log L\log K)\end{gathered}
\tag{8.22}
\]

title: 2 Aggregati economici e conti nazionali
text:
Il Sistema dei Conti Nazionali presenta in termini contabili le attività economiche e finanziarie che caratterizzano un intero Paese o porzioni di esso; in quest’ultimo caso si preferisce il termine di Conti Territoriali, anche se lo schema di riferimento è naturalmente quello della Contabilità Nazionale. I conti possono riferirsi all’anno o a frazioni di esso (usualmente il trimestre).
La Contabilità Nazionale viene definita nell’ambito delle regole europee del SEC2010 che, a partire da settembre 2014, sostituisce il precedente SEC95 in accordo con le linee guida internazionali stabilite nel Sistema dei conti nazionali delle Nazioni Unite.
Il SEC2010, dunque, stabilisce in modo sistematico e dettagliato come si definiscono e si misurano le grandezze che descrivono il funzionamento contabile di un Paese. Esso, in sostanza, è un sistema integrato dei conti economici, poiché fa ricorso a convenzioni contabili omogenee tra i Paesi europei con l’obiettivo di misurare contabilmente le operazioni economiche che avvengono all’interno delle nazioni.
La logica del SEC è quella della partita doppia, in cui ogni posta è registrata in uscita per l’operatore che la origina e in entrata per quello che la riceve. Pertanto, tutti i conti registrano operazioni in entrata e in uscita che si bilanciano per mezzo di un opportuno saldo contabile. Poiché sono costruiti a cascata, il saldo di un conto sarà riportato nel conto successivo. Essi registrano operazioni di produzione, di distribuzione e di redistribuzione degli attori coinvolti, fondamentalmente famiglie, imprese, pubbliche amministrazioni e resto del mondo.
Rispetto alla precedente versione del 1995 (in vigore dal 1999), il SEC2010 presenta alcune importanti differenze riguardo sia l’ambito di applicazione sia i concetti. In particolare: la capitalizzazione delle spese in ricerca e sviluppo; la riclassificazione da consumi intermedi a investimenti della spesa per armamenti sostenuta dalle amministrazioni pubbliche; una differente tecnica di stima degli scambi con l’estero di merci da sottoporre a lavorazione (si registra il valore del solo servizio di trasformazione); un aggiornamento e una verifica delle unità classificabili come amministrazioni pubbliche. In aggiunta, una serie di piccole modifiche tecniche sul calcolo di alcuni aggregati con limitate ricadute pratiche, e una un po’ più consistente legata all’inclusione di tutte le attività che producono reddito, incluse quelle illegali (principio già enunciato nel SEC95). Nello specifico, si introduce una stima del traffico di sostanze stupefacenti, della prostituzione e del contrabbando di sigarette o alcol. Infine, il SEC2010, rispetto al suo predecessore, ha accresciuto l’integrazione di differenti fonti informative e l’uso di dati amministrativi, con un generale miglioramento di tutte le stime e delle attività sommerse e irregolari. Naturalmente, l’applicazione del nuovo SEC2010 in chiave storica, cioè ai dati degli anni precedenti diffusi con il SEC95, ha determinato alcune revisioni delle informazioni in serie storica, con una generale rivalutazione di alcuni aggregati macroeconomici.
In una rappresentazione semplificata che mantiene una forte connessione con la versione precedente, possiamo presentare il SEC in base a una struttura su 6 conti principali, a loro volta divisi in 3 categorie, come di seguito elencato; tra parentesi è riportato il corrispondente saldo del conto.
A) Conti delle operazioni correnti

Conto della produzione (valore aggiunto)
Conto della distribuzione e utilizzazione del reddito

2.1 distribuzione primaria (risultato di gestione)
2.2 distribuzione secondaria (reddito disponibile)
2.3 redistribuzione in natura (reddito disponibile corretto)
2.4 utilizzazione del reddito (risparmio)


B) Conti dell’accumulazione

Formazione di capitale (accreditamento / indebitamento sull’estero)
Finanziario (accreditamento / indebitamento)
Variazioni delle attività e passività (variazione netta del patrimonio)

C) Conti patrimoniali

Patrimoniale (patrimonio netto)

6.1 patrimoniale di apertura
6.2 variazioni del patrimonio
6.3 patrimoniale di chiusura


Per i diversi conti, proseguiamo con le poste costituenti in una rappresentazione volutamente non dettagliata, omettendo anche le formali e puntuali definizioni degli aggregati, per le quali occorrerebbe un ulteriore approfondimento sui temi di contabilità nazionale che ci porterebbe fuori strada rispetto agli obiettivi del testo. D’altronde, gli studenti ai quali è indirizzato questo volume dovrebbero già avere nel proprio bagaglio di conoscenze un corso base di contabilità e statistica economica.


\[
Y + V = X + \mathit{Inn}
\tag{2.1}
\]

\(Y\) = PIL (prodotto interno lordo) ai prezzi di mercato
\(V\) = consumi intermedi
\(X\) = produzione totale (ai prezzi base)
\(\mathit{Inn}\) = imposte indirette nette (imposte sulla produzione e importazioni al netto dei contributi ai prodotti)

Questo conto confronta la produzione con l’ammontare dei costi necessari per ottenerla. La differenza tra produzione e costi intermedi (per branca) fornisce il valore aggiunto (pari alla remunerazione dei fattori produttivi capitale, lavoro e impresa). La somma del valore aggiunto per branca fornisce il PIL.
Ricordiamo che il PIL (o Prodotto Interno Lordo) è il valore di tutti i beni e servizi finali prodotti in un Paese in un determinato periodo di tempo, ma non può essere considerato una misura del benessere della società. Per dirla alla Robert Kennedy (1968): «… il PIL comprende l’inquinamento dell’aria, la pubblicità delle sigarette, […] programmi televisivi che valorizzano la violenza […]. Il PIL non tiene conto della salute delle nostre famiglie, della qualità della loro educazione e della gioia dei loro momenti di svago […]. Non misura né la nostra arguzia né il nostro coraggio né la nostra saggezza né la nostra conoscenza né la nostra compassione. Misura tutto, eccetto ciò che rende la vita degna di essere vissuta…». Ciò nonostante, il PIL è considerato ancora oggi il migliore indicatore statistico della produzione e dello sviluppo di una nazione.



\[
Y + \mathit{Cp} = \mathit{RLD} + \mathit{Ipi} + \mathit{RLG}
\tag{2.2}
\]

\(Y\) = PIL (Prodotto Interno Lordo) ai prezzi di mercato
\(\mathit{Cp}\) = contributi alla produzione
\(\mathit{RLD}\) = redditi interni da lavoro dipendente
\(\mathit{Ipi}\) = imposte sulla produzione e importazioni
\(\mathit{RLG}\) = risultato lordo di gestione

Questo conto registra la distribuzione funzionale (primaria) del reddito, cioè mostra come il valore aggiunto viene ripartito tra i fattori di produzione (lavoro, capitale, impresa) sotto forma di salari e stipendi, interessi, rendite e dividendi, profitti. Se dal PIL si sottraggono i redditi da lavoro dipendente, si ottiene quale saldo la remunerazione degli altri fattori, cioè il risultato lordo di gestione.
Va notato che alcuni aggregati possono essere, e talvolta vengono, rappresentati anche al netto di certi contributi e/o imposte, sottraendo o aggiungendo le poste corrispondenti tra le risorse e gli impieghi dei diversi conti. Per esempio, la “sequenza dei conti” pubblicata dall’ISTAT predilige la scomposizione delle poste lorde in modo da evidenziare, ove possibile, il contributo netto degli aggregati al conto.



\[
\mathit{RLD} + \mathit{RLG} + \mathit{Ipi} + \mathit{RLG}_{dn} + \mathit{RLG}_{drm} = Y_{nl} + \mathit{RLG}_{aN} + \mathit{RLG}_{arm} + \mathit{Cp}
\tag{2.3}
\]

\(Y_{nl}\) = reddito nazionale lordo
\(\mathit{Ipi}\) = imposte indirette
\(\mathit{RLG}_{drm}\) = redditi da capitale e impresa dal resto del mondo
\(\mathit{RLG}_{arm}\) = redditi da capitale e impresa al resto del mondo
\(\mathit{RLG}_{dn}\) = redditi da capitale da altri settori nazionali
\(\mathit{RLG}_{aN}\) = redditi da capitale ad altri settori nazionali

Questo conto presenta l’acquisizione del reddito dei soggetti proprietari dei fattori di produzione. È un conto che interessa gli operatori residenti, indipendentemente da dove hanno prestato la loro opera. Il saldo è il reddito nazionale lordo.



\[
Y_{nld} + T_{drm} + T_{dn} = Y_{nl} + I_{red} + \mathit{Cs} + T_{an} + T_{arm}
\tag{2.4}
\]

\(Y_{nl}\) = reddito nazionale lordo
\(Y_{nld}\) = reddito nazionale lordo disponibile
\(I_{red}\) = imposte sul reddito e sul patrimonio
\(\mathit{Cs}\) = contributi sociali
\(T_{drm}\) = trasferimenti correnti dal resto del mondo
\(T_{arm}\) = trasferimenti correnti al resto del mondo
\(T_{dn}\) = altri trasferimenti correnti da settori nazionali
\(T_{an}\) = altri trasferimenti correnti a settori nazionali

Questo conto descrive la formazione del reddito disponibile per via dei trasferimenti correnti. Il saldo è il reddito disponibile per consumo o risparmio.



\[
Y_{nldc} = Y_{nld} + \mathit{Trnat}_{netti}
\tag{2.5}
\]

\(Y_{nldc}\) = reddito nazionale lordo disponibile corretto
\(Y_{nld}\) = reddito nazionale lordo disponibile
\(\mathit{Trnat}_{netti}\) = saldo dei trasferimenti sociali in natura

I trasferimenti in natura sono oneri sostenuti dalla Pubblica Amministrazione per offrire alla collettività beni e servizi individuali acquistati da terzi o prodotti direttamente.



\[
Y_{nld} + \mathit{Rett} = C + S
\tag{2.6}
\]

\(Y_{nld}\) = reddito nazionale lordo disponibile corretto
\(S\) = risparmio nazionale lordo
\(C\) = consumi finali nazionali effettivi
\(\mathit{Rett}\) = rettifica per variazione dei diritti netti delle famiglie sui fondi pensione

Il saldo è il risparmio nazionale; entra nel conto della formazione del capitale.



\[
S + T_{ke} = I_f + I_s + O_v + T_{ku} + A_n + B
\tag{2.7}
\]

\(T_{ke}\) = trasferimenti in conto capitale dal resto del mondo
\(T_{ku}\) = trasferimenti in conto capitale al resto del mondo
\(A_n\) = acquisti netti di terreni o di beni immateriali
\(B\) = accreditamento (+) / indebitamento (−) del Paese con il resto del mondo
\(S\) = risparmio nazionale lordo
\(I_f\) = investimenti fissi lordi
\(I_s\) = variazione delle scorte
\(O_v\) = variazione degli oggetti di valore

Il saldo del conto misura la capacità del Paese di finanziare gli investimenti con il risparmio. Un saldo positivo indica un risparmio superiore agli investimenti; questo valore positivo si riversa all’estero sotto forma di impieghi nel resto del mondo. Viceversa, un saldo negativo indica una necessità di finanziamento degli investimenti con debiti contratti all’estero.



\[
\mathit{Ofa} + B = \mathit{Ofp}
\tag{2.8}
\]

\(\mathit{Ofa}\) = operazioni finanziarie attive
\(\mathit{Ofp}\) = operazioni finanziarie passive

Questo conto, redatto dalla Banca d’Italia, registra le modificazioni delle attività e passività finanziarie. Dobbiamo notare che generalmente il saldo (\(B\)) delle attività finanziarie non coincide con quello presente nel conto della formazione del capitale, in ragione delle diverse fonti statistiche utilizzate; spesso, per risolvere questa incongruenza, si aggiunge una posta di rettifica “errori ed omissioni”.



Il conto registrerebbe variazioni di volume legate a scoperta o esaurimento di miniere, bonifica di terreni, rinvenimento di reperti archeologici, registrazione di nuovi brevetti o scadenza di altri, ecc., ma anche le variazioni di valore causate da variazioni di prezzo. Limiti statistici non consentono ancora una redazione completa del conto.



Come nel caso precedente, anche il conto patrimoniale (con i suoi 3 sottoconti) viene pubblicato solo parzialmente, in ragione di irrisolte difficoltà statistiche.
Esisterebbero anche una serie di conti con il resto del mondo, in base ai quali vengono analizzate specificamente le operazioni in essere tra la nazione e il resto del mondo. Spesso le operazioni vengono sintetizzate in un unico conto detto per l’appunto “resto del mondo” o delle “transazioni internazionali”; il saldo è l’accreditamento o indebitamento della nazione, fermo restando le solite differenze dovute a effetti di bilanciamento e alle diverse fonti statistiche utilizzate, saldo che consente il bilanciamento delle due sezioni, sostanzialmente sintetizzabili in “entrate dell’Italia” e “uscite dell’Italia”.
